f: 1072. What is the ruling when a person makes an exception immediately connected to his admission?
b: The exception is valid, and only the remaining amount becomes binding.

f: 1073. Why is a directly connected exception accepted in an admission?
b: Because the admission together with the exception expresses the remaining amount intended.

f: 1074. What condition must exist for an exception in an admission to be valid?
b: The exception must be directly connected to the admission without separation.

f: 1075. Does the size of the excluded amount affect whether an exception in an admission is valid?
b: No, it does not matter whether the excluded amount is small or large.

f: 1076. If a person admits owing one hundred dirhams and immediately excludes ten, is the exception valid?
b: Yes, the exception is valid and ninety remains binding.

f: 1077. If a person admits owing one hundred dirhams and immediately excludes ninety, is the exception valid?
b: Yes, the exception is valid and ten remains binding.

f: 1078. If a person excludes the entire amount he admitted owing, is the exception valid?
b: No, the exception is invalid and the entire admission remains binding.

f: 1079. Why is excluding the entire admitted amount invalid?
b: Because nothing remains after the exception, so it becomes a retraction from the admission rather than a true exception.

f: 1080. What does a complete exception from an admission legally resemble?
b: It resembles a withdrawal or retraction from the admission.

f: 1081. Why must an exception leave some amount remaining in order to be valid?
b: Because an exception explains what is excluded from an existing admission, and if everything is removed, there is no admission left.

f: 1082. If a person admits, “I owe him one hundred dirhams except a dinar,” what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: He owes one hundred dirhams minus the value of the dinar.

f: 1083. If a person admits, “I owe him one hundred dirhams except a measure (qafīz) of wheat,” what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: He owes one hundred dirhams minus the value of the wheat measure.

f: 1084. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why is an exception of a dinar from one hundred dirhams valid?
b: Because both the dinar and dirhams are used as prices and can be valued against each other.

f: 1085. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why is an exception of wheat from one hundred dirhams valid?
b: Because measured and weighed goods can also function as prices and can be valued in dirhams.

f: 1086. If a person admits, “I owe him one hundred dirhams except a garment,” what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: The exception is invalid.

f: 1087. According to Muḥammad, is an exception of a dinar, wheat, or garment from one hundred dirhams valid?
b: No, Muḥammad considers the exception invalid in all these cases.

f: 1088. According to al-Shāfiʿī, is an exception of a dinar, wheat, or garment from one hundred dirhams valid?
b: Yes, al-Shāfiʿī considers the exception valid in all these cases.

f: 1089. Why does Muḥammad say an exception from one hundred dirhams using a dinar, wheat, or garment is invalid?
b: Because an exception only applies to something that would have originally been included in the wording, and these items are not included in the term “dirhams.”

f: 1090. According to Muḥammad, why cannot a dinar be excluded from an admission of dirhams?
b: Because a dinar is a different type of wealth and is not included in the word “dirhams.”

f: 1091. According to Muḥammad, why cannot wheat be excluded from an admission of dirhams?
b: Because wheat is not included in the wording “dirhams” and belongs to a different category.

f: 1092. According to Muḥammad, why cannot a garment be excluded from an admission of dirhams?
b: Because a garment is not included in the meaning of “dirhams.”

f: 1093. What is al-Shāfiʿī’s reasoning for allowing exceptions of dinars, wheat, or garments from dirhams?
b: He considers them all part of the same category because they are all forms of wealth.

f: 1094. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why is the exception of a dinar from dirhams different from the exception of a garment?
b: Because a dinar is naturally used as a price, while a garment is not originally a price.

f: 1095. Why can a dinar be excluded from dirhams according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Because both currencies function as prices and can be measured against each other in value.

f: 1096. Why can wheat be excluded from dirhams according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Because measured and weighed goods can serve as prices and have a known value in dirhams.

f: 1097. Why cannot a garment be excluded from dirhams according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Because a garment is not normally a price, so its value in dirhams is not automatically understood.

f: 1098. What happens if the excluded item from dirhams is something whose value cannot be determined clearly?
b: The exception becomes unknown and therefore invalid.

f: 1099. Why is an unknown exception invalid in an admission?
b: Because the remaining obligation cannot be determined.

f: 1100. If a person admits owing a right and immediately says, “If Allah wills,” does the admission become binding?
b: No, the admission does not become binding.

f: 1101. Why does saying “If Allah wills” after an admission prevent it from becoming binding?
b: Because it either cancels the admission or makes it conditional.

f: 1102. How can saying “If Allah wills” function as a cancellation of an admission?
b: It removes the effect of the admission entirely.

f: 1103. How can saying “If Allah wills” function as making an admission conditional?
b: It suspends the admission upon something whose occurrence is unknown.

f: 1104. Why does an admission not accept being suspended upon a condition?
b: Because an admission is a binding acknowledgment and cannot depend on an uncertain future event.

f: 1105. Why is a condition such as “if Allah wills” problematic in an admission?
b: Because whether the condition occurs cannot be known, similar to the issue discussed in divorce.

f: 1106. If a person acknowledges a debt and says “if Allah wills” immediately after the acknowledgement, does the debt become binding?
b: No, the acknowledgement does not become binding.

f: 1107. Why does adding “if Allah wills” to an acknowledgement prevent it from becoming binding?
b: Because it either cancels the acknowledgement or makes it conditional upon something uncertain.

f: 1108. What are the two possible meanings of saying “if Allah wills” after an acknowledgement?
b: It can mean cancellation or making the acknowledgement conditional.

f: 1109. Why is an acknowledgement cancelled if “if Allah wills” is understood as cancellation?
b: Because the acknowledgement itself is removed and no obligation remains.

f: 1110. Why is an acknowledgement invalid if “if Allah wills” is understood as a condition?
b: Because an acknowledgement cannot be suspended upon a condition, or because the occurrence of the condition cannot be known.

f: 1111. Why is saying “if Allah wills” after an acknowledgement compared to issues in divorce?
b: Because in both cases the condition depends on something whose occurrence cannot be determined.

f: 1112. If a person says, “So-and-so has one hundred dirhams due from me if I die,” is this treated as a true condition?
b: No, it is treated as a postponement of the debt.

f: 1113. If a person says, “So-and-so has one hundred dirhams due from me when the month begins,” is this a true condition?
b: No, it is treated as a time limitation and deferment.

f: 1114. If a person says, “So-and-so has one hundred dirhams due from me when people break their fast,” is this a true condition?
b: No, it is treated as a time limitation and deferment.

f: 1115. Why are phrases such as “if I die” or “when the month begins” treated differently from “if Allah wills”?
b: Because they specify a time period for payment rather than making the obligation dependent on an uncertain condition.

f: 1116. If a claimant denies the deferment of a debt that was acknowledged as payable after a certain time, what happens?
b: The debt becomes immediately due.

f: 1117. If a person acknowledges owning a house but excludes the building for himself, who receives the house and building?
b: The person to whom the acknowledgement was made receives both the house and the building.

f: 1118. Why does excluding the building from an acknowledgement of a house not work?
b: Because the building is included in the meaning of the acknowledgement, even though it was not explicitly mentioned.

f: 1119. Why is an implied part of a property included in an acknowledgement despite not being mentioned in the wording?
b: Because the exception only applies to things explicitly included in the wording.

f: 1120. Does an exception apply to the building of a house when someone acknowledges ownership of the house?
b: No, because the building is included implicitly rather than explicitly.

f: 1121. Does an exception apply to the stone of a ring when someone acknowledges ownership of a ring?
b: No, because the stone is considered part of the ring by implication.

f: 1122. Does an exception apply to the palm trees when someone acknowledges ownership of an orchard?
b: No, because the trees are included as subordinate parts of the orchard.

f: 1123. Why is excluding one-third of a house different from excluding the building of a house?
b: Because one-third is explicitly included in the wording of the acknowledgement, while the building is only included by implication.

f: 1124. Why is excluding one room from a house different from excluding the building itself?
b: Because a room is part of the wording’s meaning of division, while the building is a subordinate attached element.

f: 1125. If a person says, “The building of this house belongs to me and the empty land belongs to so-and-so,” who owns the empty land?
b: The person named as owner of the empty land owns it.

f: 1126. What does the term ʿarṣah (عرصة) refer to?
b: The bare plot of land itself, excluding the building.

f: 1127. Why does ʿarṣah exclude the building?
b: Because it refers specifically to the open land or courtyard area.

f: 1128. If a person acknowledges ownership of arḍ (land), does the acknowledgement include the building upon it?
b: Yes, the building is included.

f: 1129. Why does acknowledging ownership of land include the building upon it?
b: Because land in common usage includes what is attached to it.

f: 1130. How does acknowledgement of land differ from acknowledgement of ʿarṣah?
b: Land includes the building, while ʿarṣah refers only to the bare land.

f: 1131. If a person acknowledges owing one thousand dirhams as the price of a slave he bought but never received, what must happen if the slave is specified?
b: The claimant may either deliver the slave and take the one thousand dirhams, or he receives nothing.

f: 1132. In the case where someone acknowledges owing the price of a slave but never took possession of the slave, what choice does the claimant have?
b: He may deliver the slave and receive the price, or leave the matter and receive nothing.

f: 1133. Why is the claimant required to deliver the slave before receiving the price?
b: Because the acknowledgement connects the payment to the exchange of the slave.

f: 1134. In the case of an acknowledged sale where both parties confirm the transaction and the claimant delivers the slave, what is the ruling?
b: The claimant receives the one thousand dirhams.

f: 1135. Why is a mutually acknowledged transaction treated like something directly witnessed?
b: Because both parties’ agreement establishes the matter with certainty.

f: 1136. If a person acknowledges owing one thousand dirhams as the price of a specific slave, and the claimant later says, “The slave is yours; you did not sell this slave to me, but another slave,” does the debt remain binding?
b: Yes, the one thousand dirhams remain binding upon the person who made the acknowledgement.

f: 1137. Why does the one thousand dirhams remain binding when the claimant says a different slave was sold?
b: Because the slave has remained safely retained by the person who made the acknowledgement, and once the purpose of the transaction is achieved, disagreement over the cause does not affect the obligation.

f: 1138. If a person acknowledges owing money as the price of a specific slave, but the slave himself says, “I belong to the seller and was not sold to him,” what is the ruling?
b: Nothing is owed by the person who made the acknowledgement.

f: 1139. Why is no money owed when the slave himself denies that he was sold?
b: Because the acknowledged payment was only compensation for that specific slave, and the price is not binding without the slave.

f: 1140. If a slave denies being sold and the buyer claims, “Rather, I bought another slave,” what legal process occurs?
b: The parties enter into mutual oaths (taḥāluf).

f: 1141. Why do mutual oaths occur when the slave denies the sale and another slave is claimed?
b: Because the parties have conflicting claims: one claims delivery of the specific slave and the other denies it, while the buyer claims another sale and the other denies that claim.

f: 1142. In the case of mutual oaths over a disputed slave sale, what does the acknowledging party claim?
b: He claims that he delivered the specific slave mentioned in the acknowledgement.

f: 1143. In the case of mutual oaths over a disputed slave sale, what does the other party deny?
b: He denies that he received the specific slave.

f: 1144. In the case of mutual oaths over a disputed slave sale, what does the claimant claim regarding the one thousand dirhams?
b: He claims that the thousand dirhams are owed from another slave sale.

f: 1145. After mutual oaths in the case of a disputed specific slave sale, what happens to the obligation of the money?
b: The obligation of the money is cancelled.

f: 1146. Does the ruling of mutual oaths apply when the slave in the acknowledgement was not specified?
b: No, the ruling applies only when a specific slave was mentioned.

f: 1147. If a person says, “I owe him one thousand dirhams from the price of a slave whom I bought from him,” without specifying which slave, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The one thousand dirhams become binding.

f: 1148. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, is a person believed if he says, “I did not take possession of the slave,” after acknowledging the price of an unspecified slave?
b: No, he is not believed.

f: 1149. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does it matter whether the denial of possession is connected immediately to the acknowledgement or stated later?
b: No, it is rejected in both cases.

f: 1150. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject the statement “I did not take possession” after acknowledging the price of an unspecified slave?
b: Because it is considered a retraction from his acknowledgement.

f: 1151. Why is denying possession considered a retraction according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because the acknowledgement established a debt, while denying possession removes the basis for that debt.

f: 1152. Why does possession matter in determining whether the price of a slave becomes due?
b: Because a sale price becomes binding after the exchanged item is received.

f: 1153. In an unspecified slave sale, why would lack of possession prevent the price from becoming due?
b: Because the slave was not identified and possession never occurred, so the purchased item may be unknown or unavailable.

f: 1154. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consider a denial of possession after acknowledgement invalid even if it is immediately connected?
b: Because once an acknowledgement creates an obligation, a connected denial that removes it is treated as a retraction.

f: 1155. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, if a person immediately says “I did not take possession” after acknowledging the price of an unspecified slave, is he believed?
b: Yes, he is believed if the statement is connected.

f: 1156. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, if a person says “I did not take possession” separately after acknowledging the price of an unspecified slave, is he believed?
b: No, he is not believed unless the claimant denies that the money was the price of a slave.

f: 1157. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad accept a connected denial of possession?
b: Because the person acknowledged the debt and then explained its cause, and a connected explanation is accepted.

f: 1158. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, why does denial of possession prevent the debt from being established?
b: Because the obligation depends on the sale and possession, and the person denies that possession occurred.

f: 1159. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, why is a separated denial of possession normally rejected?
b: Because a modifying explanation is only accepted when it remains connected to the original acknowledgement.

f: 1160. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, when can a separated explanation after an acknowledgement be accepted?
b: When the claimant denies that the acknowledged amount was the price of a slave.

f: 1161. What is the difference between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله/Muḥammad regarding denial of possession after acknowledging a slave’s price?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله considers it a forbidden retraction, while Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad accept it as a valid explanation if connected.

f: 1162. If a person says, “I bought from him in a sale, but I did not take possession,” is his statement accepted?
b: Yes, his statement is accepted according to all scholars.

f: 1163. Why is a person believed when he says he bought something but did not take possession?
b: Because possession is not a necessary condition for the existence of a sale.

f: 1164. Why is denying possession different when acknowledging a sale price is owed?
b: Because the obligation of the price depends upon completion of the sale, which requires establishing the relevant conditions.

f: 1165. If a person says, “So-and-so has one thousand dirhams owed to me from the price of wine or pork,” what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The one thousand dirhams remain binding, and his explanation is not accepted.

f: 1166. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does it matter whether the explanation “from the price of wine or pork” is connected or separated from the acknowledgement?
b: No, it is rejected in both cases.

f: 1167. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject the explanation that the debt came from the price of wine or pork?
b: Because it is considered a retraction from an obligation already established by his acknowledgement.

f: 1168. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, why is saying “from the price of wine or pork” a retraction?
b: Because the first part establishes a debt, while the explanation attempts to remove that debt by attributing it to something not legally owed.

f: 1169. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, if someone says “from the price of wine or pork” immediately after acknowledging the debt, is anything owed?
b: No, nothing is owed if the explanation is connected.

f: 1170. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad accept the connected explanation regarding wine or pork?
b: Because the final words explain that the speaker did not intend a legally binding obligation.

f: 1171. How do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad compare a connected explanation of wine or pork to saying “if Allah wills”?
b: They treat it as a clarification of the intended meaning rather than a separate invalid statement.

f: 1172. What is the author’s response distinguishing “from the price of wine or pork” from “if Allah wills”?
b: Saying “if Allah wills” suspends the acknowledgement, while mentioning wine or pork cancels the acknowledgement.

f: 1173. If a person says, “I owe him one thousand from the price of merchandise,” then explains that the payment was in counterfeit or defective dirhams, and the claimant says they were good dirhams, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The good dirhams become binding.

f: 1174. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, if a person explains that the dirhams were counterfeit or defective immediately after the acknowledgement, is he believed?
b: Yes, he is believed if the explanation is connected.

f: 1175. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, if a person explains that the dirhams were counterfeit or defective after a delay, is he believed?
b: No, he is not believed if the explanation is separated.

f: 1176. What other types of defective currency have the same ruling as counterfeit dirhams?
b: Stūqah (mixed/defective coins), lead coins, and other specified inferior currencies.

f: 1177. If a person says, “I owe him one thousand counterfeit dirhams from the price of merchandise,” what disagreement applies?
b: The same disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله/Muḥammad applies.

f: 1178. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad accept a connected explanation about defective currency?
b: Because it is considered a modifying explanation of the original acknowledgement, and connected modifications are accepted.

f: 1179. What examples are given for connected modifying explanations accepted by Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Exceptions and conditions.

f: 1180. Why can the word “dirham” technically include inferior coins according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Because the word can linguistically apply to currency generally, including defective forms.

f: 1181. How can stūqah be included under the term dirham according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Through figurative usage.

f: 1182. Why does specifying defective currency change the apparent meaning of the word “dirham”?
b: Because when used without qualification, dirham normally refers to good-quality currency.

f: 1183. What is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله main reasoning for rejecting the explanation about defective currency?
b: He considers it a retraction from the original acknowledgement.

f: 1184. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consider defective currency a retraction?
b: Because an unrestricted obligation normally requires sound currency, and claiming defects removes part of what was originally acknowledged.

f: 1185. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله compare defective currency to a defective item in a sale?
b: He compares it to a seller claiming he sold a defective item while the buyer claims it was sound; the buyer’s statement is accepted.

f: 1186. Why is a sale normally understood to involve sound currency according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because unrestricted contracts are understood according to their normal and complete form, free from defects.

f: 1187. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله say stūqah is even weaker than defective dirhams?
b: Because stūqah is not even considered a valid category of currency, while a sale is concluded using a valid price.

f: 1188. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consider stūqah a retraction rather than a clarification?
b: Because it removes the basis of the acknowledged obligation rather than merely explaining it.

f: 1189. If a person acknowledges owing a debt and says, “Except that it weighs five,” is this exception valid?
b: Yes, the exception is valid.

f: 1190. Why is the exception “except that it weighs five” valid?
b: Because it relates to quantity, not quality or description.

f: 1191. Why is an exception concerning quantity treated differently from an exception concerning description?
b: Because quantity is included in the wording of the obligation, while a description is not.

f: 1192. Why is excluding a description from an acknowledgement invalid according to the text?
b: Because a description is not included in the original wording, just as excluding the building from a house is not valid.

f: 1193. If a person says, “I owe him a kurr of wheat from the price of a slave, except that it is poor quality,” is the exception valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Yes, the exception is valid.

f: 1194. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consider “poor quality wheat” a valid exception?
b: Because poor quality is a type or category of wheat, not merely a defect.

f: 1195. Why does a normal sale not require a specific quality of goods unless stated?
b: Because the unrestricted contract does not automatically require a particular quality.

f: 1196. What is another narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding defective currency in loans?
b: He accepts the borrower’s statement that the currency was inferior if he says it immediately after the acknowledgement.

f: 1197. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله accept the statement about inferior currency in a loan when connected?
b: Because a loan requires repayment of the equivalent of what was received, and the received currency itself may have been inferior.

f: 1198. What analogy is used for accepting inferior currency in a loan?
b: The analogy of usurpation (ghaṣb), where the person returns the equivalent of what was taken.

f: 1199. What is the apparent reasoning that unrestricted currency terms refer to good-quality currency?
b: Because people normally conduct transactions using good-quality currency.

f: 1200. If a person says, “So-and-so has one thousand counterfeit dirhams owed to me,” without mentioning a sale or loan, what is one view regarding his statement?
b: He is believed by consensus because the term “dirhams” can include counterfeit dirhams.

f: 1201. Why do some scholars say a person is believed when he acknowledges counterfeit dirhams without mentioning a contract?
b: Because the word “dirhams” includes counterfeit forms linguistically.

f: 1202. What is the other view regarding an acknowledgement of one thousand counterfeit dirhams without mentioning a sale or loan?
b: He is not believed.

f: 1203. Why do some scholars reject the explanation of counterfeit dirhams in an unrestricted acknowledgement?
b: Because unrestricted acknowledgements are understood according to lawful causes of obligation, not unlawful consumption.

f: 1204. If a person says, “I forcibly took one thousand dirhams from him,” and later says they were counterfeit or inferior, is he believed?
b: Yes, he is believed whether he says it connected or separately.

f: 1205. If a person says, “He entrusted me with one thousand dirhams,” and later says they were counterfeit or inferior, is he believed?
b: Yes, he is believed whether he says it connected or separately.

f: 1206. Why is a person believed when specifying defective currency in theft or trust cases?
b: Because there is no assumption that the money must have been good-quality currency.

f: 1207. Why is there no established custom requiring good-quality currency in theft or trust cases?
b: Because a person takes whatever he finds by force and entrusts whatever property he owns.

f: 1208. Why is specifying defective currency in theft or trust considered merely an explanation?
b: Because it explains the object already acknowledged rather than removing an established obligation.

f: 1209. If stolen property or entrusted property is later found to be defective, whose statement is accepted?
b: The statement of the person holding the property is accepted.

f: 1210. What is narrated from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding a separated explanation of defective currency in theft or trust?
b: He says the person is not believed if the explanation is separated.

f: 1211. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله reject a separated explanation in theft or trust?
b: Because possession creates liability in both theft and loans, so he compares them.

f: 1212. If a person acknowledges theft or a trust of “one thousand dirhams” and then says they were stūqah coins or lead coins, when is he believed?
b: He is believed if he says it connected, but not if he says it separately.

f: 1213. Why is a connected explanation about stūqah or lead coins accepted but a separated one rejected?
b: Because stūqah is not actually from the category of dirhams, so it is a modifying explanation that requires connection.

f: 1214. How is stūqah treated in relation to the term “dirham”?
b: It may be called a dirham metaphorically, but not literally.

f: 1215. If a person acknowledges owing “one thousand” and says, “except that it is short by such-and-such amount,” is he believed?
b: Only if he says the exception immediately connected to the acknowledgement.

f: 1216. Why must a quantity exception such as “short by such-and-such amount” be connected?
b: Because exceptions are only valid when connected to the original statement.

f: 1217. Why is a quantity exception different from an exception about inferior currency?
b: Because quantity is part of what the wording includes, while descriptions are not.

f: 1218. Why is “one thousand except that it is short by such-and-such amount” considered a valid type of adjustment?
b: Because it changes the amount, not the description of the thing owed.

f: 1219. If a person pauses briefly to breathe between an acknowledgement and an exception, is the exception still considered connected?
b: Yes, it is still considered connected.

f: 1220. Why is a pause for breathing considered a connected statement?
b: Because avoiding such an interruption is impossible, so it does not break continuity.

f: 1221. If a person acknowledges that he unlawfully took a garment and later brings a defective garment, is his statement accepted?
b: Yes, his statement is accepted.

f: 1222. Why is a person accepted when he brings a defective garment after acknowledging unlawful taking?
b: Because unlawful taking (ghaṣb) is not restricted to sound or perfect items.

f: 1223. If a person says, “I took one thousand dirhams from you as a trust and it was destroyed,” and the owner says, “No, you took it as a loan,” what is the ruling?
b: He is liable for the money.

f: 1224. Why is a person liable when he claims a trust but the owner claims it was a loan?
b: Because he acknowledged taking possession, which creates the basis of liability, then claimed a circumstance removing liability.

f: 1225. In the dispute over whether money was a trust or a loan, what does the person claiming liability deny?
b: He denies the claimed trust arrangement and asserts that it was a loan.

f: 1226. In the dispute between trust and loan, whose statement is accepted according to the text?
b: The statement of the person denying the removal of liability is accepted with an oath.

f: 1227. If a person says, “You gave me one thousand dirhams as a trust,” and the other says, “No, you stole it from me,” what is the ruling?
b: The person denying liability is accepted with an oath, and he is not liable.

f: 1228. Why is a person not liable when he claims he was given something as a trust and the other claims theft?
b: Because he attributes the action to the other person, while the other person is trying to establish a cause of liability against him.

f: 1229. What is the difference between saying “I took it as a trust” and saying “You gave it to me as a trust”?
b: In the first, he acknowledges taking possession himself; in the second, he attributes the transfer to the other person.

f: 1230. In these disputes, what is taking (akhdh) equivalent to?
b: Taking is equivalent to receiving possession.

f: 1231. In these disputes, what is giving (iʿṭāʾ) equivalent to?
b: Giving is equivalent to handing over possession.

f: 1232. Why does merely giving something not always establish liability?
b: Because giving can occur by making something available or placing it before someone, without a legally significant transfer of liability.

f: 1233. If someone argues that giving cannot occur without the other person taking possession, what is the response?
b: Giving can occur through making the item available or placing it before him, and any implied possession is only incidental and does not establish liability.

f: 1234. Why is implied possession from giving different from acknowledged taking as a trust?
b: Because implied possession from giving does not necessarily create a cause of liability.

f: 1235. If a person says, “I took one thousand dirhams from you as a trust,” and the owner says, “No, it was a loan,” what do both parties agree upon?
b: They both agree that possession occurred with permission.

f: 1236. Why is the dispute between trust and loan different from the dispute between trust and theft?
b: Because in the trust-loan dispute, both agree on permitted taking, while they disagree over whether that taking created liability.

f: 1237. If a person says, “This thousand was my trust with so-and-so, and I took it,” and the other person says, “It belongs to me,” who receives the money?
b: The first person receives it.

f: 1238. Why does the first person receive the money when he claims it was his trust with another person?
b: Because he acknowledged that the other person had possession but claimed ownership against him, and the other person denied that claim.

f: 1239. In the dispute over whether property held by another person belongs to the holder or the claimant, whose statement is accepted?
b: The statement of the person denying the claim is accepted with an oath.

f: 1240. What principle is applied when one person admits another had possession but claims ownership over the item?
b: The person denying the ownership claim is believed because he is the one denying an asserted right.

f: 1241. If a person says, “I rented my animal to another person, he rode it, and he returned it,” while the other person says, “You are lying; the animal belongs to me,” whose statement is accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The statement of the person claiming ownership of the animal is accepted.

f: 1242. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, if a person claims he rented an animal to someone and that person claims ownership of the animal, whose statement is accepted?
b: The statement of the person who took the animal is accepted.

f: 1243. What is the basis of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad’s opinion in the dispute over rented property ownership?
b: Their opinion is based on analogy (qiyās).

f: 1244. Which other transactions have the same disagreement as the dispute over rented animals and garments?
b: Borrowing (ʿāriyah) and allowing someone to live in a house.

f: 1245. If a person says, “So-and-so stitched my garment for half a dirham, then I took it,” and the other person says, “The garment belongs to me,” which disagreement applies?
b: The same disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله/Muḥammad applies.

f: 1246. Why does analogy give preference to the person who received the rented or borrowed item?
b: Because possession is established through the transaction, and the acknowledgement of that possession affects the ruling.

f: 1247. According to the preferred Hanafi view (istiḥsān), why is the person who rented out an item believed when he claims ownership?
b: Because the other person only possessed the item to obtain its benefit, not as an owner.

f: 1248. According to istiḥsān, why does possession in rental not indicate ownership?
b: Because possession in rental exists only as a necessity for using the item.

f: 1249. What is the purpose of possession in a rental contract?
b: The purpose is obtaining the contracted benefit, such as riding an animal or wearing a garment.

f: 1250. Why is possession in a trust deposit different from possession in rental?
b: Because possession itself is the purpose of a trust deposit.

f: 1251. Why does acknowledging a trust deposit acknowledge another person’s possession?
b: Because entrusting an item means intentionally giving another person possession of it.

f: 1252. According to the second explanation, why is a person’s statement about possession accepted in rental and borrowing cases?
b: Because he acknowledges possession that came about through his own action.

f: 1253. According to the second explanation, why is a trust deposit different from rental and borrowing?
b: Because the item in a trust deposit may have entered his possession without his own action.

f: 1254. Why is the distinction between trust deposits and rental not simply based on whether the word “took” is mentioned?
b: Because the word “took” also appears in other acknowledgement cases where the ruling is different.

f: 1255. If a person says, “I collected one thousand dirhams from someone that were owed to me,” and the other person denies this, whose statement is accepted?
b: The statement of the person denying the collection is accepted.

f: 1256. If a person says, “I lent someone one thousand dirhams and then took them back,” and the other person denies this, whose statement is accepted?
b: The statement of the person denying the repayment is accepted.

f: 1257. Why is the claimant’s statement accepted in a dispute over repayment of a debt?
b: Because repayment of debts occurs through receiving an equivalent that carries liability.

f: 1258. What does a person acknowledge when he says, “I collected the one thousand dirhams that were owed to me”?
b: He acknowledges the existence of a cause of liability and receipt of something that carries liability.

f: 1259. Why does acknowledging collection of a debt create liability?
b: Because receiving repayment means receiving property that substitutes for the original debt.

f: 1260. Why is the case of debt repayment different from rental and borrowing disputes?
b: Because debt repayment concerns establishing liability, while rental and borrowing concern possession only for obtaining benefit.

f: 1261. In the debt repayment dispute, what does the person claim after acknowledging receipt of the money?
b: He claims ownership of the received money through the alleged settlement of the debt.

f: 1262. Why is the claim of ownership rejected in the debt repayment case?
b: Because the other party denies that the payment or settlement occurred.

f: 1263. What principle distinguishes possession in rental from possession in a trust deposit?
b: In rental, possession exists only for use; in a trust deposit, possession itself is the purpose.

f: 1264. What principle distinguishes possession in rental from receiving repayment of a debt?
b: Rental creates temporary possession for benefit, while debt repayment creates liability through receiving an equivalent.

f: 1265. If a person acknowledges that another person rented, borrowed, or otherwise used an item, why is this different from acknowledging that another person merely performed an action?
b: Because in rental and borrowing cases, the item itself is the object connected to the claimed right, while an action may be performed while ownership and possession remain with another person.

f: 1266. If a person says, “So-and-so planted this land,” while the land remains in his possession, does this acknowledge the other person’s possession?
b: No, it only acknowledges that the other person performed an action.

f: 1267. If a person says, “So-and-so built this house,” while he possesses the house, does this prove that the builder owns the house?
b: No, because the building could have been done while the property remained owned and possessed by the person making the acknowledgement.

f: 1268. If a person says, “So-and-so planted this vineyard,” and the other person claims ownership of the vineyard, whose statement is accepted?
b: The statement of the person in possession is accepted.

f: 1269. Why is the statement of the possessor accepted when someone else claims ownership after planting or building?
b: Because the possessor only acknowledged an act performed by the other person, not possession or ownership belonging to that person.

f: 1270. What example is given to explain why acknowledging an action does not mean acknowledging possession?
b: The example of a tailor stitching a garment for half a dirham without the owner saying that he received the garment from the tailor.

f: 1271. Why does saying “the tailor stitched my garment for half a dirham” not prove the tailor possessed the garment?
b: Because a person can perform work on an item while it remains in another person’s possession.

f: 1272. What is the ruling if a person acknowledges that another person planted his land or built his house, but the other claims ownership?
b: The possessor’s statement is accepted.

f: 1273. What is the main distinction between acknowledging an action and acknowledging possession?
b: An action can occur without transferring possession, while possession directly relates to ownership claims.

f: 1274. What is the chapter discussed after these rulings on acknowledgement?
b: The chapter of acknowledgement by a person during his final illness (Iqrār al-Marīḍ).

f: 1275. If a person acknowledges debts during his terminal illness while he already has debts from his healthy period, which debts receive priority according to the Hanafi view?
b: The debts from his healthy period and debts arising during illness from known causes receive priority.

f: 1276. According to Imām al-Shāfiʿī, are debts acknowledged during illness equal to debts from health?
b: Yes, he considers them equal.

f: 1277. Why does Imām al-Shāfiʿī consider illness debts and health debts equal?
b: Because both arise from an acknowledgement made by a sane and religiously responsible person, and both attach to the person’s legal liability (dhimmah).

f: 1278. How does Imām al-Shāfiʿī compare a sick person’s acknowledgement to transactions such as sale and marriage?
b: He compares them because a person’s liability can accept obligations in both cases.

f: 1279. What is the Hanafi response to Imām al-Shāfiʿī’s argument about equal liability?
b: An acknowledgement is not accepted when it results in cancelling another person’s established right.

f: 1280. Why is the acknowledgement of a sick person treated differently according to the Hanafi scholars?
b: Because existing creditors already have rights attached to the person’s wealth before the acknowledgement.

f: 1281. Why can a sick person not freely give gifts or waive debts beyond one-third of his wealth?
b: Because the rights of creditors are already attached to his wealth.

f: 1282. What does the restriction of gifts during terminal illness indicate about creditors’ rights?
b: It shows that creditors’ rights have priority over voluntary transfers by the sick person.

f: 1283. Why is marriage treated differently from a sick person’s acknowledgement of debt?
b: Because marriage is considered an essential need, and it is only allowed with the normal dower (mahr al-mithl).

f: 1284. Why is selling property for its equivalent value treated differently from harmful acknowledgements during illness?
b: Because creditors’ rights are attached to the financial value of the wealth, not merely to the outward form of the transaction.

f: 1285. Why are creditors’ rights not considered attached to wealth during a person’s state of health?
b: Because a healthy person can continue earning and increasing his wealth.

f: 1286. Why are creditors’ rights considered attached during terminal illness?
b: Because illness is a state of inability and restriction (ḥajr), where increasing wealth is not expected in the same way.

f: 1287. What is the difference between a person’s state of health and state of illness according to the Hanafi reasoning?
b: Health is a state of unrestricted freedom, while illness is a state of restriction and inability.

f: 1288. Why are the two states of illness (before and after acknowledgement) treated similarly?
b: Because both are states of restriction (ḥajr), unlike the difference between health and illness.

f: 1289. What principle is used to give priority to earlier debts over debts acknowledged during terminal illness?
b: Existing rights attached to wealth take priority over later acknowledgements that would remove those rights.

f: 1290. Why are debts with known causes given priority over debts acknowledged during terminal illness?
b: Because there is no suspicion regarding their establishment, since something established by direct evidence cannot be denied.

f: 1291. Why is a witnessed or established debt stronger than a debt based only on a sick person’s acknowledgement?
b: Because the witnessed debt is already proven and does not depend solely on the person’s statement.

f: 1292. What are examples of debts with known causes that receive priority during terminal illness?
b: Compensation for consumed property, debts established without acknowledgement, and the normal dower (mahr al-mithl) in marriage.

f: 1293. Why is compensation for property consumed by a person considered a debt with a known cause?
b: Because the obligation arises from the actual consumption of another person’s property, not merely from acknowledgement.

f: 1294. Why is a debt whose obligation became known without acknowledgement given priority?
b: Because its existence is established independently of the sick person’s statement.

f: 1295. Why is marriage with the normal dower considered a debt with a known cause?
b: Because the obligation of the dower is established through the marriage contract itself.

f: 1296. Are debts from a person’s healthy period preferred over debts from known causes during illness?
b: No, neither is preferred over the other because both are established without suspicion.

f: 1297. If a sick person acknowledges that a specific item in his possession belongs to another person, is that acknowledgement valid against creditors from his healthy period?
b: No, it is not valid against them.

f: 1298. Why is a sick person’s acknowledgement of another person’s ownership not valid against health creditors?
b: Because the creditors’ rights have already attached to the wealth.

f: 1299. Why can a sick person not repay some creditors while leaving others unpaid?
b: Because favouring some creditors would result in cancelling or reducing the rights of others.

f: 1300. Do creditors from the healthy period and creditors from illness receive the same treatment regarding repayment priority?
b: Yes, they are treated the same in this ruling.

f: 1301. What exceptions allow repayment of certain illness debts before others?
b: If he repays something he borrowed during his illness or pays the price of something he purchased during illness, and this is established by evidence.

f: 1302. Why are repayment of an illness loan and payment for an illness purchase treated differently?
b: Because their causes are established through evidence rather than merely through acknowledgement.

f: 1303. After priority debts are paid, what happens to the debts acknowledged during terminal illness?
b: Any remaining wealth is given to those debts acknowledged during illness.

f: 1304. Why is an acknowledgement during illness accepted after priority creditors are paid?
b: Because the acknowledgement itself was valid; it was only prevented from affecting the rights of existing creditors.

f: 1305. Was the sick person’s acknowledgement completely invalid according to the Hanafi view?
b: No, it was only ineffective against the rights of creditors whose claims already attached to the estate.

f: 1306. If a sick person has no debts from his healthy period, is his acknowledgement of debt valid?
b: Yes, his acknowledgement is valid.

f: 1307. Why is a sick person’s acknowledgement valid when there are no prior creditors?
b: Because it does not cancel another person’s established right.

f: 1308. When there are no prior debts, who has greater priority: the person acknowledged as a creditor or the heirs?
b: The person acknowledged as a creditor has priority over the heirs.

f: 1309. What statement of ʿUmar رضي الله عنه is used to support the validity of a sick person’s acknowledgement?
b: “If a sick person acknowledges a debt, it is binding upon him regarding all of his estate.”

f: 1310. Why do heirs not have priority over debts acknowledged during illness?
b: Because heirs only inherit what remains after obligations and debts are removed.

f: 1311. Why are burial expenses given priority before inheritance?
b: Because burial is an essential need that must be fulfilled before heirs receive the estate.

f: 1312. What general principle explains why debts take priority over inheritance?
b: The deceased’s obligations are removed from the estate before heirs’ ownership begins.

f: 1313. What is the ruling if a sick person acknowledges a debt in favour of one of his heirs during his terminal illness?
b: The acknowledgement is not valid unless the remaining heirs confirm it.

f: 1314. What was one opinion of Imām al-Shāfiʿī regarding a sick person acknowledging a debt for an heir?
b: He held that it is valid because it reveals an already existing right, and truthfulness is stronger in such matters.

f: 1315. What analogy did Imām al-Shāfiʿī use to support the validity of a sick person’s acknowledgement of a debt to an heir?
b: He compared it to acknowledging a debt to a non-heir, acknowledging a debt in favour of another heir, or acknowledging a destroyed deposit belonging to an heir.

f: 1316. What hadith is used as evidence that a sick person’s acknowledgement of debt for an heir is not accepted?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “There is no bequest for an heir, nor acknowledgement of a debt for an heir.”

f: 1317. Why is a sick person prevented from giving preference to one heir through acknowledgement of debt?
b: Because the rights of all heirs become attached to his wealth during his illness, and favouring one heir cancels the rights of the others.

f: 1318. Why is acknowledgement of debt for a stranger different from acknowledgement for an heir during terminal illness?
b: Because strangers need to conduct transactions with him during health, whereas heirs already have an attachment to his wealth due to kinship.

f: 1319. Why would preventing acknowledgements to strangers during illness harm society?
b: People would avoid transactions with a person who might later become unable to acknowledge debts during illness.

f: 1320. Why is acknowledgement in favour of another heir treated differently from acknowledgement in favour of the remaining heirs?
b: Because the other heir also needs to conduct transactions, while the attachment of rights belongs to the remaining heirs.

f: 1321. What happens if the remaining heirs confirm a sick person’s acknowledgement of debt to one heir?
b: The acknowledgement becomes valid because they have waived their own rights.

f: 1322. What is the ruling if a sick person acknowledges a debt in favour of a stranger, even if the debt covers all of his wealth?
b: The acknowledgement is valid.

f: 1323. Why would analogy suggest limiting a sick person’s acknowledgement to one-third of his wealth?
b: Because the Law restricts a sick person’s voluntary disposal of wealth to one-third.

f: 1324. Why is a sick person’s acknowledgement of debt to a stranger valid beyond one-third of his estate?
b: Because acknowledgement is a binding proof, not a voluntary gift, and it is valid against the estate after debts are considered.

f: 1325. According to the text, how can an acknowledgement valid for one-third eventually encompass the entire estate?
b: One-third of what remains becomes valid, then one-third of the remaining amount after that, and so on until the entire estate is covered.

f: 1326. What happens if a person acknowledges a debt to a stranger and later claims that the creditor is his son?
b: His lineage claim is established, and the previous debt acknowledgement becomes invalid.

f: 1327. Why does a later claim of sonship invalidate a previous acknowledgement of debt to a stranger?
b: Because lineage goes back to the time of conception, meaning the acknowledgement was actually made in favour of his son, and acknowledgement for an heir is invalid.

f: 1328. Why does marrying a woman after acknowledging a debt to her not invalidate the acknowledgement?
b: Because marriage only begins from the time of the marriage contract, so the previous acknowledgement was genuinely made to a stranger.

f: 1329. What is the difference between lineage and marriage regarding previous acknowledgements of debt?
b: Lineage has retroactive effect to conception, while marriage only takes effect from the contract.

f: 1330. What is the ruling if a man divorces his wife three times during his terminal illness and later acknowledges that she has a debt against him?
b: She receives the lesser of the acknowledged debt and her inheritance share from him.

f: 1331. Why is the divorced wife’s acknowledgement of debt treated with suspicion during terminal illness?
b: Because the divorce and acknowledgement may have been used as a method to give her more than her inheritance share.

f: 1332. Why is only the lesser amount between the debt and inheritance established for the divorced wife?
b: Because there is no suspicion regarding the smaller amount, while the larger amount may involve favouring her beyond her legal inheritance.

f: 1333. Why might a person divorce his wife during terminal illness before acknowledging a debt to her?
b: To avoid the restriction against acknowledging debts in favour of an heir and make the acknowledgement appear to be for a stranger.

f: 1334. What principle is used when rejecting a sick person’s acknowledgement that harms existing creditor rights?
b: An acknowledgement is not accepted when it results in cancelling another person’s established right.

f: 1335. Why are debts from health and debts with known causes given priority over a sick person’s later acknowledgements?
b: Because their establishment is certain and they were already attached to the wealth before the later acknowledgement.

f: 1336. What are the conditions for a man's acknowledgment that a boy is his son to establish lineage?
b: Four conditions are required: the boy could have been born from him, the boy has no known lineage, the boy confirms the claim, and the acknowledgment is made by a person whose statement is valid.

f: 1337. Why must the boy be someone who could have been born from the man for lineage acknowledgment to be accepted?
b: Because otherwise the acknowledgment would contradict obvious reality and would not be legally possible.

f: 1338. Why must the boy have no known lineage for a man's acknowledgment of him as his son to be accepted?
b: Because an existing lineage from another person prevents establishing a new lineage through acknowledgment.

f: 1339. Why must the boy confirm the man's claim that he is his son?
b: Because the case concerns a person who has control over himself and can confirm or deny the claim, unlike a young child who cannot speak.

f: 1340. Does a man's terminal illness prevent his acknowledgment of a son from being valid?
b: No. His illness does not prevent it because lineage is considered among essential needs and personal rights.

f: 1341. What happens to inheritance when a man's acknowledgment of a son is accepted?
b: The acknowledged son shares in the inheritance with the other heirs because his lineage has been established.

f: 1342. Why does an acknowledged son inherit alongside the other heirs?
b: Because once his lineage is established, he becomes like any other known heir.

f: 1343. Is a man's acknowledgment of his parents, child, wife, or master valid?
b: Yes, because he is acknowledging matters connected to himself and is not assigning lineage to another person.

f: 1344. Is a woman's acknowledgment of her parents, husband, or master valid?
b: Yes, because these acknowledgments concern herself and do not assign lineage to another person.

f: 1345. Why is a woman's acknowledgment of a child generally not accepted?
b: Because it involves assigning lineage to another person, namely the child's father, since the child's lineage is connected to the husband.

f: 1346. When is a woman's acknowledgment of a child accepted?
b: When her husband confirms the child or when a midwife testifies regarding the birth.

f: 1347. Why is the testimony of a midwife sufficient for a woman's acknowledgment of a child?
b: Because the purpose is only to establish the identity and occurrence of the birth, and midwife testimony is accepted in such matters.

f: 1348. Can confirmation of lineage be accepted after the death of the person making the acknowledgment?
b: Yes, because lineage continues after death and remains a valid matter for confirmation.

f: 1349. Why is the wife's confirmation of lineage valid after the husband's death?
b: Because the legal effects of marriage, including inheritance rights, continue to exist.

f: 1350. Is a husband's confirmation of his wife's acknowledgment valid after her death according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, because marriage ends with death and inheritance does not yet exist at the time of acknowledgment.

f: 1351. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not accept confirmation based on inheritance after death?
b: Because inheritance is not present at the time of acknowledgment, and confirmation only relates back to the original acknowledgment.

f: 1352. Is acknowledgment of lineage from someone other than parents or children, such as a brother or uncle, accepted?
b: No, because it involves assigning lineage to another person rather than establishing one's own direct lineage.

f: 1353. Why is acknowledgment of a brother or uncle not accepted as establishing lineage?
b: Because lineage cannot be created through a person's claim when it concerns the lineage of another person.

f: 1354. If a person acknowledges a brother but already has a known heir, who receives the inheritance?
b: The known heir receives the inheritance, whether that heir is close or distant.

f: 1355. Why does a known heir take priority over a person acknowledged as a brother or relative?
b: Because the acknowledgment does not establish lineage, so the acknowledged person does not compete with the established heir.

f: 1356. If a person acknowledges a brother but has no known heir, who receives his inheritance?
b: The acknowledged person receives the inheritance.

f: 1357. Why does an acknowledged relative receive the inheritance when there are no heirs?
b: Because the person has authority over his wealth when no heir exists, just as he may bequeath all of it.

f: 1358. Is acknowledgment of a brother considered an actual bequest (waṣiyyah)?
b: No. It is not a true bequest, although it receives a similar ruling in some respects.

f: 1359. If someone acknowledges a brother during terminal illness and later bequeaths all his wealth to another person, who receives the wealth?
b: The person who received the bequest receives it, because the acknowledgment of the brother was not a true bequest.

f: 1360. If a person acknowledges a brother during terminal illness, the brother confirms it, then the person denies the inheritance and leaves no bequest, where does the wealth go?
b: It goes to the public treasury (Bayt al-Māl).

f: 1361. Why can a person retract his acknowledgment of a brother but not his acknowledgment of a son?
b: Because lineage is not established through acknowledgment of a brother, whereas direct lineage such as fatherhood becomes established and cannot be revoked.

f: 1362. Why does retraction invalidate acknowledgment of a brother?
b: Because the acknowledgment only created a right similar to a bequest, not an established lineage. Once retracted, no permanent lineage remains.

f: 1363. Why does acknowledgment of a son differ from acknowledgment of a brother?
b: A son involves direct lineage, which is permanent and cannot be revoked, whereas a brother's acknowledgment does not establish lineage.

f: 1364. If a deceased man leaves two sons and one son acknowledges that their father received fifty out of a one hundred dirham debt owed to him, what is the ruling?
b: The acknowledging son receives nothing, and the other son receives the remaining fifty dirhams.

f: 1365. Why does the son who acknowledges that his father received fifty dirhams receive nothing from that amount?
b: Because his acknowledgment concerns a debt owed to the deceased, and repayment is only established through a guaranteed receipt. Since his brother denies receiving the amount, the acknowledgment consumes his own share.

f: 1366. Why is an acknowledgment by one heir about a debt owed to the deceased treated as affecting his own share?
b: Because the debt belonged to the deceased, and after death the heirs share in the right. The acknowledging heir cannot impose his acknowledgment upon the other heir who rejects it.

f: 1367. If one of two heirs claims that their deceased father already received part of a debt owed to him, why does the other heir receive the remaining amount instead of the first heir?
b: Because the acknowledgment is binding only upon the person making it, not upon the other heir who denies it.

f: 1368. What legal problem would occur if the acknowledging son could reclaim the fifty dirhams from the debtor despite his brother’s denial?
b: It would create a circular legal contradiction: the son would reclaim from the debtor, the debtor would reclaim from the deceased's estate, and the estate would reclaim from the acknowledging son.

f: 1369. Why is repayment considered to require a guaranteed receipt in this case?
b: Because a debt is only considered discharged when payment is received in a manner that establishes certainty and liability.

f: 1370. What two aspects are contained in an acknowledgment by an heir regarding a debt of the deceased?
b: It contains acknowledgment of a financial right and an attempt to impose its consequences upon the other heirs. The first may be valid, but the second cannot bind those who deny it.

f: 1371. Why does an heir not have authority to impose his acknowledgment regarding the deceased’s debt upon another heir?
b: Because each heir only controls his own share of the estate, not the rights belonging to the other heirs.

f: 1372. What is the principle illustrated by the case of a person acknowledging that a seller emancipated a slave?
b: An acknowledgment may be accepted for one consequence but rejected for another consequence depending on whether the person has authority over that matter.

f: 1373. Why is a person's acknowledgment that a seller emancipated a slave accepted regarding the emancipation but not regarding recovering the price?
b: Because emancipation concerns the slave’s status, while recovering the price affects the seller’s financial rights. The person making the acknowledgment has no authority to impose financial consequences upon the seller.

f: 1. What are the three types of settlement (ṣulḥ) mentioned in Islamic law according to the text?
b: Settlement with acknowledgment, settlement with silence (where the defendant neither acknowledges nor denies), and settlement with denial.

f: 2. Are all three types of settlement (acknowledgment, silence, and denial) permissible according to the author?
b: Yes, all three are permissible.

f: 3. What Qur’anic verse is used as evidence for the permissibility of settlement?
b: “And reconciliation is better.” (Qur’an 4:128)

f: 4. What prophetic statement is used as evidence for the permissibility of settlement?
b: “Every settlement is permissible among the Muslims, except a settlement that makes lawful what is unlawful or makes unlawful what is lawful.”

f: 5. What is the position of al-Shāfiʿī regarding settlement with denial or silence?
b: He considers settlement with denial or silence impermissible.

f: 6. Why does al-Shāfiʿī argue that settlement with denial or silence is not permissible?
b: Because the compensation is lawful for the person giving it but unlawful for the person taking it, making the matter reversed; he also considers giving wealth to end a dispute similar to bribery.

f: 7. How does the author respond to al-Shāfiʿī’s argument against settlement with denial or silence?
b: The author argues that the hadith only prohibits settlements involving something inherently unlawful, not settlements after a valid claim where the claimant takes compensation for his perceived right and the defendant gives wealth to remove a dispute.

f: 8. What is meant by the phrase “making lawful what is unlawful or making unlawful what is lawful” in the hadith about settlement?
b: It refers to making something unlawful in itself lawful, such as wine, or making something lawful in itself unlawful, such as preventing marital relations with a co-wife through a settlement condition.

f: 9. Why is settlement after a valid claim considered permissible according to the author?
b: Because the claimant receives compensation for a right he believes he possesses, and the defendant pays to remove a dispute, both of which are legislated purposes.

f: 10. Why is giving wealth to remove oppression or a dispute not considered bribery?
b: Because wealth serves as protection for people, and paying to remove an unjust dispute is permissible.

f: 11. If settlement occurs with acknowledgment in exchange for wealth for wealth, what type of contract does it resemble?
b: It resembles a sale contract.

f: 12. Why is settlement with acknowledgment in exchange for wealth treated like a sale?
b: Because it involves exchanging wealth for wealth through mutual agreement between the parties.

f: 13. What legal rulings apply to settlement with acknowledgment when it resembles a sale?
b: Pre-emption (shufʿah) applies in real estate, defects allow return, and the option of condition and inspection apply.

f: 14. Why does ignorance of the compensation invalidate a settlement based on acknowledgment?
b: Because unknown compensation can lead to dispute.

f: 15. Why does ignorance of the thing being settled over not invalidate settlement?
b: Because the right being disputed is dropped through the settlement.

f: 16. What condition is required regarding the compensation in a settlement treated like a sale?
b: The compensation must be something deliverable.

f: 17. If settlement is exchanged for wealth in return for benefits, what type of contract does it resemble?
b: It resembles a lease (ijārah).

f: 18. Why is settlement for wealth in return for benefits treated like a lease?
b: Because it involves granting ownership of benefits in exchange for wealth.

f: 19. What requirement applies to settlement that resembles a lease?
b: A specific time period must be defined.

f: 20. Why does settlement resembling a lease become invalid if either party dies during the agreed period?
b: Because it is treated as a lease contract.

f: 21. In settlement with silence or denial, what is the purpose of the settlement for the defendant?
b: To avoid taking an oath and to end the dispute.

f: 22. In settlement with silence or denial, what is the purpose of the settlement for the claimant?
b: It is based on the meaning of exchange, as he receives compensation in place of his claimed right.

f: 23. Why can the legal ruling of settlement differ between the claimant and defendant?
b: Because contracts may have different legal effects for different parties, similar to how cancellation may differ between contracting parties and others.

f: 24. Why is settlement with denial clearly capable of having different rulings for the two parties?
b: Because the defendant denies the claim while the claimant treats the settlement as compensation for his right.

f: 25. Why does settlement with silence also allow different rulings for the two parties?
b: Because silence may indicate either acknowledgment or rejection, so the defendant’s status is uncertain and cannot be treated as a clear offer or acknowledgment.

f: 26. In which type of settlement regarding a house does pre-emption (shufʿah) not apply according to the text?
b: In settlement based on denial or silence.

f: 27. Why does pre-emption not apply when settlement regarding a house is based on denial or silence?
b: Because the defendant takes the house based on his original right and only gives compensation to remove the claimant’s dispute, not as an exchange acknowledging the claimant’s ownership.

f: 28. Why does pre-emption apply when a person gives a house itself as settlement compensation?
b: Because the claimant receives it as compensation for wealth, making it an exchange contract for him.

f: 29. Why does settlement based on giving the house itself become subject to pre-emption even if the defendant denies the claim?
b: Because from the claimant’s perspective it functions as an exchange of property, and exchange contracts trigger pre-emption.

f: 30. What is the ruling if a settlement based on acknowledgment is made and part of the settled property is later found to belong to someone else?
b: The defendant returns a proportional amount of the settlement compensation.

f: 31. Why does a defendant return a proportional amount of compensation when part of settled property in an acknowledgment settlement belongs to another person?
b: Because acknowledgment settlement is treated like a sale, and the rules of sale apply when another person’s ownership is discovered.

f: 32. What is the ruling if settlement based on silence or denial is made and the disputed property is later found to belong to another person?
b: The claimant returns to the original dispute and returns the compensation.

f: 33. Why does the claimant return to the dispute after another person's ownership is discovered in a silence or denial settlement?
b: Because the defendant only paid to remove the dispute, and once it is clear there was no valid claim against him, the purpose of the compensation disappears.

f: 34. What happens if only part of the disputed property in a silence or denial settlement is found to belong to another person?
b: The claimant returns the portion of compensation corresponding to that part and returns to the dispute regarding that portion.

f: 35. What is the difference between finding another person’s ownership in acknowledgment settlement and in denial/silence settlement?
b: In acknowledgment settlement, it is treated like a sale and compensation is adjusted; in denial/silence settlement, the original dispute returns because the settlement was only to remove conflict.

f: 36. If the entire property given in an acknowledgment settlement is found to belong to another person, what happens?
b: The person who received the settlement returns the entire property because the exchange was invalid.

f: 37. If only part of the property given in an acknowledgment settlement is found to belong to another person, what happens?
b: The equivalent portion of compensation is returned.

f: 38. Why is settlement different from selling property while denying the claimant’s right?
b: Because a sale itself acknowledges an exchange of ownership, while settlement may only be intended to remove a dispute without admitting the claimant’s right.

f: 39. If a person sells property to a claimant while denying the claim, what happens if the sale is later challenged?
b: He returns to the disputed claim because entering into the sale indicates acknowledgment that the claimant had a right to the property.

f: 40. What happens if the compensation given in settlement is destroyed before it is delivered?
b: The ruling is the same as the ruling for discovering another person's ownership in the settlement property.

f: 41. If a person claims a right in a house without specifying the exact part, settles over it, and later part of the house is found to belong to another person, does he return compensation?
b: No, he does not return any compensation because his original claim may have concerned the remaining part of the house.

f: 42. Why does a claimant not return compensation when an unspecified part of the claimed house is found to belong to another person?
b: Because his claim was general and may have been directed toward the part that remains validly owned.

f: 43. What happens if the entire house in an unspecified settlement is found to belong to another person?
b: The claimant returns all compensation because the settlement becomes completely without a corresponding subject.

f: 44. Why does discovery that the entire house belongs to another person require returning all compensation?
b: Because the compensation no longer corresponds to any valid right, similar to the rules of sale.

f: 45. Is it valid for someone who claims ownership of an entire house to settle by taking only a piece of that same house while still maintaining his claim over the rest?
b: No, such a settlement is invalid.

f: 46. Why is settlement over part of the claimed property invalid when the claimant still maintains his claim over the remainder?
b: Because the claimant received compensation from the very thing he is claiming, while the dispute over the remaining part continues.

f: 47. How can a valid settlement be made when someone claims an entire house but wants only part of it as settlement?
b: Either an additional one dirham is added as compensation for the remaining claim, or the settlement includes a statement that he releases the claim regarding the remainder.

f: 48. Why does adding one dirham make such a settlement valid?
b: Because it makes the settlement compensation for the remaining right rather than merely taking part of the disputed property itself.

f: 49. Why does adding a release of the remaining claim make the settlement valid?
b: Because it removes the remaining dispute and completes the purpose of settlement.

f: 50. For what types of rights is settlement (ṣulḥ) valid according to the chapter?
b: Settlement is valid regarding claims of wealth, benefits, intentional injuries, and accidental injuries.

f: 51. Why is settlement valid regarding claims of wealth?
b: Because settlement has the meaning of sale, as it involves exchanging something of value by mutual agreement.

f: 52. Why is settlement valid regarding benefits (manāfiʿ)?
b: Because benefits can be owned through leasing, and settlement can also transfer ownership of benefits.

f: 53. What principle is used to determine the legal ruling of settlement contracts?
b: Settlement is interpreted according to the contract most similar to it, so that the parties’ actions can be made legally valid whenever possible.

f: 54. Is settlement valid for intentional injuries (jināyāt ʿamd)?
b: Yes, settlement is valid for intentional injuries.

f: 55. What Qur’anic verse is used as evidence for settlement regarding intentional injuries?
b: “But if something is pardoned for him by his brother, then there should be a suitable follow-up…” (Qur’an 2:178).

f: 56. According to Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنهما, what matter was the verse about pardon and follow-up revealed regarding?
b: It was revealed regarding settlement over the blood-money of intentional killing.

f: 57. Why is settlement over intentional injury compared to marriage?
b: Because both involve exchanging wealth for something that is not itself wealth.

f: 58. What similarity exists between compensation in marriage and compensation in settlement over intentional injury?
b: Anything valid to specify as a dowry in marriage is valid to specify as compensation in settlement over intentional injury.

f: 59. If the specified compensation in settlement over intentional injury is invalid, what replaces it?
b: The blood-money (diyah) is required because it is the original right connected to the injury.

f: 60. What happens if a person settles over an intentional injury using wine as compensation?
b: Nothing is required because an unrestricted pardon does not require compensation.

f: 61. Why is this different from marriage where invalid or unspecified dower still requires mahr al-mithl?
b: Because mahr al-mithl is the original obligation in marriage, whereas compensation in injury settlement only arises through the settlement agreement.

f: 62. Does the ruling of valid settlement for injuries include only killing or also lesser injuries?
b: It includes both injuries to life and injuries less than killing.

f: 63. Why is settlement not valid for the right of pre-emption (shufʿah) in exchange for wealth?
b: Because shufʿah is only a right to acquire ownership, and no right is attached to the property before ownership is obtained.

f: 64. Why is settlement valid for retaliation (qiṣāṣ) but not for pre-emption (shufʿah)?
b: Because retaliation is a direct right connected to an act, whereas pre-emption is only a future right of acquiring ownership.

f: 65. What happens to the right of pre-emption if settlement over it is invalid?
b: The right of pre-emption becomes void because it can be lost through abandonment and silence.

f: 66. Is a guarantee of a person (kafālah bi al-nafs) treated like shufʿah regarding settlement?
b: Yes, it is treated similarly, so wealth is not required through settlement over it.

f: 67. Are there different narrations regarding cancellation of a personal guarantee through settlement?
b: Yes, there are two narrations regarding its invalidation.

f: 68. Why is settlement valid for accidental injuries?
b: Because the obligation in accidental injury is financial, so it resembles a sale.

f: 69. Is an increase beyond the legally fixed blood-money valid in settlement for accidental injury?
b: No, an increase beyond the fixed blood-money is not valid.

f: 70. Why is an increase beyond blood-money invalid in accidental injury settlement?
b: Because blood-money is fixed by the Lawgiver, and it is not permissible to invalidate or alter a fixed legal obligation.

f: 71. What happens to an invalid excess amount added above the blood-money in accidental injury settlement?
b: The excess amount is returned.

f: 72. Why is settlement over retaliation (qiṣāṣ) different from settlement over accidental injury regarding extra compensation?
b: Because retaliation itself is not wealth, so its value is determined by the agreement between the parties.

f: 73. If a person settles over one of the specified blood-money amounts, what restriction applies?
b: Any amount beyond the specified blood-money is not valid.

f: 74. If a person settles for something other than the specified blood-money amounts, is the settlement valid?
b: Yes, because it is treated as an exchange for the blood-money right.

f: 75. What condition is required when settling for something other than the specified blood-money amounts?
b: The compensation must be received in the same session.

f: 76. Why must possession occur in the same session when settling for another type of compensation?
b: To prevent it from becoming an exchange of one deferred debt for another deferred debt.

f: 77. If a judge has already ruled with a specified blood-money amount and the parties settle for another type of compensation with an increase, is it valid?
b: Yes, it is valid.

f: 78. Why is an increase valid after a judge’s ruling fixing blood-money?
b: Because the right has already become established through judgment, making the settlement an exchange contract.

f: 79. Why is an initial settlement different from settlement after judicial determination?
b: Because in an initial settlement, agreement over the blood-money amount functions like the original specification, so an increase beyond it is not allowed.

f: 80. What is the difference between settlement before judgment and settlement after judgment regarding blood-money?
b: Before judgment, the parties’ agreement fixes the amount and prevents increase; after judgment, the right is already fixed and can be exchanged for another compensation.

f: 81. Why is settlement (ṣulḥ) not permissible regarding a prescribed punishment (ḥadd)?
