b: No. Liability remains because the trust relationship ended when he denied possessing the deposit.

f: 55. Why does later admitting possession not restore the original deposit contract after an earlier denial?
b: Because the owner's demand ended the owner's consent, and the deposit holder's denial terminated the trust relationship from his own side.

f: 56. How is denying possession of a deposit similar to an agent denying his agency?
b: Both acts terminate the underlying legal relationship, so it does not automatically revive afterward.

f: 57. What is the ruling if a deposit arrangement has ended, and the custodian later admits possessing the deposit?
b: The original deposit arrangement does not revive automatically. Once it has ended through denial in the owner's presence, it can only be restored through a new deposit agreement.

f: 58. Does denying possession of a deposit before someone other than the owner make the custodian liable according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: No. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, denying possession before a third party does not create liability because it may serve to protect the deposit from others, and the custodian cannot remove himself from responsibility except before the owner or after the owner's demand.

f: 59. Why does denying possession of a deposit before a third party not terminate the deposit agreement according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Because only the owner can effectively remove the custodian from the deposit arrangement, either through direct interaction or by demanding the deposit. Denial before someone else does not terminate the agreement.

f: 60. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, may a custodian travel with a deposited item?
b: Yes. He may travel with the deposit, whether or not it has burdens or expenses, provided travel is considered a safe means of preserving it.

f: 61. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may a custodian travel with a deposited item that requires transportation costs or maintenance?
b: No. They prohibit travelling with a deposit that has burdens or expenses because the owner would ordinarily not consent to bearing the cost of returning it.

f: 62. According to al-Shāfiʿī, may a custodian travel with a deposited item?
b: No. Al-Shāfiʿī does not allow travelling with a deposit, regardless of whether it has burdens or expenses, because customary preservation normally occurs in settled places rather than during travel.

f: 63. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله allow a custodian to travel with a deposited item?
b: Because the owner's permission is unrestricted, and safe travel is considered a valid method of preserving property.

f: 64. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad prohibit travelling with a burdensome deposited item?
b: Because returning such an item creates additional expense, and they assume the owner would not normally consent to those extra costs.

f: 65. Why does al-Shāfiʿī prohibit travelling with a deposited item?
b: Because he limits the custodian's authority to ordinary methods of preservation, which normally means keeping the deposit in settled areas rather than travelling with it.

f: 66. What happens if the owner expressly forbids the custodian from taking the deposit out of the city, but the custodian does so anyway?
b: The custodian becomes liable because he violated a valid restriction that benefits the preservation of the deposit.

f: 67. Why is a restriction preventing removal of a deposit from the city considered valid?
b: Because remaining in the city generally provides stronger protection for the deposited property, making the restriction beneficial and binding.

f: 68. If two people jointly deposit property with a custodian and only one owner requests his share, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله ruling?
b: The custodian must not hand over any portion until the other joint owner is also present.

f: 69. If two people jointly deposit property and one owner requests his share, what is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: The custodian should give the requesting owner his share of the deposit.

f: 70. If three people jointly deposit one thousand dirhams and only one owner appears to claim his share, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله ruling?
b: The custodian should not give him any portion until the other owners are present.

f: 71. If three people jointly deposit one thousand dirhams and one owner requests his share, what is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: The custodian may give him his proportional share of the deposited money.

f: 72. To what types of jointly deposited property does the disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and his two companions mainly apply?
b: It applies primarily to fungible goods that are measured or weighed, such as money, grain, and similar property.

f: 73. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad allow one joint depositor to receive his share before the others arrive?
b: Because each owner is merely requesting delivery of the share that already belongs to him, so the custodian should hand it over.

f: 74. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله prohibit giving one joint depositor his share before the other owners are present?
b: Because the claimant's right exists only as an undivided share. Delivering a specific separated portion effectively requires dividing the jointly owned property, and the custodian has no authority to carry out such a division.

f: 75. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish jointly deposited property from a shared debt when one owner requests his share?
b: Because debts are satisfied through equivalent amounts, allowing each creditor to receive his portion independently, whereas jointly deposited physical property requires an actual division of the object, which the custodian is not authorized to perform.

f: 76. What is the ruling if the owner of a deposit says, "Keep it in this room," but the depositary keeps it in another room of the same house?
b: The depositary does not become liable because moving the deposit to another room within the same house does not reduce its protection. The condition provides no meaningful benefit, so it is not legally binding.

f: 77. What is the ruling if one person deposits divisible property with two custodians and one custodian gives the entire deposit to the other without dividing it?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the custodian who hands over the entire deposit becomes liable because the owner consented to both custodians jointly safeguarding it, not to one person possessing all of it alone.

f: 78. How should two custodians safeguard a divisible deposit according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: They should divide the deposit so that each custodian preserves one-half, since this reflects the owner's permission for both to participate in its safekeeping.

f: 79. What is the ruling if the deposited item cannot be divided and one of the two custodians keeps the entire item with the permission of the other?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, this is permissible because continuous joint possession is impossible, and alternating custody is understood to fall within the owner's permission.

f: 80. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may one of two custodians keep the entire deposit with the other's permission?
b: Yes. They hold that since the owner trusted both custodians, either may entrust the whole deposit to the other without liability, whether the property is divisible or indivisible.

f: 81. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish between divisible and indivisible deposits entrusted to two custodians?
b: Because divisible property can be split so that each custodian fulfills the owner's intention of joint custody, whereas indivisible property cannot practically be held by both at once, making alternating custody acceptable.

f: 82. If the owner of a deposit tells the custodian, "Do not give it to your wife," but the wife is the only practical person available to care for that type of property, is the custodian liable?
b: No. If giving the deposit to that family member is practically unavoidable for normal preservation, the restriction is disregarded and the custodian is not liable.

f: 83. If the owner forbids the custodian from giving the deposit to anyone in his household, but the custodian gives it to someone he could easily have avoided using, what is the ruling?
b: The custodian becomes liable because the owner's condition can reasonably be observed and may protect the deposit from an untrustworthy person.

f: 84. Why are some restrictions imposed by the owner of a deposit considered legally ineffective?
b: Restrictions that provide no real protective benefit or make ordinary preservation impractical are disregarded because the law does not enforce conditions that serve no meaningful purpose.

f: 85. Why are some restrictions imposed by the owner of a deposit considered legally binding?
b: Restrictions that provide a genuine benefit in protecting the deposit and can reasonably be followed must be observed. Violating them makes the custodian liable.

f: 86. Why is moving a deposit between rooms in the same house generally permitted despite the owner's instruction to keep it in one room?
b: Because the level of security is ordinarily the same throughout the house, so moving it does not undermine the owner's interest in preserving the deposit.

f: 87. Why does handing an entire divisible deposit from one custodian to the other create liability according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because the owner entrusted both custodians with responsibility, and transferring all possession to one exceeds the permission originally granted.

f: 88. Why does the custodian who receives a deposit from another custodian not become liable according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because he received it as a deposit from the first custodian and did not himself violate the owner's instructions; the liability falls upon the one who transferred it improperly.

f: 89. How does the ruling on two custodians preserving a deposit compare to two agents appointed to purchase something?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the same principle applies: one agent may not simply hand over the entire responsibility to the other when the owner's appointment contemplated both acting together.

f: 90. How does the ruling on two custodians preserving a deposit compare to two people jointly holding a pledged item?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the same rule applies: one holder may not transfer the entire responsibility to the other when the arrangement originally required both to participate in safeguarding it.

f: 91. What is the ruling if a deposit is kept in a different house than the one specified by the owner?
b: The deposit holder becomes liable because different houses provide different levels of protection, making the owner's restriction beneficial and therefore binding.

f: 92. When does moving a deposit to another room in the same house make the deposit holder liable?
b: It normally does not create liability because the rooms provide equivalent protection, but liability arises if the specified room has a clearly different level of security or vulnerability.

f: 93. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, who is liable if a deposit holder unlawfully deposits the property with another person and it is destroyed?
b: Only the first deposit holder is liable; the second recipient is not liable because he received the property from someone who was still considered a trustee.

f: 94. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, who may the owner hold liable if a deposit holder unlawfully deposits the property with another person and it is destroyed?
b: The owner may hold either the first or second deposit holder liable. If the second pays, he may seek reimbursement from the first.

f: 95. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad hold the second recipient of an unauthorized deposit liable?
b: Because the second recipient took possession without the owner's permission, making him responsible just as one who receives property from a usurper.

f: 96. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not hold the second recipient of an unauthorized deposit liable?
b: Because the first deposit holder remains a trustee merely by handing it over, so the second receives it from a trusted hand rather than from someone already liable.

f: 97. If the owner recovers compensation from the first deposit holder after an unauthorized transfer, may the first recover from the second?
b: No. Once the first pays compensation, he is treated as having acquired ownership through liability, so he cannot seek reimbursement from the second.

f: 98. If the owner recovers compensation from the second recipient after an unauthorized transfer, what happens according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: The second recipient may recover the amount from the first deposit holder because he acted on the first person's behalf.

f: 99. Why does the first deposit holder become liable according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله after handing the deposit to another person?
b: He becomes liable only when he abandons the duty of personally safeguarding the deposit, not merely by transferring possession.

f: 100. What example does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use to illustrate why the second recipient is not liable?
b: He compares it to a garment blown by the wind into someone's lap, where mere possession without wrongful action does not create liability.

f: 101. If two people each claim ownership of the same deposited money and the custodian refuses to swear an oath to either, how is the dispute resolved?
b: The money is divided equally between the claimants, and the custodian must also pay an additional equal amount between them because of refusing the required oaths.

f: 102. Why is each claimant entitled to an oath from the custodian when both claim ownership of the same deposit?
b: Because each claim is independently possible and each claimant has a separate legal right to require an oath.

f: 103. How does the judge decide which claimant's oath is heard first when two claimants dispute the same deposit?
b: The judge may begin with either claimant, and if they dispute the order, he draws lots to remove suspicion of bias.

f: 104. What happens if the custodian swears the required oath to both claimants in a dispute over a deposit?
b: Neither claimant receives the property because neither has established ownership through evidence.

f: 105. What happens if the custodian refuses to swear the oath for one claimant in a deposit dispute?
b: Judgment is entered in favour of that claimant because refusal to swear serves as proof against the custodian.

f: 106. Why is refusal to swear treated differently from acknowledging ownership in a deposit dispute?
b: Because an acknowledgment is itself direct legal proof establishing ownership, whereas refusal to swear only operates according to the procedural rules governing oaths.

f: 107. What is the legal status of a deposit (wadīʿah) in the hands of the person entrusted with it?
b: A deposit is a trust (amānah). If it is destroyed without negligence or transgression, the custodian is not liable.

f: 108. Why is the custodian of a deposit generally not liable if the deposit is destroyed?
b: Because the Sharīʿah treats the deposit as a trust, and imposing liability would discourage people from accepting deposits, harming public interests.

f: 109. Who may a person entrusted with a deposit use to help preserve it?
b: He may preserve it himself or through members of his household, since this is considered normal and necessary.

f: 110. When does a custodian become liable for entrusting a deposit to another person?
b: If he gives it to someone outside his household without permission, he becomes liable because the owner only consented to his own custody.

f: 111. When is giving a deposit to another person without permission excused?
b: When necessity requires it, such as protecting it from fire or sinking, provided the necessity is proven.

f: 112. What happens if the owner demands the return of a deposit and the custodian refuses despite being able to return it?
b: The custodian becomes liable because withholding it after demand is wrongful.

f: 113. What is the ruling if a custodian intentionally mixes a deposit with his own identical property so that it cannot be distinguished?
b: He becomes liable for the deposit.

f: 114. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what right does the depositor have after identical property is intentionally mixed?
b: The depositor only has a claim for compensation and does not become a partner in the mixed property.

f: 115. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what option does the depositor have after identical property is intentionally mixed?
b: He may choose to claim compensation or become a partner in the mixed property.

f: 116. What happens if the person who mixed the property is released from liability by the owner?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the owner's claim ends. According to the two companions, partnership in the mixed property remains.

f: 117. What is the ruling when different liquids, such as vinegar and oil, are intentionally mixed?
b: The owner is only entitled to compensation because separation is impossible.

f: 118. What is the ruling regarding intentionally mixing wheat with barley?
b: According to the preferred view, it is treated like destruction and only compensation is due.

f: 119. How does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله rule when identical liquids are intentionally mixed?
b: The smaller amount becomes subordinate to the larger amount.

f: 120. How does Muḥammad rule when identical liquids are intentionally mixed?
b: The owner becomes a partner in the mixture regardless of quantity.

f: 121. What is the ruling if two owners' property becomes mixed accidentally without the custodian's action?
b: The owners become partners in the mixed property and the custodian is not liable.

f: 122. What happens if the custodian spends part of a deposit, later replaces it, and mixes it with the remainder?
b: He becomes liable for the entire deposit.

f: 123. What happens if a custodian rides, wears, uses, or improperly entrusts a deposited item, then later returns it to proper custody?
b: His liability ends once the transgression ceases and the deposit is restored to proper custody.

f: 124. According to al-Shāfiʿī, does liability end when the custodian returns the deposit to proper custody after transgressing?
b: No. He holds that only returning it to the owner removes liability.

f: 125. What happens if the owner asks for a deposit and the custodian falsely denies possessing it?
b: He becomes liable for the deposit.

f: 126. Does later admitting possession remove liability after previously denying it to the owner?
b: No. The original deposit arrangement has ended and must be renewed.

f: 127. What is the ruling if the custodian denies possessing the deposit before someone other than the owner?
b: According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, he does not become liable because such denial may serve to protect the property.

f: 128. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, may a custodian travel with a deposit?
b: Yes, even if the item has transportation costs, provided the journey is safe.

f: 129. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, when may a custodian not travel with a deposit?
b: He may not travel with it if it involves transportation burdens or expenses.

f: 130. According to al-Shāfiʿī, may a custodian travel with a deposit?
b: No, because preservation is ordinarily expected in settled areas.

f: 131. What happens if the owner forbids removing the deposit from the city and the custodian does so anyway?
b: The custodian becomes liable because the restriction provides a real benefit.

f: 132. If two owners jointly deposit divisible property and one requests his share, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله ruling?
b: The custodian must wait until the other owner is present.

f: 133. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may one joint owner receive his share of a divisible deposit before the other arrives?
b: Yes, he may receive his share.

f: 134. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله prevent giving one joint owner his share of an undivided deposit?
b: Because separating shares requires division, and the custodian has no authority to divide jointly owned property.

f: 135. If one person deposits divisible property with two custodians, may one custodian hand the entire property to the other according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No. They must divide the property and each preserve his own portion.

f: 136. If one person deposits indivisible property with two custodians, may one custodian preserve it alone?
b: Yes, with the permission of the other custodian.

f: 137. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may one of two custodians preserve the entire deposit with the other's permission?
b: Yes, whether the property is divisible or indivisible.

f: 138. If the owner tells the custodian not to give the deposit to his wife, when is the custodian still excused for doing so?
b: When practical necessity leaves no reasonable alternative, such as items normally cared for by women.

f: 139. When does giving the deposit to a prohibited household member make the custodian liable?
b: When another suitable person was available and the condition could have been observed.

f: 140. If the owner tells the custodian to keep the deposit in one room but he keeps it in another room of the same house, is he liable?
b: No, unless there is a meaningful difference in security between the rooms.

f: 141. If the custodian moves the deposit to another house against instructions, what is the ruling?
b: He becomes liable because protection differs between houses.

f: 142. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, if a custodian improperly deposits the property with another person and it is destroyed, whom may the owner hold liable?
b: Only the first custodian.

f: 143. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, if a custodian improperly deposits the property with another person and it is destroyed, whom may the owner hold liable?
b: The owner may hold either the first or second custodian liable.

f: 144. If the owner holds the second custodian liable according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, does the second custodian have recourse?
b: Yes. He may recover the amount from the first custodian.

f: 145. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله exempt the second custodian from liability in this case?
b: Because the second initially received the property from a trustworthy custodian and committed no independent act of transgression.

f: 146. If two people each claim that money held by a custodian belongs to them as a deposit and he refuses to swear to either claim, how is judgment given?
b: The money is divided equally between them, and the custodian must also pay another equal amount divided between them.

f: 147. Why is the custodian required to swear separately to each claimant when two people claim the same deposit?
b: Because each claim is an independent legal right requiring a separate oath.

f: 148. What happens if the custodian swears the oath for both claimants?
b: Neither claimant receives the money because neither established proof.

f: 149. Why must the custodian compensate both claimants after refusing both oaths?
b: Because by the judgment each had a valid claim, and dividing the original money deprived each of part of his established right.

f: 150. According to Imām al-Bazdawī, what happens if judgment is first given for one claimant after refusal to swear?
b: The custodian is still made to swear regarding the second claimant, and if he refuses again, the property is divided between both.

f: 151. According to al-Khaṣṣāf, what is the effect of a judgment for the first claimant after refusal to swear?
b: The judgment becomes effective immediately and later refusal regarding the second claim has no effect on ownership of that property.

f: 152. What further oath did al-Khaṣṣāf suggest may still be required after judgment for the first claimant?
b: An oath denying liability for the value of the property claimed by the second claimant.

f: 153. On what earlier legal disagreement is this final oath based?
b: It is based on the disagreement between Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad concerning liability after a custodian acknowledges a deposit that is later judicially awarded to someone else.

f: 1. What is the legal definition of an ʿāriyah (loan for use) in Islamic law?
b: It is the transfer of ownership of the benefit (usufruct) of property to another person without compensation.

f: 2. Why is an ʿāriyah considered permissible in Islamic law?
b: Because it is an act of kindness and mutual assistance, supported by the Prophet ﷺ borrowing armor from Ṣafwān.

f: 3. What evidence from the Sunnah supports the permissibility of an ʿāriyah?
b: The Prophet ﷺ borrowed coats of armor from Ṣafwān, demonstrating the legitimacy of lending property for use.

f: 4. According to the preferred Ḥanafī view, what ownership is transferred in an ʿāriyah?
b: Ownership of the benefit (usufruct), not ownership of the physical object itself.

f: 5. How did al-Karkhī define an ʿāriyah?
b: He defined it as merely granting permission to benefit from another person's property.

f: 6. Why did al-Karkhī regard an ʿāriyah as permission rather than ownership?
b: Because it is often concluded with words of permission, does not require a specified duration, and uncertain benefits cannot be fully transferred according to his reasoning.

f: 7. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject al-Karkhī's interpretation of an ʿāriyah?
b: Because the language, legal effects, and ability to conclude it with ownership wording indicate that ownership of the benefit is transferred.

f: 8. What is the linguistic origin of the word ʿāriyah used by the jurists?
b: It comes from ʿariyyah, meaning a gift.

f: 9. Why does the linguistic origin of the word ʿāriyah support the view that it transfers ownership of benefits?
b: Because the word itself is derived from a term meaning a gift, indicating transfer rather than mere permission.

f: 10. Can an ʿāriyah be concluded using wording that indicates ownership?
b: Yes. Words indicating transfer of ownership may establish an ʿāriyah when ownership of the object itself is not intended.

f: 11. Why are benefits capable of being owned according to the preferred Ḥanafī position?
b: Because benefits, like physical property, fulfill human needs and are recognized as legitimate objects of ownership.

f: 12. What are the two forms of ownership recognized by the jurists?
b: Ownership may exist either with compensation or without compensation.

f: 13. How does ownership of benefits compare to ownership of physical property?
b: Both can be owned either with compensation or without compensation.

f: 14. What common characteristic do benefits and physical property share that allows both to be owned?
b: Both satisfy human needs and therefore are capable of ownership.

f: 15. Why can wording of permission establish ownership in an ʿāriyah?
b: Because permission is understood as expressing the transfer of ownership of benefits, similar to how leasing contracts operate.

f: 16. How does leasing support the interpretation that an ʿāriyah transfers ownership of benefits?
b: Leasing may also be concluded using words of permission even though it unquestionably transfers ownership of the benefit.

f: 17. Why does uncertainty (jahālah) not invalidate an ʿāriyah?
b: Because there is no binding exchange or financial obligation that could lead to contractual disputes.

f: 18. At what point does ownership of the benefit become established in an ʿāriyah?
b: When the borrower actually takes possession by using the property.

f: 19. Why does uncertainty cease once the borrower begins using the borrowed property?
b: Because the benefit has become definite through actual possession and use.

f: 20. Does the prohibition arising from uncertainty prevent the borrower from using the property?
b: No. It only prevents broader acquisition of rights beyond the permitted benefit.

f: 21. Why may the borrower not lease out property received through an ʿāriyah?
b: Because the borrower does not acquire a transferable leasing right, and subleasing would impose additional harm upon the owner.

f: 22. Which explicit statement validly creates an ʿāriyah?
b: Saying, "I have lent it to you."

f: 23. Does saying, "I have lent it to you," validly establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because it is explicit wording for a loan for use.

f: 24. Can the statement, "I have fed you this land," establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because this expression is customarily used to grant the right to benefit from land.

f: 25. Why does saying, "I have fed you this land," create an ʿāriyah?
b: Because customary usage understands it as granting use rather than ownership of the land itself.

f: 26. Can saying, "I have granted you this garment," establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, provided the speaker does not intend to make an outright gift of the garment itself.

f: 27. Under what condition does the statement, "I have granted you this garment," create an ʿāriyah rather than a gift?
b: When the speaker intends only to grant the benefit of using the garment, not ownership of the garment itself.

f: 28. Can the statement, "I have carried you upon this animal," establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, if the speaker intends only to grant the use of the animal rather than ownership of it.

f: 29. Why are statements such as "I have granted you this garment" interpreted as loans for use instead of gifts?
b: Because the surrounding intention shows that ownership of the benefit, rather than the object itself, was intended.

f: 30. What role does intention play when wording could indicate either a gift or an ʿāriyah?
b: The speaker's intention determines whether ownership of the object or merely its benefit is transferred.

f: 31. Does saying, "I have made this slave serve you," establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because it grants permission to benefit from the slave's services.

f: 32. Why does the statement, "I have made this slave serve you," constitute an ʿāriyah?
b: Because it clearly grants the benefit of the slave's service without transferring ownership of the slave.

f: 33. Can the statement, "My house is yours for residence," establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because it grants the right to reside in the house without transferring ownership of the house itself.

f: 34. Why is the statement, "My house is yours for residence," interpreted as a loan for use?
b: Because the phrase "for residence" limits the grant to the benefit of living there.

f: 35. Can the statement, "My house is yours for residence for your lifetime," establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because it grants the benefit of residing in the house for the borrower's lifetime.

f: 36. Why does adding "for your lifetime" not convert the transaction into a gift of the house itself?
b: Because the duration relates only to the right of residence, not ownership of the property.

f: 37. How does the phrase "for residence" affect the interpretation of the statement "My house is yours"?
b: It clarifies that only the benefit of residence is being transferred, not ownership of the house.

f: 38. Why is the word "yours" interpreted in light of the later wording in these expressions?
b: Because the explanatory wording specifies that the intended ownership is ownership of the benefit rather than the object itself.

f: 39. What is the legal definition of an ʿāriyah (loan for use) in Islamic law?
b: It is a gratuitous loan that grants another person the right to benefit from property without compensation.

f: 40. Why is an ʿāriyah considered permissible in Islamic law?
b: Because it is an act of kindness and mutual assistance, supported by the Prophet ﷺ borrowing armor from Ṣafwān.

f: 41. According to al-Karkhī, what is the legal nature of an ʿāriyah?
b: It is merely permission to benefit from another person's property rather than ownership of the benefit itself.

f: 42. According to the majority of Ḥanafīs, what is the legal nature of an ʿāriyah?
b: It transfers ownership of the benefit without transferring ownership of the underlying property.

f: 43. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject al-Karkhī's view that an ʿāriyah is only permission?
b: Because benefits can be owned just as physical property can, whether with or without compensation.

f: 44. Why does uncertainty (jahālah) not invalidate an ʿāriyah according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because it is not a binding exchange contract, so uncertainty does not normally lead to disputes.

f: 45. When does ownership of the benefit in an ʿāriyah effectively arise according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: It arises through actual use and possession of the benefit.

f: 46. Why may the borrower not lease out property received through an ʿāriyah?
b: Because borrowing grants a lesser right than leasing, so it does not include authority to create a lease.

f: 47. Which expressions explicitly establish an ʿāriyah contract?
b: Statements such as "I have lent it to you."

f: 48. Does saying "I have fed you this land" establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because the expression is conventionally used for granting use of land.

f: 49. When does saying "I have granted you this garment" create an ʿāriyah instead of a gift?
b: When the speaker intends granting its use rather than transferring ownership of the garment itself.

f: 50. When does saying "I have carried you upon this animal" establish an ʿāriyah?
b: When the intention is permission to use the animal rather than gifting ownership of it.

f: 51. Does saying "I have made this slave serve you" establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because it grants permission to benefit from the slave's services.

f: 52. Does saying "My house is yours for residence" establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because it grants the right to live in the house without transferring ownership.

f: 53. Does saying "My house is yours for residence during your lifetime" establish an ʿāriyah?
b: Yes, because it grants the right to reside there for the borrower's lifetime.

f: 54. Can the lender revoke an ʿāriyah whenever he wishes?
b: Yes, because ownership of future benefits has not yet become fixed.

f: 55. What prophetic evidence supports the lender's right to revoke an ʿāriyah?
b: The ḥadīth: "The gift of milk is returned, and the borrowed item is returned."

f: 56. Why may a lender revoke an ʿāriyah before all benefits have been used?
b: Because benefits come into existence gradually, so future benefits have not yet become owned.

f: 57. Is borrowed property held as a trust (amānah) by the borrower?
b: Yes.

f: 58. Is a borrower liable if borrowed property is destroyed without negligence?
b: No, because the borrowed property is held as a trust.

f: 59. Why does Imām al-Shāfiʿī hold the borrower liable if borrowed property is destroyed?
b: Because he believes possession was taken for the borrower's own benefit without an established proprietary right.

f: 60. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject al-Shāfiʿī's view regarding liability for destroyed borrowed property?
b: Because possession was taken with the owner's permission and without transgression.

f: 61. Does the obligation to return borrowed property mean the borrower originally possessed it unlawfully?
b: No. Returning it is simply an obligation arising from the loan arrangement.

f: 62. Why is property taken under an approval-for-purchase arrangement guaranteed, unlike an ʿāriyah?
b: Because possession there arises through a commercial contract, which carries liability.

f: 63. Can a borrower lease out borrowed property?
b: No.

f: 64. What is the legal ruling if a borrower leases out borrowed property and it is destroyed?
b: The borrower becomes liable.

f: 65. Why does leasing borrowed property invalidate the borrower's protection from liability?
b: Because leasing exceeds the authority granted through borrowing and amounts to unauthorized possession.

f: 66. Why would validating a lease made by the borrower create an unacceptable consequence?
b: Because it would bind the lender and prevent him from recovering his property until the lease ends.

f: 67. When does the borrower become liable after leasing borrowed property to another?
b: Upon handing the property over to the lessee.

f: 68. May the lender claim compensation directly from the lessee if borrowed property was unlawfully leased?
b: Yes, because the lessee took possession without the owner's permission.

f: 69. If the lender claims compensation from the borrower, may the borrower recover that compensation from the lessee?
b: No, because he is treated as having leased his own property.

f: 70. If the lender claims compensation from the lessee, may the lessee recover it from the borrower?
b: Yes, if the lessee was unaware that the property was only borrowed.

f: 71. Does the lessee have a right of recourse against the borrower if he knew the property was merely borrowed?
b: No, because there was no deception.

f: 72. According to the Ḥanafīs, when may a borrower lend borrowed property to another person?
b: When the nature of the benefit does not differ according to the user.

f: 73. According to Imām al-Shāfiʿī, may a borrower lend borrowed property to another person?
b: No.

f: 74. Why does Imām al-Shāfiʿī prohibit the borrower from lending borrowed property to someone else?
b: Because he views an ʿāriyah as mere permission, and permission cannot itself be delegated.

f: 75. Why do the Ḥanafīs allow sub-lending in some cases?
b: Because they regard the borrower as owning the benefit, allowing him to transfer its use when the intended benefit is unchanged.

f: 76. Why do the Ḥanafīs allow a borrower to lend borrowed property to another person in some cases?
b: Because they regard an ʿāriyah as transferring ownership of the benefit, allowing the borrower to transfer that benefit to another person.

f: 77. How do the Ḥanafīs support the view that benefits can be transferred in an ʿāriyah?
b: They argue that benefits are capable of ownership in leasing, so they are likewise capable of ownership in borrowing to fulfill people's needs.

f: 78. When may a borrower not lend borrowed property to another person?
b: When the usefulness or wear of the item differs depending on who uses it, because this could cause additional harm to the lender.

f: 79. Why is sub-lending prohibited when different users affect the borrowed item differently?
b: Because the lender only consented to the borrower's use, not the use of someone else whose use may be more burdensome.

f: 80. How many forms of unrestricted and restricted ʿāriyah does al-Hidāyah describe?
b: Four forms.

f: 81. What is the first form of an ʿāriyah regarding restrictions?
b: It is unrestricted regarding both time and manner of use, allowing the borrower to use it however and whenever he wishes.

f: 82. What is the second form of an ʿāriyah regarding restrictions?
b: It is restricted regarding both time and manner of use, so the borrower may not exceed those restrictions except by using an equivalent or less harmful alternative.

f: 83. What is the third form of an ʿāriyah regarding restrictions?
b: It is restricted regarding time but unrestricted regarding the manner of use.

f: 84. What is the fourth form of an ʿāriyah regarding restrictions?
b: It is unrestricted regarding time but restricted regarding the manner of use.

f: 85. When may a borrower depart from the lender's specified manner of use?
b: Only when the alternative use is equivalent or more beneficial to the lender without causing additional harm.

f: 86. If an animal is borrowed without any restriction, what uses are permitted?
b: The borrower may ride it, use it for carrying loads, and lend it to another person for carrying loads.

f: 87. Why may a borrower lend an unrestrictedly borrowed animal to another person for carrying loads?
b: Because carrying loads does not materially differ according to the user.

f: 88. Why may a borrower either ride an unrestrictedly borrowed animal himself or allow someone else to ride it?
b: Because the unrestricted contract allows him to determine who will use it.

f: 89. After the borrower personally rides an unrestrictedly borrowed animal, may he then allow another person to ride it?
b: No, because his own riding has become the specified use.

f: 90. After the borrower allows another person to ride an unrestrictedly borrowed animal, may he later ride it himself?
b: No, because allowing another rider has become the specified use.

f: 91. What is the ruling if a borrower changes the specified rider after a choice has become fixed?
b: He becomes liable because he exceeded the specified use.

f: 92. Why are borrowed dirhams, dinars, measured goods, weighed goods, and counted goods treated as loans (qarḍ) rather than ʿāriyah?
b: Because they can only be beneficially used by consuming them, which requires transferring ownership of the items themselves.

f: 93. Why does borrowing consumable goods necessarily involve ownership of the items themselves?
b: Because their benefit cannot be separated from consuming or using up the actual items.

f: 94. Why is the legal ruling of qarḍ preferred over a gift when consumable goods are borrowed?
b: Because a loan is the lesser transfer of ownership needed to achieve the intended benefit while requiring repayment of an equivalent.

f: 95. What is returned in a qarḍ involving consumable goods?
b: An equivalent item rather than the identical item originally received.

f: 96. When does borrowing dirhams or similar goods remain an ʿāriyah rather than becoming a qarḍ?
b: When a specific non-consumptive use is intended, such as testing a scale or decorating a shop.

f: 97. If someone borrows coins only to decorate a shop, are they treated as a loan (qarḍ)?
b: No. They remain an ʿāriyah limited to that specific use.

f: 98. What is another example where borrowing consumable property remains an ʿāriyah rather than becoming a qarḍ?
b: Borrowing a utensil for decoration or a decorated sword to wear.

f: 99. Is borrowing land for construction or planting legally valid?
b: Yes.

f: 100. Why is borrowing land for building or planting considered valid?
b: Because the benefit is known and is a type of benefit that can also be leased.

f: 101. May the lender revoke a loan of land given for construction or planting?
b: Yes.

f: 102. What may the lender require after revoking a loan of land used for building or planting?
b: He may require the borrower to remove the buildings and trees.

f: 103. Why may the lender demand removal of buildings and trees after revoking the loan?
b: Because the borrower continues occupying the lender's land after the permission has been withdrawn.

f: 104. If land was borrowed without a specified period and the lender revokes the loan, is the borrower liable for his improvements?
b: No, because he relied on the unrestricted agreement without being deceived.

f: 105. Why is the borrower not liable when an unrestricted loan of land is revoked?
b: Because he acted based on the unrestricted contract and not on any false promise by the lender.

f: 106. If land was borrowed for a specified period, may the lender revoke the loan before the period ends?
b: Yes.

f: 107. What is the ruling on revoking a time-limited loan of land before the agreed period expires?
b: It is legally valid but disliked because it breaks a promise.

f: 108. Why is early revocation of a time-limited loan considered disliked?
b: Because it involves breaking an agreed promise, even though the lender retains the legal right to revoke the loan.

f: 109. If a lender revokes a time-limited loan of land before the agreed period ends, who bears the loss caused by removing the borrower's buildings or trees?
b: The lender is liable for the decrease in the value of the buildings and trees caused by their removal.

f: 110. Why is the lender liable for the reduction in value when buildings or trees must be removed after revoking a time-limited loan?
b: Because he induced the borrower to rely on the agreed period, creating a reasonable expectation that he would honor his promise.

f: 111. According to al-Qudūrī, what compensation is due when a lender prematurely revokes a loan of land with buildings or trees?
b: The lender compensates the borrower for the reduction in value caused by removing the buildings or trees.

f: 112. According to al-Ḥākim al-Shahīd, what happens to buildings and trees after the lender compensates the borrower?
b: The lender pays their value, and ownership of the buildings and trees passes to the owner of the land.

f: 113. According to al-Ḥākim al-Shahīd, may the borrower remove his buildings or trees instead of accepting compensation?
b: Yes. If he chooses not to claim their value, he may remove them because they remain his property.

f: 114. If removing the borrower's buildings or trees would damage the land, who decides whether they are removed?
b: The owner of the land has the choice because ownership of the land takes precedence over ownership of what is attached to it.

f: 115. Why is preference given to the landowner when removing buildings or trees would damage the land?
b: Because the land is the foundation, while the buildings and trees are dependent upon it.

f: 116. If someone borrows land to grow crops, may the lender reclaim it before the crops are harvested?
b: No. The borrower keeps possession until the crops are harvested, whether or not a period was specified.

f: 117. Why is a borrower allowed to keep borrowed land until crops are harvested?
b: Because crops have a known endpoint, allowing both parties' rights to be preserved without permanent harm.

f: 118. Why is borrowing land for crops treated differently from borrowing land for planting trees?
b: Because crops mature within a known period, whereas trees have no definite endpoint and could indefinitely burden the landowner.

f: 119. Who bears the cost of returning a borrowed item (ʿāriyah)?
b: The borrower bears the cost of returning it.

f: 120. Why must the borrower pay the cost of returning a borrowed item?
b: Because he took possession of it for his own benefit and is responsible for returning it.

f: 121. Who bears the cost of returning leased property after the lease ends?
b: The lessor bears the cost of returning it.

f: 122. Why does the lessor bear the cost of returning leased property?
b: Because the lessee's obligation is only to make the property available and relinquish control, not to transport it back.

f: 123. Who bears the expense of returning a usurped (ghaṣb) item?
b: The usurper bears the expense.

f: 124. Why is the usurper responsible for the expense of returning usurped property?
b: Because he must fully undo his wrongful act by restoring the property to the owner's possession.

f: 125. If someone returns a borrowed animal to the owner's stable and it later dies, is the borrower liable?
b: No. According to istiḥsān, he is not liable.

f: 126. Why is returning a borrowed animal to the owner's stable considered sufficient?
b: Because this is the customary method of returning such property, and the owner would normally place it there himself.

f: 127. According to strict analogy (qiyās), would returning a borrowed animal to the stable without handing it to the owner discharge liability?
b: No. Under qiyās he would remain liable because he did not personally deliver it to the owner.

f: 128. Why do the Ḥanafīs depart from analogy and apply istiḥsān regarding returning borrowed animals?
b: Because customary practice recognizes returning animals to the owner's stable as valid delivery.

f: 129. If someone borrows a slave and returns him to the owner's house without personally handing him over, is he liable if the slave later perishes?
b: No. The return is valid according to customary practice.

f: 130. If a usurper leaves usurped property at the owner's house without handing it to the owner, is he released from liability?
b: No. He remains liable.

f: 131. Why does merely leaving usurped property at the owner's house not discharge the usurper's liability?
b: Because he must restore possession directly to the owner to remove the effects of his wrongful taking.

f: 132. If a person entrusted with a deposit leaves it at the owner's house without handing it to the owner, is he free from liability?
b: No. He remains liable.

f: 133. Why is returning a deposit to the owner's house insufficient without direct delivery?
b: Because the owner specifically entrusted the property to that custodian and is not presumed to accept return merely by leaving it at the house.

f: 134. Why are borrowed items treated differently from deposits regarding return to the owner's house?
b: Because there is an established custom of returning borrowed items to the owner's home, whereas no such custom exists for deposits.

f: 135. May a borrower return a borrowed jewel necklace by simply leaving it at the lender's house?
b: No. It must be handed directly to the lender.

f: 136. Why must valuable items such as a borrowed jewel necklace be returned directly to the lender?
b: Because the customary rule allowing return to the owner's house does not apply to valuable items requiring greater care.

f: 137. If someone returns a borrowed animal through his own slave, is the borrower liable if the animal is later lost?
b: No. He is not liable because his slave is considered part of his household and acts as a trustee.

f: 138. If someone returns a borrowed animal through a hired worker employed for a month or a year, is the borrower liable?
b: No. A long-term hired worker is treated like a member of the borrower's household, so the borrower is not liable.

f: 139. Why is a borrower allowed to return a borrowed animal through his own slave or long-term hired worker?
b: Because they are regarded as trustworthy members of his household, just as with the rules governing deposits.

f: 140. Is a daily hired worker treated like a member of the borrower's household for returning borrowed property?
b: No. A daily worker is not considered part of the household, so the same rule does not apply.

f: 141. If someone returns a borrowed animal through the owner's slave, is the borrower liable?
b: No. He is not liable because the owner is presumed to be satisfied with delivery through his own slave.

f: 142. If someone returns a borrowed animal through the owner's hired worker, is the borrower liable?
b: No. He is not liable because delivery through the owner's hired worker is treated as acceptable.

f: 143. Why is returning borrowed property through the owner's slave or hired worker considered valid?
b: Because the owner is presumed to accept delivery through those who serve him and would often entrust such matters to them.

f: 144. Does the rule allowing return through the owner's slave apply only to a slave responsible for animals?
b: There are two opinions, but the preferred view is that it applies to any of the owner's slaves because the owner may sometimes use any of them to receive property.

f: 145. If a borrower returns borrowed property through an unrelated stranger, is he liable?
b: Yes. He becomes liable because the stranger is not an approved recipient for returning the borrowed property.

f: 146. Does returning borrowed property through a stranger indicate that the borrower cannot intentionally deposit the borrowed item with another person?
b: According to some scholars, yes. They understood this ruling as evidence that the borrower has no right to entrust the borrowed property to someone else.

f: 147. Did some scholars permit a borrower to entrust borrowed property to another person?
b: Yes. They argued that borrowing grants greater authority than depositing property, so such entrustment is allowed.

f: 148. How did scholars who permit entrusting borrowed property interpret the ruling about returning it through a stranger?
b: They explained that it applies specifically when the borrower is attempting to terminate the borrowing by returning the property after the borrowing period has ended.

f: 149. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what wording should be used when documenting the loan of vacant land for cultivation?
b: The contract should state: "You have fed me (aṭʿamtanī)."

f: 150. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what wording should be used when documenting the loan of vacant land for cultivation?
b: The contract should state: "You have lent it to me (aʿartanī)."

f: 151. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad prefer the wording "You have lent it to me" for land given for cultivation?
b: Because ʿāriyah is the technical legal term specifically designated for this type of contract.

f: 152. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله prefer the wording "You have fed me" for land loaned for cultivation?
b: Because "feeding" specifically refers to cultivation and therefore expresses the intended purpose more precisely than the broader term ʿāriyah.

f: 153. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish between lending land and lending a house when choosing contract wording?
b: Because land may be used for cultivation or other purposes such as building, whereas a house is normally lent only for residence, making the general term ʿāriyah sufficiently precise for a house.

f: 1. What evidence establishes that the contract of gift (hibah) is legislated in Islamic law?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Give gifts to one another and you will love one another," and there is consensus on its legitimacy.

f: 2. What are the essential elements required for a valid gift (hibah) according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Offer, acceptance, and possession (qabḍ).

f: 3. Why are offer and acceptance required for a valid gift?
b: Because a gift is a contract, and contracts are concluded through offer and acceptance.

f: 4. Why is possession (qabḍ) required before ownership transfers in a gift according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because ownership is not established until the recipient takes possession.

f: 5. What was Imām Mālik's opinion regarding ownership of a gift before possession?
b: He held that ownership is established before possession, by analogy with sale.

f: 6. Which other contract is affected by the disagreement over whether ownership of a gift transfers before possession?
b: Charity (ṣadaqah).

f: 7. What ḥadīth do the Ḥanafīs cite to prove that possession is required for ownership in a gift?
b: "A gift is not valid except when it is possessed."

f: 8. How do the Ḥanafīs interpret the ḥadīth stating that a gift is not valid until possessed?
b: They interpret it as meaning that ownership is not established until possession occurs.

f: 9. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject ownership transferring before possession in a gift?
b: Because it would obligate the donor to deliver the gift, even though he only intended a voluntary donation.

f: 10. Why is a bequest (waṣiyyah) different from a gift regarding ownership before possession?
b: Because ownership under a bequest only takes effect after death, when the testator is no longer capable of assuming legal obligations.

f: 11. If the recipient takes possession of a gifted item during the same gathering without the donor's permission, is the gift valid according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Yes. It is valid based on juristic preference (istiḥsān).

f: 12. If the recipient takes possession of a gifted item after the parties have separated without the donor's permission, is the gift valid?
b: No. It is only valid if the donor gives permission to take possession.

f: 13. What is the analogical (qiyās) ruling regarding taking possession of a gift without permission?
b: It would be invalid whether possession occurred during the gathering or afterward.

f: 14. Which jurist held that possession without the donor's permission is invalid even during the gathering?
b: Imām al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 15. Why does qiyās require the donor's permission before taking possession of a gift?
b: Because the property still belongs to the donor until possession occurs, so taking possession is a disposition of another person's property.

f: 16. Why do the Ḥanafīs allow possession during the gathering without explicit permission?
b: Because the donor's offer itself is treated as implicit permission to take possession during the contract session.

f: 17. Why does implied permission to take possession end when the parties separate?
b: Because it is linked to acceptance, and acceptance is confined to the contract gathering.

f: 18. If the donor expressly forbids the recipient from taking possession during the gathering, may the recipient still take possession?
b: No. An explicit prohibition overrides any implied permission.

f: 19. Which words explicitly create a valid gift contract?
b: "I have gifted," "I have granted," and "I have given."

f: 20. Why is the phrase "I have granted" sufficient to establish a gift?
b: Because it is commonly used to mean giving ownership as a gift.

f: 21. Is saying "I have given" sufficient to establish a gift?
b: Yes. It is commonly used to transfer ownership by gift.

f: 22. If someone says, "I have fed you this food," what contract is created?
b: A gift, because food is consumed by transferring ownership of the item itself.

f: 23. Why does saying "I have fed you this food" create a gift rather than a loan for use?
b: Because the substance of food is consumed, requiring ownership of the food itself.

f: 24. Why does saying "I have fed you this land" not create a gift of the land itself?
b: Because land is not eaten; the expression refers to benefiting from its produce rather than transferring ownership of the land.

f: 25. If someone says, "I have made this garment yours," what contract is formed?
b: A gift.

f: 26. Why does the phrase "I have made this garment yours" establish ownership?
b: Because the Arabic letter lām indicates ownership.

f: 27. If someone says, "I have given you this property for your lifetime," what contract is created?
b: A lifetime gift (ʿumrā), which transfers ownership.

f: 28. What prophetic evidence supports ownership in a lifetime gift (ʿumrā)?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever grants a lifetime gift, it belongs to the recipient and his heirs after him."

f: 29. If someone says, "This house is yours for your lifetime," what is the ruling?
b: It is a valid lifetime gift transferring ownership.

f: 30. If someone says, "I have carried you upon this animal," when does it mean a gift?
b: When the speaker intends to transfer ownership of the animal.

f: 31. Why can the phrase "I have carried you upon this animal" indicate either a gift or a loan?
b: Because it literally refers to riding the animal but is also used idiomatically for granting ownership.

f: 32. If someone says, "I have clothed you with this garment," what contract is created?
b: A gift.

f: 33. Why is "I have clothed you with this garment" interpreted as a gift?
b: Because the expression is commonly used to mean transferring ownership of clothing.

f: 34. If someone says, "I have granted you this female slave," what contract is created?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah), not a gift.

f: 35. If someone says, "My house is yours as a gift for residence," what contract is formed?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah).

f: 36. Why is the phrase "My house is yours as a gift for residence" treated as a loan for use?
b: Because the qualifying phrase "for residence" clarifies that only the benefit, not ownership of the house itself, is being transferred.

f: 37. If someone says, "Residence as a lifetime gift," what contract is created?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah).

f: 38. If someone says, "Residence as a grant," what contract is created?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah).

f: 39. If someone says, "Residence as charity," what contract is created?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah).

f: 40. If someone says, "Charity as a loan," what contract is created?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah).

f: 41. If someone says, "A loan as a gift," what contract is created?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah), because the wording referring to use clarifies the intended meaning.

f: 42. If someone says, "This is a gift that you may reside in," what contract is created?
b: A gift (hibah).

f: 43. Why is the phrase "that you may reside in it" interpreted as creating a gift rather than a loan for use?
b: Because it merely expresses the intended purpose of the gift and does not limit or explain the transfer of ownership.

f: 44. Why is the phrase "a gift for residence" interpreted differently from "a gift that you may reside in"?
b: Because "for residence" explains and restricts the gift to the benefit of residence, making it a loan for use rather than a transfer of ownership.

f: 45. According to the Ḥanafīs, when is a gift of divisible property valid?
b: Only after the property has been separated and divided.

f: 46. According to the Ḥanafīs, is a gift of an undivided share in indivisible property valid?
b: Yes.

f: 47. What was Imām al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding gifts of undivided shares?
b: He held that they are valid whether the property is divisible or indivisible.

f: 48. Why did Imām al-Shāfiʿī consider gifts of undivided shares valid?
b: Because a gift transfers ownership, and an undivided share is capable of being owned just like in a sale.

f: 49. Why do the Ḥanafīs invalidate a gift of an undivided share in divisible property?
b: Because complete possession is required for a gift, and complete possession cannot occur until the property is divided.

f: 50. Why does the requirement of possession prevent the validity of gifting an undivided share in divisible property?
b: Because possession would necessarily include another person's share, which was not part of the gift.

f: 51. Why do the Ḥanafīs say that validating a gift of an undivided share would impose an unintended obligation on the donor?
b: Because it would require him to bear the burden and expense of dividing the property, which he did not undertake.

f: 52. Why is a gift of an undivided share in indivisible property valid according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because complete separate possession is impossible, so the only possible form of possession is accepted.

f: 53. Why does indivisible property not create the same burden as divisible property in gifts?
b: Because no division is possible, so the donor is not burdened with dividing the property.

f: 54. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject relying on alternating use (muhāya’ah) to validate gifts of undivided shares?
b: Because alternating use grants a benefit the donor did not intend to give, whereas the gift concerns ownership of the property itself.

f: 55. Why is a bequest (waṣiyyah) treated differently from a gift regarding undivided shares?
b: Because possession is not a condition for the validity of a bequest.

f: 56. Why is a valid sale treated differently from a gift regarding undivided shares?
b: Because possession is not a condition for the validity of a normal sale.

f: 57. Why do invalid sales, currency exchange (ṣarf), and salam differ from gifts regarding possession?
b: Because they are contracts involving liability rather than voluntary donations.

f: 58. Why is a loan (qarḍ) treated differently from a gift regarding undivided property?
b: Because a loan resembles both a donation and a contract of liability, so incomplete possession is sufficient.

f: 59. If someone gives an undivided share of jointly owned property to his own partner, is the gift valid according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: No. The existence of undivided ownership itself prevents its validity.

f: 60. What is the ruling if someone gives an undivided share of divisible property as a gift?
b: The gift is invalid.

f: 61. If an undivided share is later divided and delivered, does the original gift become valid?
b: Yes. Once the property is divided and possession is completed, the gift becomes valid.

f: 62. Why does dividing the property later validate the gift of an undivided share?
b: Because the obstacle of undivided ownership is removed and complete possession becomes possible.

f: 63. Is the gift of flour contained within wheat valid?
b: No.

f: 64. Is the gift of oil contained within sesame seeds valid?
b: No.

f: 65. Is the gift of clarified butter contained within milk valid?
b: No.

f: 66. If the donor later extracts the flour from the wheat and delivers it, does the original gift become valid?
b: No. A new gift contract is required because the original subject matter did not legally exist.

f: 67. Why is the gift of flour within wheat invalid?
b: Because the flour does not yet exist as a separate legal object capable of ownership.

f: 68. Why does later extracting the gifted substance not validate the original gift?
b: Because the original contract was void and a void contract cannot later become effective without a new agreement.

f: 69. Why is gifting flour within wheat different from gifting an undivided share?
b: Because an undivided share is an existing object capable of ownership, whereas the flour does not yet exist independently.

f: 70. Is the gift of milk still inside an animal's udder valid?
b: No.

f: 71. Is the gift of wool still attached to a sheep valid?
b: No.

f: 72. Is the gift of crops still growing in the ground valid?
b: No.

f: 73. Is the gift of dates still attached to a palm tree valid?
b: No.

f: 74. Why are gifts of milk in the udder, wool on sheep, crops in the ground, and dates on trees invalid?
b: Because their attachment prevents valid possession, similar to undivided ownership.

f: 75. If the recipient already possesses the gifted property before the gift contract is made, must he take possession again?
b: No. His existing possession is sufficient.

f: 76. Why does existing possession satisfy the requirement of possession in a gift?
b: Because the property is already in the recipient's possession, fulfilling the condition of qabḍ.

f: 77. Why does existing possession suffice in a gift but not in a sale?
b: Because possession in a sale involves liability, whereas possession in a gift does not.

f: 78. If a father gives property to his minor son as a gift, when does the son become the owner?
b: Immediately upon the gift contract.

f: 79. Why does a minor child not need separate possession when receiving a gift from his father?
b: Because the father's possession legally substitutes for the child's possession.

f: 80. If the gifted property is deposited with someone else on behalf of the father, does the minor child still become owner through the gift?
b: Yes. The depositary's possession is treated as the father's possession.

f: 81. If the gifted property is pledged, usurped, or sold through an invalid sale, does the father's possession still substitute for the child's possession?
b: No. In those cases the property is under someone else's possession or ownership.

f: 82. Does the same rule regarding possession apply to charity (ṣadaqah) given to a minor child?
b: Yes. Charity follows the same ruling as a gift.

f: 83. If a mother gives a gift to her minor child while the father is deceased and there is no executor, does the child acquire ownership through the contract?
b: Yes.

f: 84. Besides the mother, who else may substitute for a minor child's possession when giving him a gift?
b: Anyone who has custody of, supports, and maintains the child.

f: 85. If a stranger gives a gift to a minor child, whose possession completes the gift?
b: The father's possession completes the gift.

f: 86. Why does the father's possession complete a gift made by a stranger to his minor child?
b: Because the father has legal authority over matters that may benefit or harm the child, so he certainly has authority over matters that are purely beneficial.

f: 87. If a gift is made to an orphan, who may validly take possession on the orphan's behalf?
b: The father's executor, the paternal grandfather, or the grandfather's executor.

f: 88. Why may the father's executor or paternal grandfather take possession of a gift for an orphan?
b: Because they possess legal guardianship and stand in the place of the father.

f: 89. If an orphan is under the care of his mother, may she take possession of a gift on his behalf?
b: Yes.

f: 90. Why may a mother take possession of a gift for an orphan in her care?
b: Because she has guardianship over preserving both the child and his wealth, and acquiring wealth is necessary for his welfare.

f: 91. If an orphan is raised by someone unrelated to him, may that caretaker take possession of a gift on the orphan's behalf?
b: Yes.

f: 92. Why may a non-relative caretaker take possession of a gift for the orphan he is raising?
b: Because he has recognized legal authority over the child's care and custody.

f: 93. If a discerning minor personally takes possession of a gift, is the gift valid?
b: Yes.

f: 94. Under what condition may a minor child personally take possession of a gift?
b: The child must be intelligent enough to understand and benefit from the transaction.

f: 95. After marriage has been consummated, may a husband take possession of a gift on behalf of his young wife?
b: Yes.

f: 96. Why may a husband take possession of a gift for his wife after consummation?
b: Because the father's entrusting of her affairs to him is treated as implied authorization.

f: 97. May a husband take possession of a gift for his wife before consummation of the marriage?
b: No.

f: 98. Does the husband's authority to receive gifts on behalf of his wife depend upon the father's presence?
b: No. He may do so even if the father is alive.

f: 99. Why do the mother and other caretakers lose authority to receive gifts when the father is present?
b: Because their authority exists only out of necessity, whereas the father's authority is primary.

f: 100. When do the mother or other caretakers have authority to receive gifts for a child?
b: After the father's death or prolonged absence, according to the preferred opinion.

f: 101. Why is the authority of the mother and other caretakers considered secondary?
b: Because it is based upon necessity rather than delegation from the father.

f: 102. If two people jointly give one house as a gift to a single recipient, is the gift valid?
b: Yes.

f: 103. Why is a joint gift of one house from two donors to one recipient valid?
b: Because the donors deliver the whole property together and the recipient takes possession of it as a whole, so no problematic undivided ownership arises.

f: 104. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, if one person gives one house as a gift to two recipients, is the gift valid?
b: No.

f: 105. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, if one person gives one house as a gift to two recipients, is the gift valid?
b: Yes.

f: 106. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad consider one donor's gift to two recipients valid?
b: Because they viewed it as one transfer of ownership of the whole property to both recipients together.

f: 107. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله invalidate one person's gift of one house to two recipients?
b: Because each recipient actually receives only a share, resulting in undivided ownership in divisible property.

f: 108. What evidence did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use to show that each recipient receives only a share of the property?
b: If the property were indivisible and only one recipient accepted, that recipient's acceptance would still be effective for his portion.

f: 109. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, why does ownership arising in separate shares invalidate the gift?
b: Because the transfer of ownership follows the actual shares acquired, producing prohibited undivided ownership.

f: 110. Why is a pledge to two people treated differently from a gift to two people?
b: Because the legal effect of a pledge is detention of the property, which is complete for each pledgee rather than divided.

f: 111. What evidence shows that a pledge is not divided between multiple pledgees?
b: If one creditor's debt is repaid, he does not receive part of the pledged property.

f: 112. According to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, if someone gives ten dirhams in charity to two poor people, is it valid?
b: Yes.

f: 113. According to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, if someone gives ten dirhams as a gift to two poor people, is it valid?
b: Yes.

f: 114. According to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, if someone gives ten dirhams in charity to two wealthy people, is it valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No.

f: 115. According to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, if someone gives ten dirhams as a gift to two wealthy people, is it valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No.

f: 116. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding gifts or charity to two wealthy people?
b: They held that such gifts are valid.

f: 117. Why are charity and gifts compared in this discussion?
b: Because both involve transferring ownership without compensation.

f: 118. According to the original text, what prevents the validity of both gifts and charity in these cases?
b: Undivided ownership, since both contracts depend upon valid possession.

f: 119. According to one narration, why is charity distinguished from gifts in this issue?
b: Because charity seeks the pleasure of Allah, which is one objective, whereas a gift seeks the pleasure of multiple recipients.

f: 120. According to one interpretation, which case does the original text refer to when equating charity and gifts?
b: Charity given to two wealthy people.

f: 121. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, if a house is gifted with two-thirds to one person and one-third to another, is the gift valid?
b: No.

f: 122. According to Muḥammad, if a house is gifted with two-thirds to one person and one-third to another, is the gift valid?
b: Yes.

f: 123. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله view when the donor explicitly specifies unequal shares in the gift?
b: He held that the gift is invalid because specifying shares clearly creates undivided ownership.

f: 124. What are the two narrations from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding gifting half of a house to each of two recipients?
b: One narration agrees with validity, while another follows the ruling that it is invalid.

f: 125. What principle does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consistently apply regarding gifts to multiple recipients?
b: Any gift that creates undivided ownership in divisible property is invalid.

f: 126. What principle does Muḥammad consistently apply regarding gifts to multiple recipients?
b: Such gifts are valid despite the resulting shared ownership.

f: 127. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله distinguish between equal and explicitly specified unequal shares?
b: Because explicitly specifying portions demonstrates that ownership is intended in separate shares, making the undivided ownership more evident.

f: 128. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why is a pledge with specified shares to two people invalid?
b: Because specifying the shares likewise creates the same problem of divided ownership that affects gifts.

f: 129. According to the Ḥanafīs, may a person revoke a gift given to a stranger?
b: Yes. The donor has the right to revoke the gift, subject to certain obstacles.

f: 130. What was Imām al-Shāfiʿī's ruling regarding revoking a gift given to a stranger?
b: He held that it cannot be revoked, except for a father's gift to his child.

f: 131. Which ḥadīth did Imām al-Shāfiʿī cite to support the prohibition of revoking gifts?
b: "The giver of a gift does not take back his gift except for the father regarding what he gives to his child."

f: 132. Why did Imām al-Shāfiʿī argue that gifts cannot normally be revoked?
b: Because revocation contradicts the transfer of ownership created by the gift contract.

f: 133. Why did Imām al-Shāfiʿī make an exception for a father's gift to his child?
b: Because he regarded the child's ownership as not being completely separate from the father's, since the child is considered part of him.

f: 134. Which ḥadīth do the Ḥanafīs cite to support the donor's right to revoke a gift?
b: "The giver of a gift has more right to his gift as long as he has not been compensated for it."

f: 135. How do the Ḥanafīs interpret the ḥadīth stating that the donor has more right to his gift until compensated?
b: They understand it to mean that the donor may revoke the gift until he receives compensation for it.

f: 136. Why do the Ḥanafīs allow revocation of an uncompensated gift?
b: Because customary gifts often anticipate reciprocal compensation, so the absence of compensation justifies annulment.

f: 137. How do the Ḥanafīs interpret the ḥadīth prohibiting taking back gifts except for a father?
b: They interpret it as denying unilateral revocation while recognizing the father's special authority, rather than denying judicial revocation altogether.

f: 138. Does the donor's legal right to revoke a gift mean that revocation is encouraged?
b: No. It remains disliked (makrūh).

f: 139. Which ḥadīth shows that revoking a gift is disliked?
b: "The one who returns to his gift is like the one who returns to his vomit."

f: 140. Why is revoking a gift considered disliked despite being legally permitted?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ likened it to the repulsive act of returning to one's vomit.

f: 141. What happens to the donor's right of revocation if he receives compensation for the gift?
b: The right of revocation is extinguished.

f: 142. Why does receiving compensation prevent revocation of a gift?
b: Because the intended purpose of the gift transaction has been fulfilled.

f: 143. Does a connected increase (ziyādah muttaṣilah) prevent revocation of a gift?
b: Yes.

f: 144. Why does a connected increase prevent revocation?
b: Because the donor cannot recover the original property without the increase, nor reclaim the increase since it was never included in the gift contract.

f: 145. Does the death of either the donor or the recipient prevent revocation of a gift?
b: Yes.

f: 146. Why does the recipient's death prevent revocation?
b: Because ownership has passed to the heirs through inheritance.

f: 147. Why does the donor's death prevent revocation?
b: Because the heir was not a party to the original gift contract and cannot exercise the donor's personal right of revocation.

f: 148. If the recipient transfers ownership of the gifted property to someone else, may the donor still revoke the gift?
b: No.

f: 149. Why does transferring ownership to another person prevent revocation?
b: Because the transfer occurred with the recipient's authority and created a new ownership through a separate legal cause.

f: 150. If the recipient plants palm trees on gifted land, may the donor revoke the gift?
b: No.

f: 151. If the recipient builds a house on gifted land, may the donor revoke the gift?
b: No.

f: 152. If the recipient builds a shop on gifted land, may the donor revoke the gift?
b: No, provided the construction constitutes a genuine increase in the property's value.

f: 153. If the recipient constructs a water channel on gifted land, may the donor revoke the gift?
b: No, if it constitutes a connected increase.

f: 154. Why do buildings and trees prevent revocation of gifted land?
b: Because they are connected increases attached to the gifted property.

f: 155. Why did the author specifically state that the construction must be "an increase" in the land?
b: Because a very small structure or one built on a vast tract of land may not constitute an increase affecting the entire property.

f: 156. If only part of gifted land has received a connected increase, may the donor revoke the unaffected part?
b: Yes.

f: 157. If the recipient sells an undivided half of the gifted property, may the donor revoke the remaining half?
b: Yes.

f: 158. Why may the donor revoke only the remaining half after half has been sold?
b: Because the obstacle to revocation exists only with respect to the portion that left the recipient's ownership.

f: 159. If none of the gifted property has been sold, may the donor revoke only half of it?
b: Yes.
