f: 160. Why may a donor revoke only part of a gift if he could revoke the whole?
b: Because the authority to revoke the whole necessarily includes authority to revoke a portion.

f: 161. May a donor revoke a gift given to a maḥram (an unmarriageable close relative)?
b: No.

f: 162. Which ḥadīth prohibits revoking gifts given to close unmarriageable relatives?
b: "When the gift is to a close unmarriageable relative, he does not revoke it."

f: 163. Why may gifts to close relatives not be revoked?
b: Because their purpose is maintaining family ties, and that objective has already been achieved.

f: 164. May one spouse revoke a gift given to the other spouse?
b: No.

f: 165. Why may gifts between spouses not be revoked?
b: Because their purpose is strengthening affection and marital bonds.

f: 166. At what point is the relationship between the donor and recipient considered when determining whether revocation is allowed?
b: At the time the gift contract is concluded.

f: 167. If a man gives a gift to a woman and later marries her, may he revoke the earlier gift?
b: Yes.

f: 168. Why may a donor revoke a gift given before marrying the recipient?
b: Because they were not spouses when the gift was made.

f: 169. If a husband gives a gift to his wife and later divorces her irrevocably, may he revoke the gift?
b: No.

f: 170. Why does an irrevocable divorce not restore the right to revoke a gift between spouses?
b: Because the marital relationship existed when the gift contract was concluded, and that is the relevant time for determining the ruling.

f: 171. What words from the recipient establish compensation that extinguishes the donor's right of revocation?
b: Statements such as "Take this as compensation for your gift," "as a replacement for it," or "in exchange for it."

f: 172. When does compensation offered by the recipient actually eliminate the donor's right to revoke the gift?
b: When the donor takes possession of the compensatory item.

f: 173. What is the ruling on revoking a gift given to a stranger according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: A donor may revoke a gift given to a stranger, although doing so is disliked.

f: 174. Why does the Ḥanafī school permit revocation of a gift to a stranger?
b: Because gifts are customarily given with the expectation of compensation or reciprocal goodwill, so if this purpose is absent the donor is granted the right to rescind the gift.

f: 175. Why does al-Shāfiʿī prohibit revocation of a gift?
b: Because of the ḥadīth stating that a giver should not take back his gift except a father regarding what he gives his child, and because revocation contradicts completed ownership.

f: 176. What ḥadīth do the Ḥanafīs cite to support revocation of a gift?
b: The ḥadīth: "The giver of a gift has more right to his gift so long as he has not been compensated for it."

f: 177. Why is revoking a gift considered disliked even though it is legally permitted?
b: Because of the Prophet's ﷺ comparison of one who returns to his gift to a dog returning to its vomit.

f: 178. Does receiving compensation for a gift prevent revocation?
b: Yes. Once the donor has received compensation, the right of revocation ends.

f: 179. Why does compensation prevent revocation of a gift?
b: Because the customary objective of the gift has been fulfilled through receiving compensation.

f: 180. Does a connected increase to the gifted property prevent revocation?
b: Yes. A connected increase prevents revocation.

f: 181. Why does a connected increase prevent revoking a gift?
b: Because the increase cannot practically be separated from the original gift, yet it was not included in the original contract.

f: 182. Does the death of either the donor or recipient prevent revocation of a gift?
b: Yes. The death of either party prevents revocation.

f: 183. Why does the recipient's death prevent revocation?
b: Because ownership has passed to the heirs, making the property no longer belong to the original recipient.

f: 184. Why does the donor's death prevent revocation?
b: Because the heir is a stranger to the original contract and did not make the gift.

f: 185. Does transferring ownership of the gifted property to someone else prevent revocation?
b: Yes. Once the recipient transfers ownership, the donor may no longer revoke the gift.

f: 186. Why does transferring ownership of the gifted item prevent revocation?
b: Because the transfer occurred with the donor's original authorization and new ownership has arisen through a separate legal cause.

f: 187. If the recipient plants trees or constructs permanent buildings on gifted land, may the donor revoke the gift?
b: No. Permanent improvements such as trees, houses, shops, or canals are treated as connected increases that prevent revocation.

f: 188. If improvements affect only part of gifted land, may the donor revoke the remainder?
b: Yes. Revocation remains possible regarding portions unaffected by the connected increase.

f: 189. If the recipient sells half of gifted land, may the donor revoke the remaining half?
b: Yes. The obstacle to revocation applies only to the portion that has been transferred.

f: 190. If the donor may revoke all of a gift, may he choose to revoke only half?
b: Yes. The right to revoke the whole includes the right to revoke part of it.

f: 191. May a donor revoke a gift made to a maḥram relative?
b: No. Gifts to close unmarriageable relatives cannot be revoked.

f: 192. Why are gifts to maḥram relatives irrevocable?
b: Because they are intended to maintain family ties, and that objective has already been achieved.

f: 193. May one spouse revoke a gift given to the other spouse?
b: No. Gifts exchanged between spouses are not revocable.

f: 194. Why are gifts between spouses irrevocable?
b: Because their purpose is to strengthen affection and marital bonds.

f: 195. If the donor marries the recipient after making the gift, does that prevent revocation?
b: No. Since the marital relationship did not exist when the gift was made, revocation remains possible.

f: 196. If spouses later divorce irrevocably, may the donor revoke a gift made during marriage?
b: No. The gift remains irrevocable because the relevant relationship existed when the gift was made.

f: 197. What wording from the recipient counts as offering compensation that removes the donor's right of revocation?
b: Statements such as "Take this as compensation," "as a replacement," or "in exchange for your gift," followed by the donor taking possession of it.

f: 198. Can a third party provide compensation that prevents revocation of a gift?
b: Yes. A stranger may voluntarily provide compensation, and once the donor accepts it, revocation is barred.

f: 199. Why is compensation from a third party valid?
b: Because compensation serves only to extinguish the donor's right of revocation, similar to compensation in khulʿ or settlement.

f: 200. If half of the gifted property is later found to belong to someone else, what happens to the compensation?
b: The donor returns half of the compensation because he did not transfer ownership of that half.

f: 201. If half of the compensation is discovered to belong to someone else, may the donor revoke the gift immediately?
b: No. He must first return the remaining compensation before revoking the gift.

f: 202. Why must the donor return the remaining compensation before revoking the gift when part of the compensation fails?
b: Because the remaining compensation was initially sufficient for the whole gift, but the donor only surrendered revocation expecting complete compensation.

f: 203. If the donor is compensated for only half of a gifted house, may he revoke the uncompensated half?
b: Yes. Revocation remains possible regarding the portion for which no compensation was received.

f: 204. How may a gift be validly revoked according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: Only by mutual agreement of both parties or by the judgment of a judge.

f: 205. Why is judicial judgment or mutual agreement required for revocation?
b: Because scholars differed over revocation and the right itself contains legal ambiguity, requiring formal resolution.

f: 206. If the recipient frees a gifted slave before judicial revocation, is the emancipation valid?
b: Yes. The emancipation is valid because ownership remained with the recipient until revocation occurred.

f: 207. If the gifted property dies while the recipient prevents the donor from taking it before judgment, is the recipient liable?
b: No, unless he prevented the donor after a valid demand for its return, in which case he becomes liable through transgression.

f: 208. After judicial revocation or mutual agreement, how is the revocation legally classified?
b: It is treated as a rescission of the contract from the beginning.

f: 209. Does the donor need to retake physical possession after judicial revocation?
b: No. Physical repossession is not required because the revocation operates as rescission.

f: 210. After judicial revocation, can the gift be revoked even if it is an undivided share?
b: Yes. Because the revocation is treated as rescinding the original contract.

f: 211. Why is revocation after judicial judgment treated differently from rescission for defects?
b: Because revocation exercises an original contractual right of rescission, whereas rescission for defects is based only upon lack of soundness.

f: 212. If the gifted property is taken by its true owner and the recipient must compensate that owner, may the recipient recover anything from the donor?
b: No. The recipient has no recourse against the donor.

f: 213. Why does the recipient have no recourse against the donor when the gifted property is claimed by its true owner?
b: Because a gift is a gratuitous contract and does not guarantee freedom from third-party claims.

f: 214. How is a gift made on condition of compensation classified before possession?
b: It is treated as a gift before possession.

f: 215. Before possession, does a gift conditioned upon compensation become invalid because of undivided ownership?
b: Yes. Before possession it follows the rules of gifts, including invalidity due to prohibited undivided ownership.

f: 216. How is a compensated gift treated after both parties take possession?
b: It takes the legal rulings of a sale.

f: 217. What legal consequences apply to a compensated gift after possession?
b: It may be rescinded for defects, the option of inspection applies, and pre-emption (shufʿah) is established.

f: 218. How did Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī classify a gift made on condition of compensation?
b: They regarded it as a sale from its beginning and its end because ownership is exchanged for compensation.

f: 219. Why do the Ḥanafīs classify a compensated gift as both a gift initially and a sale after possession?
b: Because it combines characteristics of both contracts, so each set of rulings is applied where appropriate.

f: 220. Why is a compensated gift not treated purely as a sale from the outset according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because its ownership is initially delayed until possession like a gift, while its binding nature arises after compensation like a sale.

f: 221. What is the ruling if someone gifts a female slave but excludes her unborn child (pregnancy) from the gift?
b: The gift of the slave is valid, but the exception of the pregnancy is invalid because a gift cannot operate upon the fetus, making the exception a corrupt condition. Corrupt conditions do not invalidate gifts.

f: 222. Why is the exception of a fetus from the gift of a pregnant slave invalid?
b: Because the fetus is considered an attribute rather than an independently transferable object of gift, so the contract cannot operate upon it. An exception is only valid where the contract itself could operate.

f: 223. Do corrupt conditions invalidate a gift contract?
b: No. Corrupt conditions are ignored in gifts, although they invalidate contracts such as sales, leases, and pledges.

f: 224. Which other contracts resemble gifts in not being invalidated by corrupt conditions?
b: Marriage, khulʿ (divorce settlement), and settlements concerning intentional homicide compensation are not invalidated by corrupt conditions.

f: 225. Which contracts are invalidated by corrupt conditions?
b: Sales, leases, and pledges are invalidated by corrupt conditions.

f: 226. What is the ruling if someone emancipates the unborn child of a slave and then gifts the pregnant slave?
b: The gift is valid because the fetus is no longer owned by the donor, so it is no longer excluded from the transfer.

f: 227. What is the ruling if someone makes the unborn child of a slave a mudabbar and then gifts the slave?
b: The gift is invalid because the fetus remains under the donor's ownership due to the tadbīr, preventing the gift from fully operating.

f: 228. Why does making the unborn child a mudabbar invalidate the gift of the pregnant slave?
b: Because the fetus remains owned by the donor, making the gift incomplete and resembling a gift of property still occupied by the donor's ownership.

f: 229. What is the ruling if someone gifts a slave on condition that the recipient later returns the slave?
b: The gift is valid, but the condition requiring the slave's return is invalid.

f: 230. What is the ruling if someone gifts a slave on condition that the recipient emancipates the slave?
b: The gift is valid, but the condition requiring emancipation is invalid.

f: 231. What is the ruling if someone gifts a slave on condition that the recipient makes her an umm walad?
b: The gift is valid, but the condition is invalid because it contradicts the nature of the gift contract.

f: 232. What is the ruling if someone gifts or gives charity of a house on condition that part of it be returned or compensated?
b: The gift or charity remains valid, while the condition is invalid.

f: 233. Why are these conditions attached to gifts considered invalid?
b: Because they contradict the requirements of complete transfer of ownership that a gift entails.

f: 234. Why do corrupt conditions invalidate sales but not gifts?
b: Because corrupt conditions resemble ribā, which affects contracts of exchange such as sales, whereas gifts are contracts of donation.

f: 235. How does the Prophet's ﷺ approval of the ʿumrā (lifetime gift) support the validity of gifts despite corrupt conditions?
b: The Prophet ﷺ approved the gift itself while invalidating the attached condition, showing that corrupt conditions do not invalidate gifts.

f: 236. What is the ruling if a creditor says to his debtor, "If tomorrow comes, the debt is yours," or "You are free from it"?
b: The conditional release is invalid because release from debt cannot be suspended upon a future condition.

f: 237. What is the ruling if a creditor says, "If you pay me half the debt, you are free from the remaining half"?
b: The condition is invalid because conditional release from debt is not legally effective.

f: 238. Why is conditional release (ibrāʾ) from debt invalid?
b: Because release from debt combines aspects of ownership transfer and relinquishment, and conditional future suspensions are only recognized in pure acts of relinquishment like divorce and emancipation.

f: 239. Why can release from debt be viewed as both ownership transfer and relinquishment?
b: A debt is considered wealth from one perspective and merely an obligation from another, giving ibrāʾ characteristics of both transfer and relinquishment.

f: 240. Does release from debt require acceptance by the debtor?
b: No. Since it functions as relinquishment, it does not depend upon acceptance, although it may be rejected.

f: 241. What is the ruling of an ʿumrā (lifetime gift)?
b: It is valid. The recipient owns it during his lifetime, and after his death it passes to his heirs. The condition that it return to the donor is invalid.

f: 242. Why does the condition requiring return after the recipient's death fail in an ʿumrā?
b: Because the gift transfers ownership immediately, while the condition contradicting that transfer is invalid.

f: 243. What is the ruling of a ruqbā according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله considers it valid, treating it like an ʿumrā in which the gift is valid and the condition is ignored.

f: 244. What is the ruling of a ruqbā according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: They consider it invalid because ownership is suspended upon an uncertain future event.

f: 245. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad invalidate the ruqbā?
b: Because it effectively says, "If I die before you, it becomes yours," making ownership contingent upon uncertainty, which invalidates the transfer.

f: 246. What does the term ruqbā literally refer to?
b: It comes from murāqabah ("watching"), meaning each party watches to see who dies first so ownership will pass accordingly.

f: 247. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what is the legal effect of an invalid ruqbā?
b: It is treated as a loan for use (ʿāriyah), since although ownership does not transfer, permission to benefit from the property remains.

f: 248. Is charity (ṣadaqah) valid before the recipient takes possession?
b: No. Charity is only valid after the recipient takes possession, just like a gift.

f: 249. Why does charity require possession to become valid?
b: Because it is a contract of donation, like a gift, and ownership is only completed through possession.

f: 250. Is a charitable donation of an undivided share in property that can be divided valid?
b: No. It is invalid because complete possession cannot occur without first dividing the property.

f: 251. Why is charity of an undivided share in divisible property invalid?
b: Because, like a gift, charity requires complete possession, which is impossible until the divisible property has been separated.

f: 252. Can the donor revoke a charitable donation after it has been completed?
b: No. Charity cannot be revoked once completed.

f: 253. Why is revocation not allowed in charity?
b: Because the intended objective of charity is earning reward from Allah, and that objective has already been achieved.

f: 254. Can charity given to a wealthy person be revoked?
b: No. According to juristic preference (istiḥsān), it cannot be revoked because the donor may still have intended the reward of giving charity.

f: 255. Why is charity to a wealthy person treated as irrevocable?
b: Because the donor may have intended spiritual reward rather than financial assistance, and that purpose has already been fulfilled.

f: 256. Can a gift given to a poor person be revoked?
b: No. According to the text, a gift to a poor person is treated like charity, since the donor's intended purpose is reward, which has already been achieved.

f: 257. Why is a gift to a poor person treated like charity regarding revocation?
b: Because the donor is presumed to seek reward from Allah, making the purpose identical to that of charity.

f: 258. If someone vows to give charity from his "wealth" (māl), what property must he give in charity?
b: He must give charity from the type of wealth upon which zakāt is obligatory.

f: 259. If someone vows to give charity from all his "property" (mamlūkāt), what must he give?
b: He is required to give charity from all of his property.

f: 260. Is there another narration regarding the distinction between vowing to give charity from one's wealth and from one's property?
b: Yes. Another narration states that both vows receive the same ruling, although the school distinguishes between them in the preferred narration.

f: 261. Where does the practical difference between the two narrations regarding vows of charity become apparent?
b: The difference appears in issues relating to judicial rulings.

f: 262. What advice is given to someone who vows to give away all of his property in charity?
b: He is told to keep enough to support himself and his family until he earns more wealth, then later give charity equal to what he temporarily retained for their maintenance.

f: 1. What is the definition of hiring (ijārah)?
b: Ijārah is a contract for obtaining benefits in exchange for compensation.

f: 2. What does the word "ijārah" mean linguistically?
b: Linguistically, ijārah means the sale of benefits.

f: 3. Why would analogy (qiyās) reject the validity of ijārah?
b: Because its subject matter is a future benefit that does not yet exist, and ownership normally cannot attach to something nonexistent.

f: 4. Why is ijārah nevertheless considered valid in Islamic law?
b: It is permitted because people need it, and its validity is established by the Sunnah.

f: 5. Which ḥadīth instructs employers to pay workers promptly?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Give the worker his wage before his sweat dries."

f: 6. Which ḥadīth requires employers to specify a worker's wage?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever hires a worker, let him inform him of his wage."

f: 7. How does an ijārah contract take effect over time?
b: It takes effect gradually as the contracted benefit comes into existence.

f: 8. Why is the leased property treated as the subject of the contract before the benefit exists?
b: It serves as a substitute for the future benefit so that offer and acceptance can validly attach to something present.

f: 9. When does ownership of the leased benefit actually arise?
b: Ownership arises as each portion of the benefit comes into existence.

f: 10. What two things must be known for an ijārah contract to be valid?
b: Both the benefit being leased and the wage must be known.

f: 11. Why must both the benefit and the wage be known in an ijārah contract?
b: Because uncertainty about either leads to disputes, just as uncertainty regarding the sold item or price invalidates a sale.

f: 12. What may be used as a wage in an ijārah contract?
b: Anything that is valid as a price in a sale is also valid as a wage.

f: 13. Why is the wage judged by the same standards as a sale price?
b: Because the wage is considered the price paid for the benefit.

f: 14. Can something that is not a valid sale price serve as a wage?
b: No. Anything unsuitable as a sale price is likewise unsuitable as a wage.

f: 15. How can benefits be made sufficiently known when leasing houses or farmland?
b: By specifying a known rental period.

f: 16. Why does specifying the rental period make the benefit sufficiently known?
b: Because the amount of benefit received during that known period becomes determinable.

f: 17. Is it permissible to lease property for either a long or short period?
b: Yes, as long as the period is known.

f: 18. Why are long-term leases of endowed (waqf) property restricted?
b: To prevent tenants from later claiming ownership of the endowed property.

f: 19. According to the preferred opinion, what length of lease is considered too long for waqf property?
b: A lease exceeding three years.

f: 20. How can benefits become known in contracts involving work, such as tailoring or dyeing?
b: By specifying the work to be performed and all relevant details, such as the garment, color, type of sewing, or amount of work.

f: 21. What details must be specified when hiring someone to dye a garment?
b: The garment, the color, and the amount of dye must be specified.

f: 22. What details must be specified when hiring someone to sew a garment?
b: The garment and the type of sewing must be specified.

f: 23. What details must be specified when hiring an animal to carry goods?
b: The amount and type of the load, together with the travel distance, must be specified.

f: 24. What details must be specified when hiring an animal for riding?
b: The distance to be traveled must be specified.

f: 25. How is the benefit determined when hiring someone to transport goods?
b: By specifying the goods being transported and the destination.

f: 26. What is an example of a contract in which the benefit is known through specification and indication?
b: Hiring someone to transport specified food to a specified destination.

f: 27. What is the difference between hiring a shared worker (ajīr mushtarak) and an exclusive worker (ajīr khāṣṣ)?
b: A shared worker is hired for a specified task or work, while an exclusive worker is hired for his time and service.

f: 28. What must be specified when hiring a shared worker (ajīr mushtarak)?
b: The work to be performed must be clearly specified.

f: 29. What must be specified when hiring an exclusive worker (ajīr khāṣṣ)?
b: The period of employment must be specified.

f: 30. Does the wage become due merely by concluding the ijārah contract?
b: No. The contract alone does not make the wage immediately due.

f: 31. What are the three ways in which a wage becomes due in an ijārah contract?
b: By stipulating immediate payment, by voluntarily making immediate payment, or by taking possession of the contracted benefit.

f: 32. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله school hold that the wage is not owed immediately upon contract?
b: Because the benefit arises gradually, and compensation should correspond to the gradual receipt of that benefit.

f: 33. Why did al-Shāfiʿī hold that the wage becomes owned immediately upon contract?
b: Because the future benefits are legally treated as existing for the purpose of validating the contract.

f: 34. Why does the gradual nature of benefits delay entitlement to the wage according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because exchange contracts require equality between what is given and what is received, so payment corresponds to the gradual receipt of benefits.

f: 35. When does ownership of the wage become fully established according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: As the benefit is actually received or enjoyed, since equality between benefit and payment has then been realized.

f: 36. Why does the wage become due if the parties stipulate immediate payment in an ijārah contract?
b: Because the party entitled to delay payment has voluntarily waived that right through the condition.

f: 37. Why does the wage become due if the tenant pays immediately without any stipulation?
b: Because he has voluntarily waived his right to delay payment.

f: 38. Why must a tenant pay rent after taking possession of a rented house even if he never lives in it?
b: Because possession of the house substitutes for delivery of the benefit, as it gives him the ability to use it.

f: 39. Why is taking possession of the leased property treated as delivery of the benefit?
b: Because the benefit itself cannot be physically delivered, so delivery of the property is treated as its legal substitute.

f: 40. What happens to the rent if a usurper seizes the rented house from the tenant?
b: The rent for the affected period is cancelled.

f: 41. Why does rent cease when the leased property is usurped?
b: Because the tenant loses the ability to benefit from the property, so legal delivery is lost and the contract is annulled for that period.

f: 42. What happens if the leased property is usurped during only part of the rental period?
b: Rent is cancelled only for the portion of the period during which the tenant was deprived of its use.

f: 43. Why is rent reduced proportionally when usurpation lasts for only part of the lease?
b: Because the annulment of the lease applies only to that part of the contract.

f: 44. When may a landlord demand rent from the tenant of a house?
b: The landlord may demand rent for each day of the tenancy.

f: 45. When may a landlord not demand daily rent from the tenant?
b: When the contract specifies a different payment date.

f: 46. Why does specifying a payment date prevent daily collection of rent?
b: Because the agreed date functions as a postponement of payment.

f: 47. Does the same rule regarding daily rent apply to leased farmland?
b: Yes. The same ruling applies to leasing land.

f: 48. When may the owner of a hired camel demand payment for its hire?
b: The owner may demand payment after each stage of the journey.

f: 49. Why may the owner of a hired camel demand payment after each stage?
b: Because each stage of the journey is considered an independently intended benefit.

f: 50. What was Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله earlier opinion regarding payment for hiring a riding animal?
b: The wage became due only after the entire journey or rental period was completed.

f: 51. Which jurist agreed with Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله earlier opinion regarding payment after the journey?
b: Zufar.

f: 52. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله originally delay payment until the journey was completed?
b: Because he viewed the contracted benefit as the entire journey rather than its individual stages.

f: 53. What is the basis of the later Ḥanafī opinion that payment becomes due gradually?
b: The benefit is received gradually, so payment should correspond to each portion of the benefit.

f: 54. Why did the jurists reject demanding payment every hour despite the benefit arising gradually?
b: Because requiring hourly payment would create unnecessary hardship and inconvenience.

f: 55. When does a washer become entitled to his wage?
b: Only after completing the work.

f: 56. When does a tailor become entitled to his wage?
b: Only after completing the work.

f: 57. Why do a washer and tailor earn no wage before completing the work?
b: Because partially completed work is not yet useful for its intended purpose.

f: 58. Does the same rule apply when the worker performs the work in the employer's house?
b: Yes. He earns no wage until the work is completed.

f: 59. When may a worker receive payment before completing the work?
b: If immediate payment was expressly stipulated in the contract.

f: 60. Why is a condition of immediate payment binding in an ijārah contract?
b: Because the parties agreed to it, making the condition enforceable.

f: 61. When does a baker hired to bake flour in the customer's house become entitled to his wage?
b: When the bread has been removed from the oven.

f: 62. Why is removing the bread from the oven considered completion of the baker's work?
b: Because the work is not complete until the bread is fully baked and taken out.

f: 63. What happens if the bread burns or is destroyed before it is removed from the oven?
b: The baker receives no wage because the work was destroyed before completion and delivery.

f: 64. Why does the baker receive no wage if the bread is destroyed before removal from the oven?
b: Because destruction occurred before delivery of the completed work.

f: 65. What happens if the bread burns after it has been removed from the oven without any fault by the baker?
b: The baker receives his wage.

f: 66. Why is the baker entitled to his wage if the bread burns after removal from the oven?
b: Because the completed work had already been delivered by placing it in the customer's house.

f: 67. Is the baker liable if the bread burns after delivery without negligence on his part according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No. It is considered a trust in his possession, so he bears no liability.

f: 68. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what is the baker's liability if the bread burns after removal but before actual delivery?
b: He must replace the equivalent amount of flour and receives no wage.

f: 69. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad hold the baker liable for the flour?
b: Because they regard the bread as remaining under his guarantee until actual delivery is completed.

f: 70. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what alternative does the customer have after the bread is destroyed?
b: He may accept the bread as delivered, hold the baker liable for the bread, and pay him the agreed wage.

f: 71. How is the compensation of a cook hired to prepare food for a wedding determined?
b: It is determined according to customary practice (ʿurf).

f: 72. Why is custom relied upon in determining the cook's compensation?
b: Because matters not specified in the contract are interpreted according to prevailing custom.

f: 73. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, when does a person hired to make bricks become entitled to his wage?
b: As soon as he sets up (forms) the bricks.

f: 74. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, when does a person hired to make bricks become entitled to his wage?
b: Only after he stacks the bricks.

f: 75. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad require a brickmaker to stack the bricks before earning his wage?
b: Because stacking completes the work, protects the bricks from being spoiled, and is customarily part of the worker's task.

f: 76. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله hold that a brickmaker earns his wage once the bricks are set up?
b: Because setting up the bricks completes the contracted work, while stacking is an additional task similar to transportation.

f: 77. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله compare stacking bricks to transporting them?
b: Because both are additional tasks performed after the contracted work has already been completed.

f: 78. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish brickmaking from baking bread when determining when the wage becomes due?
b: Because bricks can already be benefited from after being set up, whereas bread cannot be benefited from until it is removed from the oven.

f: 79. Why are bricks not considered complete before they are set up?
b: Because before being set up they are only scattered mud and cannot yet serve their intended purpose.

f: 80. Which craftsmen have the legal right to retain a customer's property until they receive their wage?
b: Craftsmen whose work leaves a lasting effect on the item, such as washers and dyers.

f: 81. Why do washers and dyers have the right to retain the customer's property until payment?
b: Because the contracted work creates an attribute in the item itself, giving them a right of retention similar to that of a seller.

f: 82. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, is a washer or dyer liable if the retained item is destroyed without negligence?
b: No. The item remains a trust in his possession because his retention of it is lawful.

f: 83. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does a washer or dyer receive a wage if the retained item is destroyed before delivery?
b: No. He receives no wage because the contracted work was destroyed before it could be delivered.

f: 84. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله deny the craftsman his wage if the retained item is destroyed before delivery?
b: Because the contracted work was never delivered to the customer.

f: 85. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, does a washer or dyer remain liable for the retained item if it is destroyed?
b: Yes. They consider the item to remain under his guarantee even while it is lawfully retained.

f: 86. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what options does the customer have if a retained item is destroyed while in the craftsman's possession?
b: The customer may claim its value without the work (and pay no wage), or claim its value including the work and pay the agreed wage.

f: 87. Which craftsmen do not have the right to retain the customer's property until payment?
b: Craftsmen whose work leaves no lasting effect on the item, such as porters and sailors.

f: 88. Why do porters and sailors not have the right to retain the customer's property until payment?
b: Because the contracted subject matter is the work itself rather than an attribute established in the item.

f: 89. Why is the person who returns a runaway slave allowed to retain the slave until receiving the reward?
b: Because returning the slave is treated as saving him from destruction, giving the rescuer a right of retention similar to that of a seller.

f: 90. Which jurists held that the finder of a runaway slave has the right to retain him until payment?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, and Muḥammad.

f: 91. What was Zufar's opinion regarding a craftsman's right to retain a customer's property until payment?
b: He held that no craftsman has a right of retention in either case.

f: 92. Why did Zufar deny craftsmen any right of retention?
b: Because he regarded delivery as complete once the item became connected with the owner's property, thereby ending the right of retention.

f: 93. How did the majority of the Ḥanafī jurists answer Zufar's argument against the right of retention?
b: They argued that merely connecting the item to the owner's property does not constitute accepted delivery, just as a buyer taking possession without the seller's consent does not remove the seller's rights.

f: 94. May a craftsman hire someone else to perform the work if the contract specifically requires him personally to do it?
b: No. He must perform the work himself.

f: 95. Why may a craftsman not delegate the work when the contract specifically requires his personal performance?
b: Because the contract makes his own performance the contracted subject matter.

f: 96. May a craftsman hire someone else to perform the work if the contract does not require his personal performance?
b: Yes. He may employ another person to perform it.

f: 97. Why may a craftsman delegate the work when the contract does not require his personal performance?
b: Because the obligation is a debt upon his liability that may be fulfilled either personally or through another person.

f: 98. If a person is hired to bring a specified number of family members from Basra, but some have died before his arrival, how much of the wage does he receive?
b: He receives the wage in proportion to the number of family members he successfully brings back.

f: 99. Why is a worker hired to bring family members from Basra paid only a proportional wage if some family members have died?
b: Because he completed only part of the contracted task.

f: 100. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does a messenger hired to deliver a letter and return with a reply receive any wage if the intended recipient dies before the letter can be delivered?
b: No. He receives no wage.

f: 101. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, does a messenger hired to deliver a letter and return with a reply receive any wage if the intended recipient dies before delivery?
b: No. He receives no wage.

f: 102. According to Muḥammad, what wage does a messenger receive if the intended recipient dies before the letter can be delivered?
b: He receives the wage for the outward journey to Basra.

f: 103. Why does Muḥammad award the messenger payment for the outward journey when the intended recipient has died?
b: Because he completed part of the contracted task by undertaking the journey, and the wage compensates the hardship of travel rather than merely carrying the letter.

f: 104. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why does a messenger hired to deliver a letter and bring back a reply receive no wage if the recipient dies before delivery?
b: Because the contracted matter is the delivery of the letter—or the knowledge obtained through it—and that purpose became impossible, so the wage falls away.

f: 105. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what is considered the contracted subject matter in hiring someone to deliver a letter and return with a reply?
b: The delivery of the letter, or the means to obtaining the information contained in it.

f: 106. According to all three Ḥanafī jurists, what happens if the messenger leaves the letter at its intended destination and then returns?
b: He is entitled to the wage for the journey by consensus.

f: 107. Why does a messenger receive the wage by consensus if he leaves the letter at its destination before returning?
b: Because he successfully completed the contracted task of delivering the letter.

f: 108. According to all three Ḥanafī jurists, does a person hired to carry food to someone receive a wage if the recipient dies before the food is delivered?
b: No. He receives no wage.

f: 109. Why does a person hired to deliver food receive no wage if the recipient dies before delivery?
b: Because the contracted subject matter—delivering the food—became impossible to complete.

f: 110. Why did Muḥammad distinguish between delivering a letter and delivering food?
b: Because he regarded the journey itself as the contracted subject matter in the letter case, whereas carrying and delivering the food remained the contracted subject matter in the food case.

f: 111. Is it permissible to rent a house or shop for residence without specifying the exact activities that will be carried out inside it?
b: Yes. The lease is valid because the customary use is residence.

f: 112. Why is it permissible to lease a house or shop without specifying every activity that will occur inside it?
b: Because residence is the customary use, and the benefit does not significantly vary.

f: 113. What activities are excluded from the unrestricted lease of a house or shop for residence?
b: Using it as a blacksmith's workshop, a washer's workplace, or a mill.

f: 114. Why may a tenant not use a rented house as a blacksmith's workshop, washer's workplace, or mill under an unrestricted residential lease?
b: Because these uses cause obvious harm by weakening the structure of the building.

f: 115. May a tenant generally use a rented house for any ordinary residential purpose if the lease is unrestricted?
b: Yes, except for uses that cause apparent structural harm.

f: 116. Is it permissible to lease land for agricultural purposes?
b: Yes. Agriculture is a recognized and intended benefit of land.

f: 117. Does a tenant leasing agricultural land automatically acquire rights to water access and pathways even if they are not mentioned in the contract?
b: Yes. These rights are included automatically.

f: 118. Why are water access and pathways included in an unrestricted lease of agricultural land?
b: Because the intended agricultural benefit cannot normally be obtained without them.

f: 119. Why are water rights and pathways automatically included in a lease but not necessarily in a sale?
b: Because leasing aims at immediate use and benefit, whereas sale aims at transferring ownership of the property itself.

f: 120. Must the type of crop be specified when leasing land for cultivation?
b: Yes, unless the landlord allows the tenant to plant whatever he wishes.

f: 121. Why must the type of crop normally be specified in an agricultural lease?
b: Because different crops place different demands on the land, and specification prevents future disputes.

f: 122. How can the parties avoid specifying a particular crop in an agricultural lease?
b: By agreeing that the tenant may plant whatever he wishes.

f: 123. Why does allowing the tenant to plant whatever he wishes remove the need to specify a crop?
b: Because giving the tenant complete choice removes the uncertainty that would otherwise lead to dispute.

f: 124. Is it permissible to lease vacant land for the purpose of constructing buildings or planting trees?
b: Yes. These are recognized benefits of land.

f: 125. What must a tenant do with buildings or trees when the lease of vacant land expires?
b: He must remove them and return the land vacant.

f: 126. Why must buildings and trees generally be removed when the lease ends?
b: Because they have no definite endpoint, and leaving them would harm the landowner's rights.

f: 127. Why are crops treated differently from buildings and trees when an agricultural lease expires?
b: Because crops have a known harvest time, making it possible to preserve the interests of both parties until harvest.

f: 128. What happens if the lease ends while crops are still growing and not yet ready for harvest?
b: The crops remain until harvest, and the tenant pays the equivalent rent for that period.

f: 129. May the owner of leased land acquire the tenant's buildings or trees instead of requiring their removal?
b: Yes, if he compensates the tenant for their value after removal and the owner of the buildings or trees agrees.

f: 130. Under what condition may the landowner take ownership of the tenant's buildings or trees by paying their value?
b: When the owner of the buildings or trees consents to that arrangement.

f: 131. What happens if removing the tenant's buildings or trees would damage the land itself?
b: The landowner may take ownership of them without the tenant's consent.

f: 132. May the landowner simply allow the buildings or trees to remain after the lease ends?
b: Yes. The building or trees remain the tenant's property while the land remains the landowner's property.

f: 133. Why may a landowner allow a tenant's buildings or trees to remain after the lease expires?
b: Because the right to demand vacant possession belongs to the landowner, and he may choose to waive that right.

f: 134. What happens if the lease of agricultural land ends while ruṭab (fresh palm shoots or similar crops without a fixed harvest time) remain in the land?
b: They must be removed.

f: 135. Why must ruṭab be removed when the lease of agricultural land expires?
b: Because they have no fixed endpoint and are therefore treated like trees rather than seasonal crops.

f: 136. Is it permissible to lease animals for riding or carrying loads?
b: Yes. Riding and carrying are recognized and customary benefits.

f: 137. If a lease for riding is unrestricted, may the tenant allow another person to ride the animal?
b: Yes, provided he has not already specified the rider through his own use or by allowing another specific person to ride it.

f: 138. Why may a tenant initially allow anyone to ride an animal when the riding lease is unrestricted?
b: Because the unrestricted wording gives him the authority to choose the rider.

f: 139. After the tenant rides a leased animal himself, may he allow someone else to ride it?
b: No. His own riding makes him the specifically intended rider.

f: 140. After the tenant allows one particular person to ride a leased animal, may he substitute another rider?
b: No. The first rider becomes specifically designated under the contract.

f: 141. Why does allowing one person to ride a leased animal prevent substituting another rider?
b: Because people differ in their riding abilities, making the first rider effectively specified.

f: 142. Does the same ruling apply to leasing a garment for wearing without specifying the wearer?
b: Yes. The tenant may initially choose the wearer, but once one person is designated, another may not replace him.

f: 143. Why are riding animals and wearing garments treated similarly regarding the identity of the user?
b: Because people differ in the way they ride animals and wear garments, which may affect the property.

f: 144. If the lease specifically states that a named person must ride the animal or wear the garment, may another person do so instead?
b: No. If another person uses it and it is destroyed, the tenant is liable.

f: 145. Why is the tenant liable if someone other than the specified person rides the animal or wears the garment?
b: Because the specified user was part of the agreement, and different users may cause different levels of wear or harm.

f: 146. What general rule applies to leased property whose use varies depending on the user?
b: The tenant must not substitute another user if the contract specifies one.

f: 147. If a house is leased for residence and the landlord specifies that one particular person should live there, may another person reside there instead?
b: Yes, provided the substitute does not cause greater structural harm.

f: 148. Why may another person reside in a leased house even if the contract names a specific resident?
b: Because ordinary residence does not materially differ between people in a way that benefits the restriction.

f: 149. What limitation remains when substituting another resident in a leased house?
b: The substitute may not use the property in a way that causes structural harm beyond ordinary residence.

f: 150. If an animal is leased to carry five qafīz of wheat, what other loads may the tenant carry?
b: He may carry goods that are equally or less harmful, such as barley or sesame.

f: 151. Why may barley or sesame replace wheat when carrying a specified load?
b: Because they are no more harmful than wheat and therefore fall within the granted permission.

f: 152. May a tenant carry salt or iron instead of wheat when an animal was leased to carry wheat?
b: No.

f: 153. Why may salt or iron not replace wheat when carrying a specified load?
b: Because they are more harmful to the animal than wheat and were not included in the owner's consent.

f: 154. If an animal is leased to carry a specified weight of cotton, may the tenant instead carry the same weight of iron?
b: No.

f: 155. Why may the tenant not substitute iron for cotton even if the weight is the same?
b: Because iron concentrates its weight in one place, whereas cotton spreads its weight, making iron more harmful to the animal.

f: 156. If an animal is leased for one rider but the tenant carries a second rider and the animal dies, how much is the tenant liable for?
b: Half of the animal's value.

f: 157. Why is the tenant liable for only half the animal's value when carrying an unauthorized second rider?
b: Because the destruction resulted partly from the permitted rider and partly from the unauthorized rider.

f: 158. Why is a rider's weight not considered when determining liability for carrying an unauthorized second rider?
b: Because harm depends on riding ability as well as weight, and people are not measured by weight alone.

f: 159. What factor determines liability when too many riders are placed on a leased animal?
b: The number of riders rather than their individual weights.

f: 160. If an animal is leased to carry a specified amount of wheat but the tenant carries more than the agreed amount, how is liability determined if the animal dies?
b: He is liable only for the additional weight beyond what was permitted.

f: 161. Why is liability limited to the additional weight when the tenant overloads a leased animal?
b: Because the destruction resulted from both permitted and unauthorized loading, so liability is apportioned accordingly.

f: 162. When does the tenant become liable for the entire value of an overloaded leased animal?
b: When the load is so excessive that such an animal could not normally bear it.

f: 163. Why does an extremely excessive load make the tenant liable for the entire value of the animal?
b: Because such loading falls completely outside the owner's permission and ordinary usage.

f: 164. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, is a tenant liable if he strikes or forcefully pulls a leased animal and it dies?
b: Yes.

f: 165. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, is a tenant liable if he drives a leased animal using customary methods and it dies?
b: No, provided his actions were customary.

f: 166. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad exempt the tenant from liability for customary driving of a leased animal?
b: Because customary methods are understood to be included within the owner's permission.

f: 167. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله hold the tenant liable for striking or forcefully pulling a leased animal?
b: Because permission is conditioned upon safe use, and such actions go beyond what is necessary.

f: 168. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what limits the tenant's permission to use a leased animal?
b: The permission is limited by the condition that the animal be used safely.

f: 169. If a person leases an animal to travel only as far as al-Ḥīrah but continues to al-Qādisiyyah before returning to al-Ḥīrah, and the animal later dies, is he liable?
b: Yes.

f: 170. Why is a tenant liable for taking a leased animal beyond the agreed destination even if he later returns it to that destination?
b: Because the lease ended upon reaching the agreed destination, and the unauthorized journey constituted a breach of the contract.

f: 171. In what case does returning to the agreed destination remove liability after exceeding it?
b: When the lease originally covered both the outward and return journeys, making it analogous to a depositary who returns to compliance after a violation.

f: 172. Why does a depositary escape liability by returning to compliance after violating the terms of the deposit, whereas a borrower or tenant does not?
b: Because preservation is the primary purpose of a deposit, so returning to compliance restores him as the owner's representative. In leasing and loans for use, preservation is only incidental to use, so liability is not removed merely by returning.

f: 173. According to the preferred Ḥanafī view, why does returning a leased or borrowed item after unauthorized use not remove liability?
b: Because the user's authority ended when the permitted use ended, so he is no longer acting as the owner's representative.

f: 174. If a person rents a donkey with a saddle and replaces it with another equivalent donkey saddle, is he liable?
b: No, provided the replacement saddle is equivalent.

f: 175. Why is a tenant not liable for replacing a rented donkey's saddle with an equivalent saddle?
b: Because the owner's permission is understood to include an equivalent replacement.

f: 176. When does replacing the saddle of a rented donkey make the tenant liable?
b: When the replacement saddle is heavier than the original, to the extent of the additional burden.

f: 177. Why is the tenant liable if the replacement saddle is heavier than the original?
b: Because the owner's permission does not extend to the additional weight.

f: 178. What happens if a tenant replaces the donkey's saddle with something that is not normally used as a donkey saddle?
b: He becomes liable.

f: 179. Why is the tenant liable for using equipment that is not normally used as a donkey saddle?
b: Because such use falls outside the owner's permission.

f: 180. What is the ruling if the tenant replaces the donkey's saddle with a pack saddle (ikāf) that is not normally used for donkeys?
b: He is liable.

f: 181. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if the tenant replaces the saddle with a pack saddle that is normally used for donkeys?
b: He is liable.

f: 182. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what is the ruling if the tenant replaces the saddle with a normal donkey pack saddle?
b: He is liable only according to the proportion of any additional burden caused.

f: 183. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad limit liability when a normal donkey pack saddle replaces a saddle?
b: Because both are customary equipment for donkeys, so only any additional weight exceeds the owner's permission.

f: 184. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله hold the tenant fully liable for replacing a saddle with a pack saddle?
b: Because a saddle is intended for riding while a pack saddle is intended for carrying loads, making them different types of use.

f: 185. What analogy does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use to explain liability for replacing a saddle with a pack saddle?
b: It is like carrying iron when permission was given only to carry wheat, since both involve a materially different use.

f: 186. If a porter is instructed to use a specific road but instead takes another commonly used road with no meaningful difference, is he liable if the goods perish?
b: No.

f: 187. Why is a porter not liable for taking a different commonly used road when there is no real difference between the routes?
b: Because the restriction has no practical benefit, so it is not legally significant.

f: 188. If a porter successfully delivers the goods after using a different but equivalent public road, is he entitled to his wage?
b: Yes.

f: 189. When does a porter become liable for using a road different from the one specified in the contract?
b: When the alternative road differs in a way that makes the original restriction meaningful.

f: 190. Why does using a materially different road make the porter liable?
b: Because he violated a beneficial contractual restriction.

f: 191. What is the ruling if the porter uses a road that people do not normally travel and the goods are destroyed?
b: He is liable.

f: 192. Why is the porter liable for using an uncommon road?
b: Because he acted contrary to the agreed restriction by taking a route outside ordinary usage.

f: 193. If the porter successfully delivers the goods after taking an unauthorized route, does he still receive his wage?
b: Yes.

f: 194. Why does the porter still receive his wage after successfully delivering the goods despite using an unauthorized route?
b: Because the intended purpose of the contract was ultimately achieved, making the disagreement only formal rather than substantive.

f: 195. What is the ruling if a carrier transports goods by sea when that type of cargo is normally transported by land?
b: He is liable if the goods are destroyed.

f: 196. Why does transporting goods by sea instead of land make the carrier liable?
b: Because the difference between sea and land transport is substantial and falls outside the owner's permission.

f: 197. If the carrier successfully delivers the goods after transporting them by sea instead of land, is he entitled to his wage?
b: Yes.

f: 198. Why does a carrier still earn his wage after successfully delivering goods by an unauthorized mode of transport?
b: Because the intended purpose of the contract—delivery—has been fulfilled.

f: 199. What happens if a tenant leases land to grow wheat but instead plants ruṭbah (fresh vegetation)?
b: He is liable for any decrease in the value of the land caused by the different crop.

f: 200. Why is planting ruṭbah instead of wheat considered a breach of the lease?
b: Because ruṭbah harms the land more through deeper roots and greater water requirements.

f: 201. Does a tenant who plants ruṭbah instead of the agreed wheat receive the agreed rent or wage?
b: No.

f: 202. Why does the tenant receive no wage or rental entitlement after planting ruṭbah instead of wheat?
b: Because he is treated as having wrongfully occupied (usurped) the land by exceeding the agreed use.

f: 203. If a tailor is hired to sew a garment into a shirt but instead makes it into a cloak, what options does the customer have?
b: He may either claim the value of the garment or accept the cloak and pay the tailor the reasonable value of his work, not exceeding the agreed wage.

f: 204. If the customer accepts the cloak made instead of the agreed shirt, how much must he pay the tailor?
b: The value of the tailor's work, not exceeding the agreed wage of one dirham.

f: 205. Why may the customer recover the value of the garment when the tailor makes a cloak instead of a shirt?
b: Because the tailor acted contrary to the contract by producing something different from what was agreed.

f: 206. Why did some jurists interpret the cloak (qabāʾ) mentioned in this case as a qurṭuf?
b: Because a qurṭuf is used similarly to a shirt and therefore is closer to the agreed work.

f: 207. What is the broader opinion regarding the tailor who sews a cloak instead of a shirt?
b: The ruling applies generally because the shirt and cloak are sufficiently similar in their intended benefit.

f: 208. According to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if a tailor is instructed to make a shirt but instead makes a cloak?
b: The tailor is liable for the garment without giving the customer a choice, because the cloak is considered a different type of garment.

f: 209. According to the apparent (ẓāhir al-riwāyah) Ḥanafī view, what options does the customer have if a tailor makes a cloak instead of the agreed shirt?
b: The customer may either hold the tailor liable for the garment or accept the cloak and pay the equivalent wage, not exceeding the agreed wage.

f: 210. Why does the apparent Ḥanafī view give the customer a choice when a tailor makes a cloak instead of a shirt?
b: Because the cloak resembles the shirt in some respects but differs in others, so both agreement and disagreement exist.

f: 211. In what way does a cloak resemble a shirt according to the apparent Ḥanafī view?
b: It serves a similar basic purpose of clothing and is worn in a comparable manner.

f: 212. In what way does a cloak differ from a shirt according to the apparent Ḥanafī view?
b: A cloak is fastened around the waist, unlike a shirt, making it different from what was agreed.

f: 213. If the customer accepts the cloak instead of the agreed shirt, how much is the tailor entitled to receive?
b: The equivalent wage for the work, not exceeding the agreed one dirham.

f: 214. Why is the tailor entitled only to the equivalent wage when the customer accepts the altered garment?
b: Because the agreement was only partially fulfilled, making the contractual basis weaker.

f: 215. Why may the equivalent wage not exceed the originally agreed wage in this case?
b: Because this is the rule governing compensation in invalid leases.

f: 216. If a tailor is instructed to make a cloak but instead makes trousers, what is one reported opinion?
b: The tailor is fully liable without giving the customer a choice because the benefit differs significantly.

f: 217. What is the preferred Ḥanafī opinion if a tailor makes trousers instead of the agreed cloak?
b: The customer has a choice because both garments share the same fundamental benefit.

f: 218. Why does the preferred opinion give the customer a choice when trousers are made instead of a cloak?
b: Because both garments provide the basic benefit of clothing despite their differences.

f: 219. What analogy is used to support giving the customer a choice when a tailor makes trousers instead of a cloak?
b: It is compared to a craftsman who is told to make a brass basin but instead makes a brass cup.

f: 220. Why does making a brass cup instead of a brass basin support giving the customer a choice?
b: Because both objects share the same fundamental material and general utility despite differing in form.

f: 221. What is the general rule regarding invalid conditions in a lease contract?
b: Invalid conditions corrupt the lease just as they corrupt a sale.

f: 222. Why do invalid conditions invalidate a lease according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because leasing is analogous to sale, both being contracts that can be concluded and rescinded.

f: 223. What compensation is due under an invalid lease according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: The equivalent market wage, provided it does not exceed the agreed amount.

f: 224. According to Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī, how is compensation determined in an invalid lease?
b: The full equivalent market wage is due, even if it exceeds the agreed amount.

f: 225. Why do the Ḥanafīs cap the equivalent wage at the amount originally agreed in an invalid lease?
b: Because the parties voluntarily agreed not to exceed that amount, thereby waiving any excess.

f: 226. Why is the specified amount not increased even if the equivalent wage is lower in an invalid lease?
b: Because the contractual specification itself is invalid and cannot control the amount owed.

f: 227. Why do the Ḥanafīs distinguish invalid leases from invalid sales regarding compensation?
b: Because physical property has intrinsic value, whereas benefits derive their value only through contract.

f: 228. If a house is leased for "one dirham every month" without specifying the total number of months, how much of the lease is valid?
b: Only the first month is valid.

f: 229. Why is only the first month valid when a lease states "one dirham every month" without specifying an ending date?
b: Because the wording cannot legally extend indefinitely, so it is interpreted as referring to one month only.

f: 230. After the valid first month ends in such a lease, what rights do the parties have?
b: Either party may terminate the lease because the valid contract has ended.

f: 231. How can a lease stating "one dirham every month" become fully valid?
b: By specifying a definite number of months.

f: 232. Why does specifying the total number of months validate the lease?
b: Because the lease period becomes known and free from uncertainty.

f: 233. If the tenant remains in the house for one hour at the beginning of the second month, what happens according to the analogy mentioned in al-Hidāyah?
b: The lease becomes valid for the entire second month.

f: 234. Why does remaining in the house at the start of the second month validate the lease for that month according to analogy?
b: Because the parties' conduct demonstrates mutual agreement to continue the lease.

f: 235. According to the apparent narration, how long does each party retain the option to terminate at the beginning of the second month?
b: During the first day and night of the second month.

f: 236. Why does the apparent narration allow an option during the beginning of the second month?
b: Because treating the lease as automatically renewed immediately would impose unnecessary hardship.

f: 237. Is it valid to lease a house for one year for a total of ten dirhams without specifying each month's share of the rent?
b: Yes.

f: 238. Why is a yearly lease valid without allocating a specific amount of rent to each month?
b: Because the total lease period is known, making monthly allocation unnecessary.

f: 239. What comparison is used to justify not dividing the rent month by month in a yearly lease?
b: It is compared to leasing for one month without specifying the rent attributable to each individual day.

f: 240. If the lease contract specifies a commencement date, when does the lease period begin?
b: It begins from the specified date.

f: 241. If no commencement date is specified in the lease contract, when does the lease period begin?
b: It begins from the time the lease contract is concluded.

f: 242. Why are corrupt conditions treated the same in leasing as in sales?
b: Because leasing, like sale, is a bilateral contract that can be concluded and invalidated, so corrupt conditions invalidate it.

f: 243. In an invalid lease, what amount of rent is owed?
b: The equivalent market wage (ujrat al-mithl), but it cannot exceed the amount originally specified in the contract.

f: 244. Why is the equivalent wage in an invalid lease limited to the agreed amount?
b: Because the parties voluntarily accepted that amount and thereby waived any claim to a higher payment.

f: 245. Why is an invalid lease treated differently from an invalid sale regarding compensation?
b: Benefits only acquire value through contract, whereas physical property has intrinsic value, so different rules apply.

f: 246. If a house is rented for "one dirham every month" without specifying how many months, what is the ruling?
b: The lease is valid only for the first month and invalid for any additional months.

f: 247. Why is such a lease valid for only one month?
b: Because the phrase "every month" without a fixed endpoint is interpreted as referring to a single month.

f: 248. Can either party terminate the lease after the first valid month ends?
b: Yes, because the original valid lease has expired.

f: 249. When is a lease for "one dirham every month" fully valid?
b: When a definite number of months is specified.

f: 250. If the tenant remains in the house for one hour at the beginning of the second month, what happens?
b: The lease for the second month becomes valid by mutual agreement.

f: 251. According to the apparent narration, how long does the option to terminate remain at the start of the second month?
b: During the first night and day of the second month.

f: 252. Is it valid to rent a house for one year for ten dirhams without assigning a monthly rent?
b: Yes, because the total rental period is clearly known.

f: 253. From what point does a lease period begin if no starting date is specified?
b: From the time the lease contract is concluded.

f: 254. If a yearly lease begins on the first day of a lunar month, how are the months calculated?
b: All months are counted as lunar months.

f: 255. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, how are the months calculated if the lease begins in the middle of a lunar month?
b: Every month of the year is counted by the number of days.

f: 256. According to Muḥammad and one narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, how is a lease beginning mid-month calculated?
b: The first month is counted by days, while the remaining months follow the lunar calendar.

f: 257. Why did Muḥammad distinguish between the first month and the remaining months?
b: Because counting by days is only necessary for the incomplete first month.

f: 258. What analogy supports Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله method of counting every month by days?
b: The rules governing the waiting period (ʿiddah).

f: 259. Is it permissible to charge admission to a public bathhouse (ḥammām)?
b: Yes, because long-standing Muslim custom establishes the validity of the contract despite uncertainty about the exact amount of benefit used.

f: 260. Why is charging for the use of a bathhouse permitted despite uncertainty?
b: Because widespread customary practice (ʿurf) removes the legal effect of that uncertainty.

f: 261. Is it permissible to charge for cupping (ḥijāmah)?
b: Yes, because the Prophet ﷺ paid a cupper, and it is a known service performed for a known wage.

f: 262. Is it permissible to charge a fee for the stud service of a male animal?
b: No, because the Prophet ﷺ prohibited taking payment for stud services.

f: 263. According to the Ḥanafī school, what general principle governs payment for acts of worship?
b: A Muslim may not be hired for acts of worship that are specifically religious duties.

f: 264. Which religious services are classically not subject to hiring according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Adhān, pilgrimage, leading prayer, teaching the Qur'an, and teaching fiqh.

f: 265. Why did the Ḥanafīs prohibit payment for these religious acts?
b: Because acts of worship are attributed to the performer himself and cannot be undertaken on behalf of another for compensation.

f: 266. Why did later Ḥanafī scholars permit payment for teaching the Qur'an?
b: Because religious commitment declined, and allowing payment became necessary to preserve Qur'anic education.

f: 267. Is it permissible to hire someone for singing or professional mourning?
b: No, because they are considered acts of disobedience or impermissible entertainment.

f: 268. What principle explains why impermissible entertainment cannot be hired for?
b: Contracts cannot lawfully establish compensation for sinful acts.

f: 269. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, may an undivided share (mushāʿ) be leased?
b: Only if it is leased to the co-owner (partner).

f: 270. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may an undivided share be leased to others?
b: Yes, they considered leasing an undivided share generally permissible.

f: 271. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad permit leasing an undivided share?
b: Because an undivided share has a usable benefit, delivery is possible through access or division of use, and equivalent rent can be determined.

f: 272. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, why is leasing an undivided share (mushāʿ) to someone other than a co-owner invalid?
b: Because the lessor cannot independently deliver possession of an undivided share, and the ability to deliver the leased benefit is a condition for a valid lease.

f: 273. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject takhliyyah (making available) as sufficient delivery for an undivided share?
b: Because merely making an undivided share available does not enable the lessee to independently benefit from it.

f: 274. Why is tahāyuʾ (division of use) not sufficient to validate leasing an undivided share according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because tahāyuʾ is a legal consequence that arises after the contract through ownership, whereas the ability to deliver must already exist before the contract is valid.

f: 275. Why is the lease of an undivided share to a co-owner valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because the entire property already exists under the co-owner's ownership, so no problematic division of delivery occurs.

f: 276. According to one narration from al-Ḥasan, what was Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله view regarding leasing an undivided share even to a co-owner?
b: He held that it is not valid even when leased to a co-owner.

f: 277. Why does newly arising shared ownership after a lease not invalidate the contract according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because the ability to deliver is only a condition for the formation of the contract, not for its continuation.

f: 278. Why is leasing an entire property jointly to two tenants valid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because delivery occurs collectively to both tenants first, and only afterward does their separate ownership produce division.

f: 279. What Qur'anic verse is used to establish the permissibility of hiring a wet nurse?
b: Allah says: "If they breastfeed for you, then give them their payment." (al-Ṭalāq 65:6).

f: 280. Besides the Qur'an, what evidence supports the permissibility of hiring a wet nurse?
b: It was a well-known practice before and during the Prophet's ﷺ time, and he approved of it.

f: 281. According to the first opinion, what is the subject matter of the contract when hiring a wet nurse?
b: Her services in caring for and nursing the child, while the milk is considered secondary.

f: 282. According to the second opinion, what is the subject matter of the wet-nursing contract?
b: The milk itself is the primary subject, while the service is secondary.

f: 283. According to the second opinion, what is the ruling if a wet nurse feeds the child sheep's milk instead of her own?
b: She does not deserve the agreed wage.

f: 284. Which interpretation of the wet-nursing contract does the author consider stronger?
b: That the contract concerns her services, while the milk is only secondary.

f: 285. Why is the view that the contract concerns service considered stronger?
b: Because ijārah is not normally concluded for the destruction or consumption of physical objects as its primary subject matter.

f: 286. What example illustrates that leasing cannot primarily concern consumable physical items?
b: Hiring a cow solely in order to consume its milk is not a valid lease.

f: 287. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, may the wage of a wet nurse consist only of food and clothing?
b: Yes, by way of juristic preference (istiḥsān).

f: 288. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad reject food and clothing alone as a wet nurse's wage?
b: Because the wage would be uncertain (majhūl).

f: 289. What analogy did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use to show that an uncertain wage is invalid?
b: They compared it to hiring someone for baking or cooking with an unspecified wage.

f: 290. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله permit food and clothing as the wet nurse's wage despite the uncertainty?
b: Because customary generosity toward wet nurses prevents disputes over the amount provided.

f: 291. What commercial analogy did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use to support allowing food and clothing as wages?
b: The sale of a qafīz from a heap of grain.

f: 292. Why does the uncertainty in a wet nurse's maintenance not invalidate the contract according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because custom removes the likelihood of dispute.

f: 293. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish wet nursing from baking and cooking contracts?
b: Because uncertainty in baking and cooking commonly causes disputes, unlike maintenance for wet nurses.

f: 294. According to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, how can the food portion of a wet nurse's wage be made valid by consensus?
b: By specifying its value in dirhams and then providing food in place of those dirhams.

f: 295. Besides specifying food by its value, what other method also makes the food wage valid?
b: Specifying the exact quantity of food.

f: 296. Why is specifying the quantity of food sufficient?
b: Because the description removes uncertainty just as price specifications do.

f: 297. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what additional condition is required for the wage besides specifying the food?
b: The place where payment will be made must also be specified.

f: 298. Did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad require specifying the place of payment for the food wage?
b: No, they did not.

f: 299. What three characteristics of clothing must be specified when clothing forms part of the wet nurse's wage?
b: Its type, its amount, and the time period for which it is provided.

f: 300. Why must the clothing be tied to a specified period?
b: Because clothing only becomes a debt on liability when it resembles a deferred sale, as in salam.

f: 301. According to the author, why is a time period necessary for clothing but not necessarily for food?
b: Because clothing becomes an enforceable liability only when deferred like a salam contract.

f: 302. May the employer prevent the wet nurse's husband from having marital relations with her?
b: No.

f: 303. Why may the employer not prevent the husband from having intercourse with his wife?
b: Because intercourse is the husband's established legal right, and the employer has no authority to remove it.

f: 304. If a husband did not know that his wife had been hired as a wet nurse, does he have the right to cancel the lease?
b: Yes. He may cancel the lease in order to protect his marital rights.

f: 305. May the tenant prevent the wet nurse's husband from having intercourse with her inside the rented house?
b: Yes. The tenant may prevent intercourse inside the house because the house is his contractual right.

f: 306. If a wet nurse becomes pregnant during the lease, when may the parties terminate the contract?
b: They may terminate the contract if they fear that her pregnancy will harm the nursing child through her milk.

f: 307. Why does a wet nurse's pregnancy give the parties the option to terminate the lease?
b: Because the milk of a pregnant woman was considered harmful to the nursing child.

f: 308. Besides pregnancy, what other event allows the parties to terminate a wet-nursing contract?
b: The wet nurse becoming ill.

f: 309. In a wet-nursing contract, who is responsible for preparing the child's food?
b: The wet nurse is responsible for preparing the child's food.

f: 310. Why is the wet nurse responsible for preparing the child's food?
b: Because preparing the child's food is part of her customary duties under the contract.

f: 311. What legal principle determines the duties of a wet nurse when there is no explicit textual ruling?
b: Custom (ʿurf) determines the parties' responsibilities.

f: 312. According to customary practice, what childcare tasks are the wet nurse expected to perform?
b: She is expected to wash the child's clothes, prepare the child's food, and perform similar customary childcare duties.

f: 313. In a wet-nursing contract, who must provide the child's food itself?
b: The child's father is responsible for providing the food.

f: 314. According to Imām Muḥammad, who must provide the child's oil and perfume?
b: The wet nurse must provide them.

f: 315. Why did Imām Muḥammad assign the cost of the child's oil and perfume to the wet nurse?
b: Because that was the customary practice among the people of Kūfah.

f: 316. If a wet nurse feeds the child sheep's milk instead of breastfeeding him herself, is she entitled to her wage?
b: No. She is not entitled to the wage.

f: 317. Why does a wet nurse lose her wage if she feeds the child sheep's milk instead of breastfeeding him?
b: Because she did not perform the contracted service, which was breastfeeding with her own milk.

f: 318. Why is feeding a child sheep's milk not considered fulfillment of a wet-nursing contract?
b: Because feeding is different from breastfeeding, and the contract specifically required breastfeeding.

f: 319. What is the ruling if someone gives yarn to a weaver to weave in exchange for half of the finished cloth?
b: The lease is invalid, and the weaver is entitled only to the equivalent market wage.

f: 320. What is the ruling if someone rents a donkey to carry food in exchange for one qafīz of that same food?
b: The lease is invalid.
