f: 41. Why is the existence of a sale sufficient for the shafīʿ (person claiming shufʿah) to exercise his right?
b: Because the sale shows the seller's desire to leave ownership, allowing the connected person to replace the buyer.

f: 42. If the seller admits that he sold the property but the buyer denies it, can the shafīʿ still claim shufʿah?
b: Yes, because the sale is established against the seller, and that is sufficient for the shafīʿ.

f: 43. When does the right of shufʿah become firmly established according to al-Hidāyah?
b: It becomes established through witnessing the claim and making the immediate request (ṭalab al-muwāthabah).

f: 44. Why must the shafīʿ immediately request shufʿah after learning of the sale?
b: Because shufʿah is a weak right that is cancelled by showing abandonment, so immediate action proves that he still wants the property.

f: 45. What is meant by ṭalab al-muwāthabah (the immediate request for shufʿah)?
b: It means requesting shufʿah immediately when the person learns of the sale.

f: 46. What happens if the shafīʿ learns about the sale but does not request shufʿah immediately?
b: His right of shufʿah is cancelled according to the Hanafi school.

f: 47. What evidence is mentioned for requiring immediate request of shufʿah?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Shufʿah belongs to the one who immediately claims it."

f: 48. If the shafīʿ receives a letter informing him of the sale and reads it completely before requesting shufʿah, what happens?
b: According to the majority of scholars, his shufʿah is cancelled because he delayed after learning of the sale.

f: 49. What is the alternative view of Muḥammad regarding reading a letter informing about the sale?
b: He held that the shafīʿ has the duration of the sitting in which he learns of the sale to decide.

f: 50. Which view regarding the time allowed after receiving news of the sale did al-Karkhī prefer?
b: He preferred the view that the shafīʿ has the same sitting in which he receives the information to decide.

f: 51. If a shafīʿ says "al-ḥamdulillāh" after hearing about the sale, does he lose his shufʿah?
b: No. It does not indicate abandonment; it may express relief from harm or another meaning.

f: 52. If a shafīʿ says "lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh" after hearing about the sale, does he lose his shufʿah?
b: No. It does not indicate that he abandoned his right.

f: 53. If a shafīʿ says "subḥān Allāh" after hearing about the sale, does he lose his shufʿah?
b: No. It can express surprise and does not indicate abandonment.

f: 54. If a shafīʿ asks "Who bought it and for how much was it sold?" does this cancel his shufʿah?
b: No. This may indicate that he is considering purchasing it depending on the price.

f: 55. What wording is sufficient to claim shufʿah?
b: Any wording that clearly indicates the desire to claim it, such as "I request shufʿah" or "I am claiming my shufʿah."

f: 56. Is witnessing required for the immediate request (ṭalab al-muwāthabah)?
b: The witnessing itself is not required; it is mainly used to prevent denial later.

f: 57. Why does the shafīʿ need witnesses after making the immediate request?
b: Because he needs evidence before the judge proving that he claimed his right.

f: 58. What are the three types of requests involved in shufʿah?
b: 1. Immediate request (ṭalab al-muwāthabah), 2. Confirmation request with witnesses, 3. Request for litigation and taking ownership.

f: 59. What is the second stage of requesting shufʿah?
b: The shafīʿ confirms his claim by taking witnesses after the initial immediate request.

f: 60. After making the immediate request, what should the shafīʿ do to establish his claim?
b: He should leave the gathering and take witnesses confirming his demand.

f: 61. Against whom should the shafīʿ take witnesses if the seller still possesses the property?
b: He should take witnesses against the seller because the seller still has possession.

f: 62. Against whom should the shafīʿ take witnesses if the buyer has possession?
b: He should take witnesses against the buyer because the buyer now owns the property.

f: 63. Why can witnesses be taken at the property itself for shufʿah?
b: Because the right is connected to the property itself.

f: 64. If the seller delivers the property to the buyer, can the shafīʿ still use the seller as a party in the claim?
b: No, because the seller no longer has possession or ownership and is no longer considered a disputing party.

f: 65. What is an example statement used for the confirmation request of shufʿah?
b: "So-and-so purchased this house, and I am the person entitled to shufʿah. I previously requested it and I request it now, so bear witness to this."

f: 66. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, must the shafīʿ specify the exact property when claiming shufʿah?
b: Yes, because a claim cannot be valid unless the subject of the claim is known.

f: 67. Does delaying the litigation after establishing shufʿah cancel the right according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and one narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, delay does not cancel it.

f: 68. According to Muḥammad, how long may the shafīʿ delay after witnessing his claim before losing shufʿah?
b: If he delays for one month without excuse, his shufʿah is cancelled.

f: 69. According to Zufar, what is the ruling on delaying litigation after witnessing the claim?
b: The shufʿah is cancelled if he delays without excuse.

f: 70. According to one narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, when does delaying litigation cancel shufʿah?
b: If the shafīʿ allows a full court session to pass without filing his claim, his shufʿah is cancelled.

f: 71. Why does Muḥammad say delay cancels shufʿah after one month?
b: Because otherwise the buyer suffers harm by being unable to freely dispose of the property due to fear of the shafīʿ reclaiming it later.

f: 72. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not cancel shufʿah through delay after it is established?
b: Because an established right is only removed by explicit relinquishment, not merely by silence or delay.

f: 73. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله respond to the concern that delay harms the buyer?
b: The same harm exists if the shafīʿ is absent, yet his right remains, so delay alone cannot cancel it.

f: 74. If the shafīʿ delays because there is no judge available in the area, does his shufʿah expire?
b: No. The lack of access to a judge is considered a valid excuse.

f: 75. Does being absent from the area automatically cancel a person's shufʿah?
b: No. Absence does not remove the right because the person may still be unable to litigate.

f: 76. When a person claims shufʿah (pre-emption) before the judge, what does the judge ask the defendant?
b: The judge asks the defendant. If he acknowledges the claimant's ownership of the property that gives him the right of shufʿah, the claim proceeds; otherwise, the claimant must provide evidence.

f: 77. Why is possession (yad) alone insufficient to establish the right of shufʿah?
b: Because possession is an indication that can have multiple possibilities, so it does not prove ownership or entitlement by itself.

f: 78. What does the judge ask the claimant before hearing the defendant in a shufʿah case?
b: The judge asks about the location and boundaries of the property, because the claimant is asserting a right connected to a specific property.

f: 79. Why does the judge ask the claimant the reason for his shufʿah claim?
b: Because the causes of shufʿah differ, such as ownership of the adjoining property, partnership in the property, or partnership in its rights.

f: 80. If someone claims shufʿah because he owns an adjoining property, what must he establish?
b: He must establish his ownership of the adjoining property that gives him the right of shufʿah.

f: 81. If the claimant cannot provide evidence of his ownership, what oath does the purchaser take?
b: The purchaser swears that he does not know the claimant to be the owner of the property through which he claims shufʿah.

f: 82. Why does the purchaser swear an oath based on knowledge in the first stage of the shufʿah dispute?
b: Because the claim concerns something established through the purchaser's possession, so the oath relates to what he knows.

f: 83. What happens if the purchaser refuses to swear the oath or the claimant produces evidence?
b: The claimant's ownership of the property giving him shufʿah and his right of adjacency are established.

f: 84. After the claimant proves his right of shufʿah, what does the judge ask the purchaser?
b: The judge asks whether he purchased the property or not.

f: 85. If the purchaser denies buying the property, what must the claimant do?
b: The claimant must provide evidence of the sale because shufʿah only becomes obligatory after the sale is established.

f: 86. If the claimant cannot prove the sale, what oath does the purchaser take?
b: The purchaser swears that he did not purchase the property or that the claimant does not have a right of shufʿah against him from the stated reason.

f: 87. Why does the purchaser swear this second oath on certainty (not knowledge)?
b: Because it concerns his own action (the purchase) and matters directly connected to his own conduct.

f: 88. Is the claimant allowed to litigate for shufʿah without bringing the purchase money to court?
b: Yes, according to the apparent narration of the school.

f: 89. What is the view of Muḥammad regarding bringing the purchase money before judgment in shufʿah?
b: Muḥammad holds that the judge should not rule until the claimant brings the money, because otherwise the purchaser's wealth may be lost if the claimant cannot pay.

f: 90. Why does the apparent Hanafi position allow litigation before bringing the money?
b: Because the claimant does not owe the price until judgment is issued, so bringing it beforehand is not required.

f: 91. After the judge rules in favor of the claimant's shufʿah, when must the claimant bring the purchase price?
b: He must bring it after the judgment.

f: 92. Can the purchaser keep the property until receiving the price after shufʿah judgment?
b: Yes, the purchaser has the right to retain it until he receives the payment.

f: 93. Does delaying payment after a shufʿah judgment cancel the claimant's right?
b: No, because his shufʿah became confirmed through the court dispute.

f: 94. If the seller still possesses the property, can the claimant bring him to court for shufʿah?
b: Yes, because the seller still has possession, which is a legally relevant connection.

f: 95. Why must the purchaser be present before the judge accepts evidence and rules against him?
b: Because the judge will invalidate the sale in his presence and issue the shufʿah ruling against him.

f: 96. Why is the seller no longer considered a party if the purchaser already received possession?
b: Because the seller no longer has ownership or possession, making him like a stranger to the dispute.

f: 97. If someone buys a property on behalf of another person, who is the defendant in a shufʿah claim?
b: The buyer (the agent) is the defendant because he is the person who made the contract.

f: 98. Why is the agent the one confronted in a shufʿah claim?
b: Because shufʿah is connected to the rights arising from the purchase contract, and the agent performed that contract.

f: 99. When does the principal become the defendant instead of the agent?
b: When the agent transfers the property to the principal and no longer has possession or ownership.

f: 100. Can a shufʿah claimant take the property from an agent who purchased for an absent principal while the agent still possesses it?
b: Yes, because the agent is still the contracting party and possesses the property.

f: 101. Who is the defendant if the seller was an agent selling on behalf of an absent owner?
b: The seller-agent can be confronted if he still possesses the property because he acted as the contracting party.

f: 102. Does the person who acquires property through shufʿah have the option of inspection (khiyār al-ruʾyah)?
b: Yes, if the judge awarded him the property and he had not previously seen it.

f: 103. Does the person who acquires property through shufʿah have the option to return it due to defects?
b: Yes, if he discovers a defect.

f: 104. Does the purchaser's previous condition that he is free from liability for defects remove the shufʿah claimant's right to return for defects?
b: No, because the shufʿah claimant is not acting as the purchaser's representative and the purchaser cannot waive his rights.

f: 105. Why are the options of inspection and defects established in shufʿah?
b: Because taking property through shufʿah functions like a purchase: it is an exchange of wealth for wealth.

f: 106. If the shufʿah claimant and purchaser disagree about the purchase price, whose statement is accepted?
b: The statement of the purchaser is accepted with an oath, because the shufʿah claimant claims the right to take the property by paying the lower amount, while the purchaser denies this claim.

f: 107. Why is the purchaser considered the one whose statement is accepted in a dispute over the price?
b: Because he is the denying party, and the principle is that the statement of the one who denies is accepted with an oath.

f: 108. Why do the purchaser and shufʿah claimant not both take oaths (taḥāluf) when they disagree about the price?
b: Because the shufʿah claimant is claiming a right against the purchaser, but the purchaser is not claiming any right against the shufʿah claimant, since he may either give up the property or accept the price.

f: 109. If both the shufʿah claimant and purchaser present evidence about the price, whose evidence is accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: The evidence of the shufʿah claimant is accepted.

f: 110. Why is the evidence of the shufʿah claimant accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Because the two pieces of evidence do not contradict each other; they can be treated as indicating two different sales, and the shufʿah claimant may take the property according to either one.

f: 111. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله view when both parties provide evidence about the purchase price?
b: He holds that the evidence of the purchaser is accepted because it establishes more.

f: 112. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله prefer the purchaser's evidence?
b: Because it is more effective in proving the price, similar to cases involving evidence from a seller, agent, or a purchaser from an enemy territory.

f: 113. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad reject Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله analogy with the seller and buyer?
b: Because in this case there is no contradiction requiring cancellation of one contract; rather, both pieces of evidence can exist together.

f: 114. If the purchaser claims a higher price and the seller claims a lower price before the seller receives payment, what price does the shufʿah claimant pay?
b: The shufʿah claimant takes the property according to the seller's statement of the lower price.

f: 115. Why is the seller's statement accepted before receiving the price?
b: Because ownership is transferred from the seller by his contract, so as long as his claim regarding the price remains connected to the transaction, his statement is considered.

f: 116. If the seller claims a higher price than the purchaser before receiving payment, what happens?
b: The seller and purchaser both swear oaths and then cancel the sale if both maintain their claims.

f: 117. If one of the seller or purchaser refuses to swear in a price dispute, what happens?
b: The statement of the other party becomes established, and the shufʿah claimant takes the property according to that price.

f: 118. If both seller and purchaser swear their oaths and the judge cancels the sale, does the shufʿah claimant lose his right?
b: No, cancellation of the sale does not invalidate the shufʿah claimant's right. He takes the property according to the seller's stated price.

f: 119. If the seller already received the purchase price, whose statement is considered regarding the price?
b: The shufʿah claimant takes according to the purchaser's statement if he wishes.

f: 120. Why is the purchaser's statement accepted after the seller receives payment?
b: Because the seller's role in the contract has ended after receiving payment, and he becomes like a stranger; the dispute remains between the purchaser and the shufʿah claimant.

f: 121. If the seller says "I sold the property for one thousand and received the payment," what price does the shufʿah claimant use?
b: He takes the property for one thousand.

f: 122. Why is the seller's statement accepted when he first admits the sale and then mentions receiving payment?
b: Because his admission establishes the shufʿah right, and his later statement is viewed as an attempt to remove the claimant's right.

f: 123. If the seller says he received the price and specifies that it was one thousand, is his statement regarding the amount considered?
b: No, because by first admitting receipt of the price he has removed himself from the dispute, so his later statement about the amount is not considered.

f: 124. If the seller reduces part of the purchase price for the buyer, does this reduction apply to the shufʿah claimant?
b: Yes, the reduction applies to the shufʿah claimant.

f: 125. Why does a partial reduction of the price apply to the shufʿah claimant?
b: Because it becomes attached to the original contract, meaning the actual remaining price is reduced.

f: 126. If the seller reduces the entire price, does this remove the shufʿah claimant's obligation to pay?
b: No, a complete reduction does not apply to the shufʿah claimant.

f: 127. Why does a complete reduction of the price not apply to the shufʿah claimant?
b: Because it cannot be attached to the original contract in the same way as a partial reduction.

f: 128. If the seller reduces the price after the shufʿah claimant already took the property, does the reduction benefit him?
b: Yes, the shufʿah claimant can recover that amount because the reduction applies to him.

f: 129. If the purchaser increases the price paid to the seller, does the increase apply to the shufʿah claimant?
b: No, the increase does not apply to the shufʿah claimant.

f: 130. Why does an increase in price not apply to the shufʿah claimant?
b: Because applying the increase would harm the shufʿah claimant by forcing him to take the property at a higher price.

f: 131. If a person purchases a property with an item of value (ʿarḍ), how does the shufʿah claimant take the property?
b: He takes it by paying the value of that item.

f: 132. Why does the shufʿah claimant pay the value of an exchanged item of value?
b: Because items of value (qīmiyyāt) are compensated according to their monetary value.

f: 133. If a person purchases property using something measurable by volume or weight (makīl or mawzūn), how does the shufʿah claimant take it?
b: He takes it by paying the equivalent item of the same type and amount.

f: 134. Why does the shufʿah claimant pay the same amount for measured or weighed goods?
b: Because such goods are fungible (mithliyyāt), where equivalents can replace one another.

f: 135. What principle determines the amount paid by the shufʿah claimant when taking the property?
b: The shufʿah claimant takes the property with the same consideration by which the purchaser acquired it, as much as possible.

f: 136. If someone exchanges one piece of real estate for another piece of real estate, how does the shufʿah claimant take the property?
b: Each property is valued according to the value of the other, and the shufʿah claimant pays that value.

f: 137. Why are two exchanged properties valued when real estate is exchanged for real estate?
b: Because real estate is from the category of items whose value differs (qīmiyyāt), so compensation is based on value.

f: 138. What options does a shafīʿ (person entitled to pre-emption) have when a property is sold with a deferred payment price?
b: The shafīʿ has two options: he may take the property immediately by paying the price in cash, or he may wait until the deferment period ends and then take it. He cannot take the property immediately while keeping the same deferred payment arrangement.

f: 139. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and his companions rule that the shafīʿ cannot take a property with the original buyer’s deferred payment terms?
b: Because the deferment was established by a condition between the original seller and buyer, and that condition does not transfer to the shafīʿ. The ability to delay payment differs between people, so the seller’s agreement with one person does not bind another.

f: 140. Why is the deferment period in a sale not considered an inherent attribute of the price according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because deferment is a right belonging to the buyer rather than a quality of the price itself. If it were an attribute of the price, it would automatically transfer whenever the price was transferred.

f: 141. What happens to the original buyer’s obligation to pay the deferred price if the shafīʿ takes the property directly from the seller by paying cash?
b: The buyer’s obligation to pay the price falls away because the shafīʿ has taken ownership directly from the seller.

f: 142. What happens to the original buyer’s deferred payment agreement if the shafīʿ takes the property from the buyer by paying the price immediately?
b: The seller may still demand the deferred price from the original buyer because the agreement between them remains valid.

f: 143. Must a shafīʿ immediately take ownership of a property sold with a deferred price?
b: No. The shafīʿ may wait until the deferment period finishes before taking the property, but he must still make his initial claim of shufʿah when he learns of the sale.

f: 144. Why must a shafīʿ announce his claim of shufʿah immediately after learning about the sale, even if he intends to delay taking the property?
b: Because the right of shufʿah can be lost through neglect. The claim must be made immediately, while the actual taking of the property may be delayed.

f: 145. How does a dhimmī shafīʿ take a property that was purchased by another dhimmī using wine as payment?
b: He takes the property by paying the same amount of wine because the transaction is considered valid between dhimmīs and wine has recognized value among them.

f: 146. How does a dhimmī shafīʿ take a property that was purchased by another dhimmī using pork as payment?
b: He takes the property by paying the value of the pork because pork is treated as a valuable item among dhimmīs.

f: 147. Why does a Muslim shafīʿ pay the value of wine instead of the equivalent amount of wine when taking a property purchased with wine?
b: Because a Muslim cannot own or transfer wine, so wine is treated as something whose value must be compensated rather than an item with a transferable equivalent.

f: 148. How is shufʿah divided when both a Muslim and a dhimmī are entitled to pre-emption over a property purchased with wine?
b: The Muslim takes his share by paying the value of the wine, while the dhimmī takes his share by paying the equivalent amount of wine.

f: 149. If a dhimmī shafīʿ becomes Muslim after having a right of shufʿah over a property purchased with wine, how does he take the property?
b: He takes it by paying the value of the wine because after becoming Muslim he cannot own or transfer wine.

f: 150. What options does a shafīʿ have if the buyer builds a structure or plants trees on the property before the shafīʿ is awarded shufʿah?
b: The shafīʿ may either take the property by paying the original price plus the value of the building or trees, or he may require the buyer to remove them.

f: 151. What was Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله opinion regarding buildings constructed by a buyer before the shafīʿ exercises his right of shufʿah?
b: Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله held that the buyer cannot be forced to remove the building. The shafīʿ may either pay its value and take the property or leave the property.

f: 152. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله not require the buyer to remove buildings constructed before the shafīʿ exercised shufʿah?
b: Because the buyer constructed the building believing that he owned the property, so he was not acting wrongfully. Requiring removal is normally a consequence of unlawful occupation.

f: 153. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad allow the shafīʿ to require removal of buildings constructed by the buyer before shufʿah?
b: Because the buyer built on property already connected to another person’s established right. The shafīʿ’s right is stronger because it can cancel the buyer’s ownership transactions.

f: 154. Why are planted crops treated differently from permanent buildings in the issue of shufʿah?
b: Crops have a known period until harvest and can remain while rent is paid, so removing them causes unnecessary harm.

f: 155. If a shafīʿ takes a property through shufʿah and later the property is proven to belong to someone else, what compensation can he recover?
b: He can recover the price he paid for the property, but he cannot recover the value of buildings or trees he added.

f: 156. Why cannot a shafīʿ recover the value of buildings he constructed after taking a property through shufʿah when the property later turns out to belong to someone else?
b: Because the buyer did not deceive him or authorize his construction. The shafīʿ was compelled to take the property through his legal right, so there is no compensation for the improvements.

f: 157. What options does a shafīʿ have if a property’s building collapses, burns, or its orchard trees dry up without anyone causing the damage before he takes it through shufʿah?
b: He may either take the property for the full original price or choose not to take it.

f: 158. Why can a shafīʿ take a property for the full price even after its building or trees have disappeared without human action?
b: Because buildings and trees are normally considered secondary additions that follow the land and do not have a separately assigned portion of the sale price.

f: 159. Why does the loss of part of the land itself affect the price in shufʿah differently from the loss of buildings or trees?
b: Because the land is the main subject of the sale. If part of the land is destroyed, the remaining property is taken according to its proportional value.

f: 160. If a buyer demolishes the building on a property before the shafīʿ exercises his right of shufʿah, what options does the shafīʿ have?
b: The shafīʿ is told: if you wish, take the land (the empty plot) according to its proportional share of the price, or leave it. This is because the building was intentionally destroyed and therefore the loss is connected to the buyer's action.

f: 161. Why can the shafīʿ not take the demolished building materials (the remains) after the buyer removes the building?
b: Because the building materials have become separated from the land and are no longer considered a dependent part of the property.

f: 162. If a person buys land with date palms that already have fruit, when does the shafīʿ take the fruit along with the land?
b: The shafīʿ takes the fruit along with the land if the fruit was included in the sale contract, because fruit does not enter the sale automatically without being mentioned.

f: 163. Why did the Ḥanafīs consider existing fruit on date palms to be included in shufʿah when it was mentioned in the sale?
b: Because its connection to the land makes it similar to a building attached to a house. Anything attached to the property as part of it is taken by the shafīʿ.

f: 164. What is the analogy (qiyās) regarding fruit on date palms sold with land in relation to shufʿah?
b: According to analogy, the shafīʿ would not take the fruit because it is not a permanent attachment and does not enter the sale unless specifically mentioned, similar to movable objects inside a house.

f: 165. If a person buys land without fruit on its date palms, then the palms produce fruit while the land is in the buyer's possession, does the shafīʿ take the fruit?
b: Yes, the shafīʿ takes the fruit because it is considered to have entered the sale as a dependent part of the property, similar to offspring of a sold animal.

f: 166. If the buyer harvests the fruit before the shafīʿ exercises shufʿah, does the shafīʿ take the fruit?
b: No, the shafīʿ does not take the fruit because it is no longer attached to the land and is no longer considered a dependent part of the property.

f: 167. If fruit already existing at the time of sale is harvested by the buyer before the shafīʿ takes the property, does the shafīʿ's price decrease?
b: Yes, because the fruit was an intended part of the sale and had a portion of the price assigned to it. The shafīʿ's share of the price is reduced accordingly.

f: 168. If fruit grows on trees after the land sale but before the shafīʿ takes the property, and the buyer harvests it, does the shafīʿ receive a reduction in price?
b: No, because the fruit was not present at the time of the sale and therefore was not an independently sold item. It only entered as a dependent attachment, so the shafīʿ takes the land for the full price.

f: 169. Is shufʿah valid for all types of real estate even if the property cannot be divided?
b: Yes, according to the Ḥanafīs, shufʿah applies to all real estate even if it cannot be divided.

f: 170. Why did al-Shāfiʿī deny shufʿah in property that cannot be divided?
b: Because he considered the purpose of shufʿah to be preventing the hardship of division, and this hardship does not exist in property that cannot be divided.

f: 171. What is the Ḥanafī response to the argument that shufʿah does not apply to indivisible property?
b: The Ḥanafīs argue that the cause of shufʿah is attachment of ownership and its purpose is preventing harm from a problematic neighbour. This applies to both divisible and indivisible property.

f: 172. What examples of indivisible properties still have shufʿah according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Examples include a bathhouse, mill, well, and private road.

f: 173. Is shufʿah valid for movable goods and ships according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: No, shufʿah is not valid for movable goods or ships because the reason for shufʿah relates to permanent neighbouring ownership, which applies to real estate rather than movable property.

f: 174. Why is there no shufʿah in movable property according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because movable ownership does not remain permanently connected in the same way as real estate ownership, so the harm of permanent neighbour relations does not apply.

f: 175. Is shufʿah valid for a building or date palm trees sold separately from the land beneath them?
b: No, according to the Ḥanafīs, there is no shufʿah in a building or date palms when sold without the land because they are movable in the sense that they have no permanent attachment to the ground.

f: 176. Why is a separate upper floor (ʿulūw) treated differently from a building sold separately?
b: Because the upper floor has a permanent right of attachment and use connected to the property, making it similar to real estate.

f: 177. Are Muslims and dhimmīs equal regarding the right of shufʿah?
b: Yes, Muslims and dhimmīs are equal in the right of shufʿah because they share the same cause and purpose of the ruling.

f: 178. Does gender, age, legal status, or social condition affect entitlement to shufʿah?
b: No, men and women, minors and adults, righteous and sinful people, free people and authorized slaves or mukātabs are equal in entitlement to shufʿah.

f: 179. When does shufʿah become obligatory according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Shufʿah becomes obligatory when real estate is transferred through compensation that is considered wealth, because the shafīʿ can take ownership by giving equivalent compensation.

f: 180. Is shufʿah established when a house is given as a marriage dowry (mahr)?
b: No, according to the Ḥanafīs there is no shufʿah because marriage compensation is not considered an exchange of wealth for wealth.

f: 181. Is shufʿah established when a house is given as compensation in khulʿ (divorce initiated by the wife)?
b: No, because the compensation in khulʿ is not considered a direct exchange of wealth for wealth according to the Ḥanafīs.

f: 182. Is shufʿah established when a person gives a house as payment for renting another property?
b: No, because the compensation is not considered a direct exchange of wealth for wealth in the way required for shufʿah.

f: 183. Is shufʿah established when a house is given as compensation for intentional homicide (qiṣāṣ settlement)?
b: No, because blood compensation is not considered a transferable monetary substitute that qualifies for shufʿah.

f: 184. Is shufʿah established when a person gives a house in exchange for freeing a slave?
b: No, because manumission is not considered an exchange of wealth for wealth.

f: 185. Why did al-Shāfiʿī allow shufʿah in cases such as marriage dowry and khulʿ compensation?
b: Because he considered these compensations to have value and believed the shafīʿ could take the property by paying their equivalent value if the exact item could not be given.

f: 186. Why did the Ḥanafīs reject shufʿah in marriage-related exchanges despite recognizing value in some benefits?
b: Because the value of benefits such as marriage relations is only recognized for specific contracts like marriage and rental, and does not establish the type of monetary exchange required for shufʿah.

f: 187. If a man marries a woman without specifying a dowry and later gives her a house as her dowry, is there shufʿah?
b: No, because the house functions as compensation for the marital relationship and is treated like a dowry established within the marriage contract.

f: 188. If a person sells a house in exchange for a specified marriage dowry, is there shufʿah?
b: Yes, because this is a direct exchange of property for property and therefore qualifies as a financial transaction.

f: 189. If a man marries a woman in exchange for a house plus an additional payment from her, is shufʿah established in the whole house according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, shufʿah is not established because the exchange is primarily a marriage contract, and the monetary aspect is only secondary.

f: 190. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding marriage in exchange for a house plus additional money?
b: They held that shufʿah applies to the portion corresponding to the monetary payment because that part represents an exchange of wealth for wealth.

f: 191. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not separate the monetary portion from the marriage exchange when determining shufʿah?
b: Because the sale-like element is only secondary; the transaction is established through the marriage contract, and shufʿah applies only to intended financial exchanges.

f: 192. If a person settles a legal dispute over a house by giving the house in exchange for a settlement while denying the other person's claim, is shufʿah established?
b: No, according to the Ḥanafīs, shufʿah is not established because the owner still claims that the house remained his property and the settlement was only to avoid the dispute.

f: 193. If a person settles a dispute over a house by admitting the claimant's ownership and giving the house as settlement, is shufʿah established?
b: Yes, shufʿah is established because the owner acknowledged that the claimant owned the right and transferred the property through a financial exchange.

f: 194. Why is shufʿah established when a house is transferred through a settlement based on admission but not through a settlement based on denial?
b: Because a settlement based on admission is considered an exchange of wealth, while a settlement based on denial is viewed as paying to end a dispute without acknowledging a transfer of ownership.

f: 195. If a person settles a dispute over a house through silence rather than explicit denial or admission, is shufʿah established?
b: According to the explanation, it is treated like denial because the payment may have been made only to avoid taking an oath or ending the dispute, so shufʿah is not established.

f: 196. If a person receives a house through a settlement claiming that it is compensation for his right, is shufʿah established?
b: Yes, because he considers the house compensation for his right, and he is treated according to his own claim when the compensation is not of the same type as the original right.

f: 197. Is shufʿah established in a normal gift (hibah)?
b: No, because a gift is not an exchange of wealth for wealth.

f: 198. When does a gift become subject to shufʿah according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: When the gift is made in exchange for a specified compensation, because it becomes effectively a sale in its final outcome.

f: 199. What conditions are required for a compensated gift (hibah with ʿiwaḍ) to be treated like a sale for shufʿah?
b: The compensation must be stipulated in the contract, the gift must be received, and neither the gifted item nor the compensation can be jointly owned shares that prevent the required conditions.

f: 200. Why is a gift with an unstipulated later compensation not subject to shufʿah?
b: Because the original transaction was a pure gift, and the later compensation does not change the nature of the original contract.

f: 201. If a person sells a property while retaining a seller's option (khiyār al-sharṭ), does the shafīʿ have a right of shufʿah?
b: No, because the seller's ownership has not yet fully ended due to the option.

f: 202. If a seller cancels his option after selling a property, does shufʿah become established?
b: Yes, because the obstacle preventing transfer of ownership has disappeared.

f: 203. When does the shafīʿ need to make his shufʿah request after the seller cancels his option?
b: He must request shufʿah after the option is cancelled because only then does the sale become effective as a cause for transferring ownership.

f: 204. If a buyer purchases a property with a buyer's option (khiyār al-sharṭ), is shufʿah established?
b: Yes, because the buyer's option does not prevent the seller's ownership from transferring.

f: 205. If a buyer exercises his option within the option period and returns the property, what happens to the shufʿah right?
b: If the shafīʿ already took it, the sale becomes binding because the buyer cannot return it after the shafīʿ's acquisition.

f: 206. Does a shafīʿ receive the buyer's contractual option when taking a property through shufʿah?
b: No, because the option was established for the buyer through a condition, and the shafīʿ does not inherit that condition.

f: 207. If a property is sold next to another property and one of the owners has a contractual option, can that owner exercise shufʿah?
b: Yes. If the option belongs to the seller, it is clear because he still owns the property used for claiming shufʿah. If it belongs to the buyer, the issue has further details discussed in sales.

f: 208. If a buyer purchases a property through a defective (fāsid) sale, is shufʿah established?
b: No, because before possession the seller's ownership has not ended, and after possession the contract remains subject to cancellation.

f: 209. Why is shufʿah not established in a defective sale after possession?
b: Because allowing shufʿah would reinforce a defective transaction that Islamic law allows to be cancelled.

f: 210. If the right to cancel a defective sale disappears, does shufʿah become established?
b: Yes, because the obstacle preventing a complete transfer of ownership has disappeared.

f: 211. If a buyer receives a property through a defective sale and another property next to it is sold while the original seller still owns the first property, who has shufʿah?
b: The original seller has shufʿah because he still owns the property used as the basis for shufʿah.

f: 212. If the original seller transfers the property from a defective sale to the buyer before claiming shufʿah, who becomes entitled to shufʿah?
b: The buyer becomes the shafīʿ because ownership has transferred to him.

f: 213. If partners divide jointly owned real estate among themselves, does a neighbour gain shufʿah because of the division?
b: No, because division (qismah) is considered separation of existing ownership rather than an exchange of wealth.

f: 214. Why does shufʿah not apply after partners divide their jointly owned property?
b: Because shufʿah was legislated for voluntary exchanges of property, whereas division only separates existing shares.

f: 215. If a buyer purchases a house, the shafīʿ gives up his shufʿah right, and then the buyer returns the house due to a court-ordered option of inspection, condition, or defect, does the shafīʿ regain shufʿah?
b: No, because the return completely cancels the sale and restores the previous ownership. Shufʿah applies to a new sale, not a cancelled transaction.

f: 216. If a buyer returns a property after discovering a defect without a judge's ruling, does the shafīʿ retain his right of shufʿah?
b: Yes, because this type of cancellation is treated as a new sale in relation to third parties, since both parties agreed to exchange wealth for wealth again.

f: 217. Why is returning a defective property without a judge's ruling treated differently from a court-ordered return?
b: Because the parties themselves chose the cancellation, making it resemble a new transaction for third parties such as the shafīʿ.

f: 218. If a property is returned before possession due to a defect, does the shafīʿ have shufʿah?
b: No, because before possession the cancellation removes the sale from its origin rather than creating a new transaction.

f: 219. What does the statement "there is no shufʿah in qismah or khiyār al-ruʾyah" mean?
b: It means there is no shufʿah due to a return based on the option of inspection, and there is no shufʿah arising from a division of property. It does not mean that options themselves are invalid in division.

f: 220. Does division of jointly owned property allow options such as khiyār al-ruʾyah or khiyār al-sharṭ?
b: Yes, because these options relate to defects in consent, and that meaning can exist in division as well.

f: 221. When does a shufʿah (pre-emption) right become invalid if the pre-emptor fails to act after learning of the sale?
b: If the pre-emptor leaves making witnesses (ishhād) when he learns of the sale while being able to do so, his shufʿah becomes invalid because this indicates abandonment of the claim.

f: 222. Why does failing to make witnesses after learning of the sale invalidate shufʿah?
b: Because abandonment is only established when the person has the ability to act but chooses not to.

f: 223. If a pre-emptor makes witnesses in the meeting where he learns of the sale but does not witness against either buyer or seller, or does not witness at the property itself, what is the ruling?
b: His shufʿah becomes invalid, as this does not fulfill the required procedure for preserving the claim.

f: 224. If a person settles his shufʿah right in exchange for compensation, what is the ruling?
b: His shufʿah becomes invalid, and the compensation must be returned.

f: 225. Why cannot the right of shufʿah be exchanged for compensation?
b: Because shufʿah is only a right of ownership acquisition, not an established property right attached to the property itself, so compensation cannot validly be taken for it.

f: 226. What happens if someone sells his shufʿah right for money?
b: The shufʿah is invalidated and the sale of the right is not valid, because the right cannot be compensated for.

f: 227. Why is shufʿah different from retaliation (qiṣāṣ) regarding compensation?
b: Qiṣāṣ is an established right, whereas shufʿah is merely a right of acquiring ownership.

f: 228. What happens to a person's shufʿah right if he dies?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, his shufʿah becomes invalid if he dies before the judge grants him the shufʿah.

f: 229. According to al-Shāfiʿī, is the shufʿah right inherited after the death of the pre-emptor?
b: Yes, al-Shāfiʿī holds that the shufʿah right is inherited.

f: 230. If the pre-emptor dies after the judge has ruled in his favour but before payment and possession, what happens?
b: The purchase becomes binding upon his heirs.

f: 231. Why does shufʿah not pass to heirs according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because after death the person's ownership transfers to the heirs, and the pre-emptor must still own the property connected to the shufʿah until the judgment is completed.

f: 232. Does the death of the buyer invalidate the pre-emptor's shufʿah?
b: No, because the right remains and the cause of the right has not changed.

f: 233. Can the buyer's property be sold for his debts or bequeathed if a pre-emptor has a valid shufʿah claim?
b: No. The pre-emptor may invalidate such transfers and take the property because his right preceded those actions.

f: 234. If the pre-emptor sells the property that gives him the right of shufʿah before judgment, what happens?
b: His shufʿah becomes invalid because the basis of his right (ownership connection to the property) no longer exists.

f: 235. Why does selling the property that gives shufʿah invalidate the claim even if the pre-emptor did not know about the sale requiring shufʿah?
b: Because the cause of entitlement is removed, just as an explicit waiver removes the right even without knowledge.

f: 236. If the pre-emptor sells his property with a condition that he retains the option of cancelling, does he lose his shufʿah?
b: No, because ownership has not fully transferred and the connection remains.

f: 237. Does a seller's agent who sells a property have a right of shufʿah in that property?
b: No, if the agent himself is the pre-emptor, he has no shufʿah because taking it back would undo the sale he carried out.

f: 238. Does a buyer's agent who purchases a property have a right of shufʿah?
b: Yes, because taking it by shufʿah does not undo his action; it is like another purchase.

f: 239. If a person guarantees the seller's liability (ḍamān al-dark) and is also the pre-emptor, does he have shufʿah?
b: No, because he is connected to the sale in a way that prevents him from claiming shufʿah.

f: 240. If a person sells a property with an option for another person and that other person approves the sale while being the pre-emptor, does he have shufʿah?
b: No, because the sale became complete through his approval.

f: 241. If someone is told that a property was sold for 1000 dirhams and he waives his shufʿah, but later discovers it was sold for less, does his waiver remain valid?
b: No, his waiver is invalid and he retains his shufʿah because he only waived due to believing the price was higher.

f: 242. If someone waives shufʿah believing the property was sold for 1000 dirhams, but later discovers it was sold for wheat or barley worth 1000 dirhams, does he still have shufʿah?
b: Yes, because he waived due to thinking the payment was in a different form, and the type of compensation affects his decision.

f: 243. If someone waives shufʿah believing the property was sold for an item worth 1000 dirhams, does he regain his shufʿah if this was true?
b: No, because the obligation is based on the value of the item, which is already considered.

f: 244. If someone waives shufʿah after being told the buyer's identity, then discovers the buyer was someone else, what is the ruling?
b: He retains his shufʿah because different buyers create different levels of harm in neighbouring property.

f: 245. If a pre-emptor is told that one person purchased a property but later discovers another person purchased it together with him, can he take the other buyer's share?
b: Yes, because his waiver did not apply to that additional buyer.

f: 246. If a pre-emptor is told that half a property was purchased and waives his shufʿah, then discovers the buyer purchased the whole property, what is the ruling?
b: He still has shufʿah because his waiver was based on the harm of partnership, which does not exist in the actual situation.

f: 247. If a pre-emptor is told the whole property was purchased and waives shufʿah, then discovers only half was purchased, does he retain shufʿah?
b: According to the apparent narration, he does not retain shufʿah because waiving the whole includes waiving parts of it.

f: 248. If a person sells a house but excludes a one-cubit strip along the boundary adjoining the neighbour, does the neighbour have shufʿah?
b: No, because the adjoining relationship has been cut off.

f: 249. Why can excluding a small strip of land remove a neighbour's shufʿah right?
b: Because shufʿah depends on continuous adjacency, and removing the boundary connection removes the cause of the right.

f: 250. Can the same strategy of removing shufʿah by transferring a small boundary strip be done through a gift?
b: Yes, gifting the strip and handing it over also removes the adjacency required for shufʿah.

f: 251. If a person buys a share of a property for a price and later buys the remainder, who has priority of shufʿah in the first and second purchases?
b: The neighbour has shufʿah in the first share but not the second, because in the second purchase the buyer has already become a partner in the property, and the partner has priority over the neighbour.

f: 252. Why does the neighbour lose shufʿah in the second purchase when the buyer already owns a share of the property?
b: Because the buyer becomes a partner in the property, and the partner's right of shufʿah is stronger than the neighbour's right.

f: 253. What legal stratagem was mentioned to avoid a partner's priority in shufʿah when purchasing a property in shares?
b: The buyer may purchase the first share for a price slightly less than the full amount (such as one dirham less), then purchase the remainder separately with the remaining price.

f: 254. If someone buys a property for a price and later gives the seller a garment instead of that price, which item is considered for shufʿah?
b: Shufʿah is taken according to the original price, not the garment, because the garment was transferred through a separate contract and the original price was the compensation for the property.

f: 255. What type of legal stratagem can remove both neighbour and partnership shufʿah?
b: Selling the property for a very high price and then giving the seller a garment worth the actual value as compensation.

f: 256. What problem exists with the stratagem of selling for a high price and replacing the price with a garment?
b: If the property is later claimed by another rightful owner (mustahaqq), the buyer remains liable for the full price because the second exchange contract remains.

f: 257. What alternative stratagem avoids the problem of liability remaining after a second exchange contract?
b: Selling the property for dirhams with the price expressed as a gold dinar exchange, so if the property is taken by another claimant, the exchange is cancelled and only the dinar is returned.

f: 258. Is using legal stratagems to avoid shufʿah considered disliked according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: No, Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله does not consider such stratagems disliked because they prevent the establishment of the right rather than harming an existing right.

f: 259. Is using legal stratagems to avoid shufʿah considered disliked according to Muḥammad?
b: Yes, Muḥammad considers such stratagems disliked because shufʿah was legislated to remove harm, and allowing these methods prevents that purpose.

f: 260. What other issue has the same disagreement between Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding legal stratagems?
b: The use of stratagems to avoid paying zakāh.

f: 261. If five people jointly buy a house from one seller, can a pre-emptor take the share of only one buyer?
b: Yes, the pre-emptor may take the share of one of the buyers.

f: 262. If one person buys a house from five sellers, can the pre-emptor take only part of the house?
b: No, the pre-emptor must either take the whole property or leave it.

f: 263. Why can the pre-emptor take only one buyer's share when five people buy a property together?
b: Because the pre-emptor replaces one of the buyers, so the purchase transaction is not divided and the remaining buyers are not harmed.

f: 264. Why cannot the pre-emptor take only part of a property when one person buys from multiple sellers?
b: Because taking part would divide the buyer's transaction and cause additional harm to him.

f: 265. Does the ruling about taking one buyer's share differ between before and after the property is received (qabḍ)?
b: The correct view is that there is no difference, although before qabḍ the pre-emptor cannot take one share unless the other buyers have also paid their portions.

f: 266. Why cannot the pre-emptor take one buyer's share before qabḍ unless the others have paid?
b: Because it would separate the seller's possession and control over the property, similar to separating the hands of joint buyers.

f: 267. If the property has already been received by the buyers, can the pre-emptor take only one buyer's share?
b: Yes, because the seller's possession has ended and separating shares no longer creates this problem.

f: 268. Does it matter whether each buyer's share had a separately stated price or whether the property had one combined price?
b: No, the ruling depends on whether the transaction is divided, not on whether the prices were separately stated.

f: 269. If someone buys half of an undivided house and then divides it with the seller, what may the pre-emptor do?
b: The pre-emptor may take the half that became the buyer's portion or leave it.

f: 270. Why is the pre-emptor allowed to take the portion created by division between buyer and seller?
b: Because division completes possession (qabḍ), and the pre-emptor does not invalidate what completes possession.

f: 271. Why does division between buyer and seller differ from division between a buyer and another partner who did not sell?
b: Because in the first case the division completes the original contract, while in the second it is a separate ownership action that the pre-emptor may invalidate.

f: 272. According to the apparent wording of the text, does it matter which side of the property the buyer receives after division?
b: No, the pre-emptor may take the buyer's portion regardless of where it falls.

f: 273. According to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, when may the pre-emptor take the portion created by division?
b: He may take it only if it remains adjacent to the property from which he has the shufʿah right.

f: 274. If a person sells a property while having an authorized slave (ʿabd مأذون) who owes debts, does the person have shufʿah?
b: Yes, because taking by shufʿah is ownership through payment, resembling a purchase.

f: 275. If an authorized slave who owes debts sells a property, does his master have shufʿah?
b: Yes, because the slave's sale benefits the creditors and resembles a purchase transaction.

f: 276. Why does an authorized slave's debt affect the ruling of shufʿah?
b: Because his transactions are carried out for the benefit of creditors, making the acquisition resemble a purchase rather than a sale purely for his master.

f: 277. Does a person have shufʿah if he sells property purely on behalf of his master when there are no debts?
b: No, because he is effectively selling to his master, and the person who sells to another does not gain shufʿah through that sale.

f: 278. Can a father or guardian waive a minor child's shufʿah right according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Yes, the father's or guardian's waiver is valid.

f: 279. According to Muḥammad and Zufar, does a minor retain shufʿah after reaching adulthood if his father or guardian waived it?
b: Yes, the minor retains the right because the waiver was not valid.

f: 280. Why do Muḥammad and Zufar reject the father's or guardian's ability to waive a child's shufʿah?
b: Because shufʿah is an established right belonging to the child, similar to blood-money and retaliation rights, which guardians cannot remove.

f: 281. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله allow the guardian to waive a child's shufʿah?
b: Because shufʿah resembles a commercial matter where there may be benefit or harm, and guardians have authority to consider the child's interests.

f: 282. Does the silence of a father or guardian after learning of a neighbouring purchase count as abandoning a child's shufʿah?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, yes, because silence indicates abandonment.

f: 283. If a property is sold at its normal market value, may a guardian waive the child's shufʿah?
b: Yes, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله.

f: 284. If a property is sold for much more than its value beyond normal tolerance, is the guardian's waiver valid?
b: Some scholars say it is valid because it is clearly beneficial, while others say it is invalid because the guardian cannot waive a right he could not acquire.

f: 285. If a property is sold far below its value as a favour to the buyer, may the guardian waive the child's shufʿah?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the waiver is not valid, and there is no narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله on this case.

f: 1. Is dividing jointly owned property (qismat al-aʿyān al-mushtarakah) legislated in Islam?
b: Yes, it is legislated. The Prophet ﷺ practiced division in spoils of war and inheritances, and Muslims continued doing so without objection.

f: 2. Why is division of jointly owned property considered a legitimate practice?
b: Because it combines two meanings: separation of ownership (ifrāz) and exchange (mubādalah).

f: 3. Why does division contain the meaning of exchange (mubādalah)?
b: Because each partner receives part that belonged to the other partner's share, making what he receives an exchange for the remaining rights of his partner.

f: 4. In which types of property is the meaning of separation (ifrāz) more apparent in division?
b: In measured and weighed items (makīlāt and mawzūnāt), because there is little or no difference between individual portions.

f: 5. Can one partner take his share of measured or weighed goods during the absence of the other partner?
b: Yes, because division in such goods is mainly separation rather than exchange.

f: 6. If two people purchase measured goods together and then divide them, can one sell his portion with murābaḥah pricing based on half the original price?
b: Yes, because his share remains equivalent to half of the original purchase price.

f: 7. In which types of property is the meaning of exchange more apparent in division?
b: In animals and other valuable items (ʿurūḍ), because their individual values differ.

f: 8. Can one partner take his share of animals or valuable goods while the other partner is absent?
b: No, because division involves exchange and requires the agreement or presence of the other partner.

f: 9. If two people purchase animals or valuable items together and then divide them, can one sell his share by murābaḥah after division?
b: No, because the value of each portion may differ and cannot simply be considered half the original price.

f: 10. When are partners forced by a judge to divide jointly owned property?
b: When the property is of one type and the purposes of the portions are close, such as similar goods, because division has the meaning of separation.

f: 11. Why can a judge compel division when the property is of the same type?
b: Because the requesting partner is asking to exclusively benefit from his own share and prevent others from using his property.

f: 12. When does a judge not force division of jointly owned property?
b: When the properties are different types and equal division cannot be achieved due to major differences in purpose and value.

f: 13. If partners agree to divide different types of property voluntarily, is the division valid?
b: Yes, because the right belongs to them and they may agree to it.

f: 14. Why should a judge appoint a state-paid divider (qāsim) to divide property among people?
b: Because division resembles judicial work by ending disputes, and its benefit extends to the public like the judge's salary.

f: 15. From where should the salary of an appointed public divider ideally come?
b: From the public treasury (Bayt al-Māl), so people are not burdened with fees and suspicion is avoided.

f: 16. If the judge does not appoint a publicly funded divider, what should he do?
b: He appoints a divider who works for payment from the people requesting division.

f: 17. Who pays the wage of a privately hired divider?
b: The partners who benefit from the division, because the benefit is specific to them.

f: 18. How much should the hired divider be paid?
b: The normal market wage (ujrat al-mithl), so he cannot demand excessive payment.

f: 19. What qualities should a person appointed as a divider have?
b: He should be trustworthy, upright, and knowledgeable about division.

f: 20. Why must the divider be knowledgeable about division?
b: Because he needs the ability to correctly distribute property.

f: 21. Why must the divider be trustworthy and just?
b: Because people must rely on his decisions, similar to judicial work.

f: 22. Can a judge force people to hire one specific divider?
b: No, because contracts cannot be forced and a designated divider might demand excessive wages.

f: 23. If partners agree among themselves and divide their property, is their division valid?
b: Yes, unless one of the partners is a minor, in which case the judge's permission is required.

f: 24. Why is a judge's permission required if a minor is among the partners?
b: Because the other partners have no authority over the minor's property.

f: 25. Can dividers form a partnership and share their work?
b: No, because this may increase fees due to laziness and reliance on each other.

f: 26. Why does preventing dividers from partnering reduce the cost of division?
b: Because each divider will compete to obtain work, leading to lower wages.

f: 27. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, how is the wage for dividing property calculated?
b: It is divided equally according to the number of partners (heads).

f: 28. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, how is the wage for dividing property calculated?
b: It is according to each person's share of ownership.

f: 29. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say division wages are according to ownership shares?
b: Because division is a cost of ownership, similar to expenses for measuring, weighing, and maintaining jointly owned property.

f: 30. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله reasoning for dividing division wages equally among partners?
b: The wage is payment for distinguishing shares, and the work of distinguishing does not vary according to the size of each person's share.

f: 31. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject comparing division wages to digging a shared well?
b: Because digging involves physical labour that varies according to the amount of work, while division is based on distinction itself.

f: 32. If measuring and weighing is performed as part of division, what is the ruling according to some scholars?
b: It follows the same disagreement as division wages.

f: 33. If measuring and weighing is performed independently of division, how is the wage determined?
b: It is based on the actual work because the payment is for measuring and weighing themselves.

f: 34. According to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, who pays the division fee if one partner requests division and another refuses?
b: The requesting partner pays because he benefits while the other is harmed.

f: 35. If heirs come before a judge with a property and claim they inherited it from a deceased person, will Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله divide the property immediately?
b: No, not for real estate. They must provide evidence of the person's death and the number of heirs.

f: 36. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may a judge divide inherited real estate based only on the heirs' admission?
b: Yes, they allow division based on their acknowledgement.

f: 37. If the inherited property is movable property rather than real estate, does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله require evidence before division?
b: No, he allows division based on their claim.

f: 38. If people claim that real estate was purchased rather than inherited, may the judge divide it based on their admission?
b: Yes, according to all three Imams.

f: 39. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad allow division of inherited real estate based on admission?
b: Because possession indicates ownership and admission is an indication of truth, with no opposing claimant present.

f: 40. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله require evidence for inherited real estate?
b: Because the judge is effectively ruling on behalf of the deceased, and the heirs' admission is not evidence against the deceased.

f: 41. Why is division of inherited property considered a judgment affecting the deceased according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because the estate remains connected to the deceased's ownership until division; debts and bequests may still apply before division.

f: 42. Why is evidence required if division affects the deceased's rights?
b: Because the heirs' admission cannot legally bind the deceased, but evidence can establish the claim.

f: 43. Why is movable inherited property treated differently from inherited real estate?
b: Because movable property needs protection and is guaranteed by whoever possesses it, whereas real estate is naturally protected and does not require the same treatment.

f: 44. Why is purchased real estate treated differently from inherited real estate?
b: Because after purchase, the property no longer remains in the seller's ownership even before division, so division is not a judgment affecting someone else's rights.

f: 45. If two people claim ownership of a property and request division without mentioning how ownership transferred to them, can the judge divide it between them?
b: Yes. The judge may divide it between them because the division does not constitute a judgment against a third party, since they have not acknowledged ownership belonging to anyone else.

f: 46. According to the narration in the Book of Division, what is the ruling if two people claim ownership of land, provide evidence that it is in their possession, and request division?
b: The land is not divided until they provide evidence that it belongs to them, because it is possible that it belongs to someone else.

f: 47. What is the correct view regarding the case of two people claiming land and requesting division based on possession and evidence of possession?
b: The correct view is that this is the position of all the scholars, because division of real estate for preservation is unnecessary, and division of ownership requires established ownership.

f: 48. If two heirs attend court, prove the death of the deceased, the number of heirs, and that the property is in their possession, while another heir is absent, may the judge divide the inheritance?
b: Yes. The judge may divide it at the request of the present heirs and appoint a representative to take possession of the absent heir's share.

f: 49. If one of the heirs in a division case is a child, may the judge divide the inheritance?
b: Yes. The judge appoints a guardian for the child who takes possession of the child's share.

f: 50. Why is division allowed when some heirs are absent but not when some purchasers are absent?
b: The heir's ownership is based on succession, so one heir can act as a representative of the deceased regarding the property. A purchaser's ownership is newly established and the present purchaser cannot represent the absent purchaser.

f: 51. If inherited property is in the possession of an absent heir, a custodian, or a child, may the judge divide it?
b: No. Division would be a judgment against the absent person or child without a present representative who can act as their opponent in court.

f: 52. Does the presence of evidence change the ruling when the property is in the possession of an absent heir, custodian, or child?
b: No. The correct view is that the ruling remains the same whether evidence is presented or not.

f: 53. If only one heir attends court, may the judge divide the inheritance even if that heir provides evidence?
b: No. There must be two opposing parties present because one person cannot simultaneously be the claimant, defendant, and co-partner in division.

f: 54. If one heir is an adult and another is a child, may the judge divide the inheritance?
b: Yes. The judge appoints a guardian for the child and divides the inheritance after evidence is established.

f: 55. If an adult heir and someone granted one-third of the estate through a bequest request division and provide evidence, may the judge divide it?
b: Yes. There are two valid parties: the adult heir representing the deceased and the beneficiary representing himself.

f: 56. When can shared property be divided by judicial compulsion?
b: When each partner can benefit from his share after division, because division is a right that must be granted in property capable of division.

f: 57. If one partner benefits from division while another is harmed because his share becomes too small, when does the judge divide?
b: If the owner of the larger share requests division, it is granted. If the owner of the smaller share requests it, it is not granted because he is acting obstinately.

f: 58. If both partners are harmed because the property is too small after division, may the judge force division?
b: No. Division only occurs by mutual agreement because compulsory division exists to complete benefit, whereas here it removes benefit.

f: 59. Can movable goods of the same type be divided by the judge?
b: Yes. When the type is the same, the objective is the same and fair division is possible.

f: 60. Why are different types of movable goods not divided by judicial compulsion?
b: Because division between different types becomes an exchange rather than a separation of ownership, and exchanges require mutual consent.

f: 61. Which types of property can be divided according to the Hanafi jurists?
b: Things such as measured goods, weighed goods, similar-counted items, gold and silver bullion, iron, copper, camels separately, cattle separately, and sheep separately can be divided.

f: 62. Why are a sheep, camel, horse, and donkey not divided together?
b: Because they are different types of property and division between them would be an exchange rather than separation.

f: 63. Why are utensils not divided by judicial compulsion?
b: Because differences in craftsmanship make them different types of goods.

f: 64. Can identical types of cloth be divided?
b: Yes. For example, certain types of uniform cloth can be divided because they are considered one category.

f: 65. Why is a single garment not divided?
b: Because division would cause harm, since it would require cutting the garment.

f: 66. Why are two garments of different values not divided?
b: Because they are unequal and division would not achieve fairness.

f: 67. Can three garments of different values be divided?
b: Yes, if the division is arranged fairly, such as one garment compared with two garments, because part of the division can be separated without dividing every item.

f: 68. According to Abu Hanifah رحمه الله, can slaves and jewels be divided among partners?
b: No. Abu Hanifah رحمه الله does not allow their compulsory division because of their great differences.

f: 69. Why do Abu Yusuf رحمه الله and Muhammad allow division of slaves?
b: They consider slaves one category of property, similar to camels and sheep, where division is possible.

f: 70. Why does Abu Hanifah رحمه الله consider humans different from animals regarding division?
b: Because differences among humans are significant due to hidden qualities and personal characteristics, making them like different categories of property.

f: 71. Why were slaves from war booty treated differently according to Abu Hanifah رحمه الله?
b: Because the partners' rights in war booty relate only to financial value, whereas in ordinary ownership the right relates to both the individual item and its value.

f: 72. According to the Hanafi school, can jewels be divided among partners by judicial compulsion?
b: There are several views: some say jewels of different types (such as pearls and rubies) cannot be divided; some say large jewels cannot be divided due to the great difference between them, while small ones can because the difference is less; and some say they cannot be divided generally because the uncertainty in jewels is greater than that of slaves.

f: 73. Why are jewels considered more problematic to divide than slaves?
b: Because the differences and unknown qualities of jewels are greater. This is shown by the fact that specifying a pearl or ruby as a dowry or settlement in divorce is invalid, whereas specifying a slave is valid. Therefore, compulsory division of jewels is even less appropriate.

f: 74. Can a bathhouse (ḥammām), well, mill, or wall shared between two properties be divided by the judge?
b: No. They cannot be divided except by mutual agreement of the partners because division would cause harm to both sides, as each portion would no longer provide the intended benefit.

f: 75. Why can a shared bathhouse, well, mill, or wall not be divided compulsorily?
b: Because after division neither portion would remain beneficial in the intended manner, whereas voluntary agreement is allowed because the partners have authority over their own rights.

f: 76. If several shared houses are located in the same city, how are they divided according to Abu Hanifah رحمه الله?
b: According to Abu Hanifah رحمه الله, each house is divided separately.

f: 77. If several shared houses are located in the same city, what is the view of Abu Yusuf رحمه الله and Muhammad?
b: They say that if it is more beneficial for the partners, the houses may be combined and divided together.

f: 78. Why do Abu Yusuf رحمه الله and Muhammad allow combining multiple shared houses in division?
b: Because they consider them one type in name and appearance, and they leave the assessment of benefit to the judge.

f: 79. Why does Abu Hanifah رحمه الله not allow combining multiple houses in one division?
b: Because the true consideration is their purpose and benefit, and houses differ greatly depending on location, neighborhood, proximity to mosques and water, and other factors, making equal division impossible.

f: 80. Why is one house with multiple rooms treated differently from multiple separate houses?
b: Because dividing each room separately would cause harm, so the entire house is divided as one unit.

f: 81. If shared houses are located in different cities, can they be combined in division according to Abu Yusuf رحمه الله and Muhammad?
b: No, according to one narration, because the difference between them is greater.

f: 82. What is Muhammad’s view regarding dividing houses in the same neighborhood together?
b: Muhammad allows houses in the same neighborhood or nearby areas to be divided together because the differences between them are small.

f: 83. Why are neighboring houses compared to rooms of one house, while distant houses are compared to separate houses?
b: Because closely connected houses have little difference, like rooms, whereas separated houses have greater differences.

f: 84. If partners share a house and agricultural land, or a house and shop, how are they divided?
b: Each is divided separately because they are considered different types of property.

f: 85. Is a house and a shop considered the same type of property or different types according to the narrations?
b: There are two possible narrations. One treats them as different types, while another suggests they may be considered one type based on discussions regarding leasing benefits.

f: 86. What should the person responsible for dividing property (the qāsim) do before dividing it?
b: He should map the property, measure and equalize the portions, separate each share with its own access and water rights, value buildings when needed, and prepare the shares for division.

f: 87. Why should the qāsim draw or record the property before dividing it?
b: So that he can preserve an accurate record of what is being divided.

f: 88. What does it mean that the qāsim should "adjust" the shares before division?
b: It means he should make the portions equal according to the shares entitled to each partner.

f: 89. Why should the qāsim measure the property before dividing it?
b: To know the exact size and amount of each portion.

f: 90. Why should the qāsim value buildings before dividing property?
b: Because their value may need to be considered when creating equal shares.

f: 91. Why should each divided portion have its own path and water access?
b: So that one person's share does not remain dependent on another person's share, ending disputes and completing the purpose of division.

f: 92. How are shares assigned after the portions have been prepared?
b: The portions are labelled as the first, second, third, etc., and lots are drawn. Whoever's name comes first receives the first portion, and so on.

f: 93. What is the purpose of drawing lots during division?
b: It is to satisfy the hearts of the partners and remove suspicion of favoritism or bias.

f: 94. Is drawing lots required for a valid division?
b: No. If each person is assigned a portion without lots, it is still valid because the division functions like a judicial judgment and can be enforced.

f: 95. How does the qāsim determine the number of portions for division?
b: He looks at the smallest share. For example, if the smallest share is one-third, he divides into thirds; if it is one-sixth, he divides into sixths.

f: 96. Are gold and silver coins included in a property division?
b: No, unless all partners agree.

f: 97. Why are gold and silver coins not included in compulsory division?
b: Because coins themselves are not jointly owned in the same way as other shared property, and including them may prevent fair division since one person may receive physical property while another receives only a debt owed to him.

f: 98. If land and a building are being divided together, what is the view of Abu Yusuf رحمه الله?
b: Abu Yusuf رحمه الله says the entire property should be divided according to value because equality cannot be achieved without valuation.

f: 99. According to Abu Hanifah رحمه الله, how is a property consisting of land and a building divided?
b: The land is divided by measurement because this is the original method for measurable properties. Then monetary compensation is paid by whoever receives the better portion or the building so that the shares become equal.

f: 100. Why does Abu Hanifah رحمه الله allow money to enter into a division of land and buildings?
b: Money enters only out of necessity, similar to cases where something normally impermissible becomes allowed due to necessity, such as a guardian having no authority over wealth or the specification of a dowry being allowed due to the necessity of marriage.

f: 101. According to Imam Muhammad رحمه الله, how is a property consisting of land and a building divided?
b: Muhammad says the partner who receives the building compensates the other partner with an equivalent portion of land. If equality cannot be achieved through land because the building's value exceeds the available land, money is paid for the remaining difference.

f: 102. Why does Muhammad only allow monetary compensation when necessary?
