f: 197. What is the ruling of performing ʿazl with one's wife?
b: A man may not perform ʿazl with his wife except with her permission.

f: 198. Why does a free wife have a right regarding intercourse?
b: Because intercourse fulfills her sexual needs and is connected to having children.

f: 199. Why does a slave woman not have the same right regarding intercourse?
b: Because she does not possess the right to intercourse in the same way a free wife does; therefore, her owner may decide regarding ʿazl.

f: 200. What is istibrāʾ?
b: Istibrāʾ is waiting to ensure that a slave woman's womb is empty before intercourse after acquiring ownership of her.

f: 201. What is the ruling after purchasing a slave woman before completing istibrāʾ?
b: The buyer may not have intercourse with her, touch her, kiss her, or look at her private parts with desire until istibrāʾ is completed.

f: 202. What had the Prophet ﷺ commanded regarding captives of Awtās?
b: He ﷺ said: "Do not have intercourse with pregnant women until they give birth, and do not have intercourse with non-pregnant women until they menstruate once."

f: 203. What does the narration about Awtās establish?
b: It establishes the obligation of istibrāʾ after acquiring ownership of a slave woman.

f: 204. What is the wisdom behind istibrāʾ?
b: Its purpose is to determine that the womb is free of pregnancy, protecting lineage from confusion and preventing the mixing of honorable bloodlines.

f: 205. Why is istibrāʾ required from the buyer rather than the seller?
b: Because the buyer is the one who intends intercourse, while the seller no longer has that intention after selling her.

f: 206. Why is the ruling attached to ownership and possession rather than intention?
b: Because intention is hidden, so the law attaches the ruling to the outward sign of intention: ownership combined with possession.

f: 207. What is the actual legal cause (sabab) of istibrāʾ according to the Hanafis?
b: The cause is acquiring ownership of the slave woman along with possession, because this gives the ability to have intercourse.

f: 208. Does istibrāʾ apply only to purchases?
b: No. It also applies to ownership gained through gifts, inheritance, wills, khulʿ, manumission agreements, and other methods of acquiring ownership.

f: 209. Does istibrāʾ apply if the purchased slave woman was a virgin?
b: Yes, because the reason is the possibility of pregnancy, and the ruling follows the existence of the cause rather than certainty.

f: 210. Is a menstruation that began before ownership counted for istibrāʾ?
b: No. A menstruation that began before purchase is not counted because the cause (new ownership) had not yet occurred.

f: 211. Is a menstruation after purchase but before receiving possession counted?
b: No, according to the Hanafis, because ownership and possession together establish the cause.

f: 212. Does childbirth after purchase but before possession count as istibrāʾ?
b: No, because the cause had not yet fully existed.

f: 213. Does istibrāʾ apply after buying a slave woman through an invalid sale before renewing the contract?
b: No, because ownership was not legally established until the valid purchase occurred.

f: 214. Is istibrāʾ required when someone regains a runaway slave woman?
b: No, because there is no new ownership being established.

f: 215. Is istibrāʾ required when a stolen slave woman is returned?
b: No, because there is no new ownership or possession being established.

f: 216. Is istibrāʾ required when a pledged slave woman is released from a pledge?
b: No, because ownership did not newly occur.

f: 217. Why are touching and kissing prohibited before istibrāʾ?
b: Because they may lead to intercourse and because of the possibility that pregnancy could later create confusion regarding lineage.

f: 218. Why are these restrictions different from a menstruating slave woman?
b: In menstruation there is no possibility of another man's pregnancy being confused, while in istibrāʾ such confusion is possible.

f: 219. According to Imam Muhammad رحمه الله, are the preliminary acts of affection prohibited for a captive woman?
b: Muhammad held that they are not prohibited because the possibility of attributing pregnancy to a previous owner does not exist in the same way.

f: 220. How long is istibrāʾ for a pregnant slave woman?
b: Until she gives birth.

f: 221. How long is istibrāʾ for a woman who normally menstruates?
b: Until she has one menstrual period.

f: 222. How long is istibrāʾ for a woman who no longer menstruates?
b: One month, because it takes the place of menstruation.

f: 223. What happens if a woman begins menstruating during the waiting period of istibrāʾ?
b: The previous calculation by days is cancelled, because the original method (menstruation) has become possible.

f: 224. What is the ruling if her menstruation stops after beginning istibrāʾ?
b: She is left until it becomes clear that she is not pregnant, after which intercourse becomes permissible.

f: 225. What different opinions were mentioned regarding how long to wait if menstruation stops?
b: Some said two or three months; Muhammad narrated four months and ten days; another narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله mentioned two months and five days; Zufar held two years.

f: 226. What is the ruling on using a legal stratagem (ḥīlah) to avoid istibrāʾ according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله permits using a legal stratagem to avoid istibrāʾ, while Muḥammad disagrees.

f: 227. What is the basis of the disagreement between Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding avoiding istibrāʾ?
b: The disagreement is based on whether the previous owner had intercourse with the slave woman during her purity period. Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله view is applied when it is known that the seller did not have intercourse with her during that period, while Muḥammad's view is applied when he did.

f: 228. What is the legal stratagem if the buyer has no free wife?
b: He may marry the slave woman before purchasing her, then purchase her afterward.

f: 229. What is the legal stratagem if the buyer already has a free wife?
b: The seller or buyer may marry the slave woman to a trustworthy person before the purchase or before possession, then after purchasing and taking possession, the husband divorces her.

f: 230. Why does this stratagem remove the obligation of istibrāʾ?
b: Because when the cause of istibrāʾ occurs (new ownership confirmed by possession), her private part was not lawful for the buyer due to another marriage, so istibrāʾ is not required.

f: 231. If the slave woman's private part becomes lawful afterward, does istibrāʾ become necessary?
b: No, because the ruling is based on the situation at the time the cause occurred, similar to a woman who is already observing another person's waiting period.

f: 232. What is the ruling for a man who has made ẓihār against his wife?
b: He may not have intercourse with her, touch her, kiss her, or look at her private parts with desire until he performs the required expiation (kaffārah).

f: 233. Why are touching and other forms of intimacy prohibited after ẓihār before expiation?
b: Because when intercourse is prohibited, the actions that lead to intercourse are also prohibited, since the means leading to something forbidden are themselves forbidden.

f: 234. What principle is used regarding prohibited acts and their means?
b: The principle is: "The means to a prohibited act are prohibited," as seen in iʿtikāf, iḥrām, and intercourse with a woman through mistaken assumption of marriage.

f: 235. Why are the preliminary acts of intimacy not prohibited during menstruation or fasting?
b: Because menstruation lasts for a large portion of a woman's life and fasting occurs regularly, so prohibiting these acts would cause hardship.

f: 236. What evidence shows that intimacy during menstruation or fasting is not completely prohibited?
b: It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ kissed his wives while fasting and was intimate with them while they were menstruating.

f: 237. What is the ruling if a man owns two female slaves who are sisters and he kissed both of them with desire?
b: He may not have intercourse with either one, kiss either one, touch either one with desire, or look at either one's private parts with desire until he removes ownership of one of them.

f: 238. What is the basis for prohibiting intercourse with two owned sisters?
b: The basis is Allah's statement: "And that you combine two sisters [in marriage]." (Qurʾān 4:23).

f: 239. Does the verse "or those whom your right hands possess" allow combining two slave sisters?
b: No. The prohibition takes precedence over the general permission because the specific prohibition is stronger.

f: 240. Are the acts leading to intercourse also prohibited between two slave sisters?
b: Yes. The preliminary acts of intimacy are treated like intercourse because they lead to it.

f: 241. Why does kissing both slave sisters count as if he had intercourse with both?
b: Because acts of desire leading to intercourse are treated similarly to intercourse in terms of prohibition.

f: 242. How can a man regain permission to have intercourse with one of the two slave sisters?
b: He must remove ownership of the other sister through sale, gift, marriage to another person, or freeing her.

f: 243. What does "removing ownership by possession" mean in this context?
b: It refers to transferring ownership of the slave woman through any valid means, such as sale or gifting.

f: 244. Does transferring only part of ownership of one sister remove the prohibition?
b: Yes, because even partial transfer prevents him from having intercourse with her.

f: 245. Does freeing part of one of the sisters remove the prohibition?
b: Yes, because partial emancipation has the same effect as complete emancipation in this matter.

f: 246. Does making one of them a mukātabah (contracted slave seeking freedom) remove the prohibition?
b: Yes, because intercourse becomes prohibited through the contract of emancipation.

f: 247. Do pledging, renting out, or making one of them a mudabbar remove the prohibition?
b: No. These do not remove ownership, so intercourse with the other sister remains prohibited.

f: 248. What type of marriage removes the prohibition between the two slave sisters?
b: A valid marriage.

f: 249. Does an invalid marriage remove the prohibition?
b: Not immediately. It only removes the prohibition if the husband actually consummates the marriage, because then a waiting period becomes necessary.

f: 250. If a man has intercourse with one of the two slave sisters, may he continue intercourse with that same one?
b: Yes. The prohibition applies to combining them, so intercourse with the other sister becomes forbidden.

f: 251. What is the general rule for women who cannot be combined in marriage?
b: Any two women who cannot be married together are treated like two sisters in this ruling.

f: 252. What is the ruling on a man kissing another man's mouth, hand, or embracing him?
b: It is disliked according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad.

f: 253. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding kissing and embracing another man?
b: He considered it permissible.

f: 254. What evidence did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله use for permitting embracing?
b: The report that the Prophet ﷺ embraced Jaʿfar رضي الله عنه when he returned from Abyssinia and kissed him between his eyes.

f: 255. What evidence did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad use for disliking such acts?
b: The report that the Prophet ﷺ prohibited "mukāmaʿah" (embracing) and "mukāʿamah" (kissing).

f: 256. How did scholars reconcile the reports about embracing?
b: They said the permissibility report was before the prohibition, or that the disagreement concerns embracing while wearing only one garment.

f: 257. When is embracing between men permissible according to the correct view?
b: When they are wearing a shirt or outer garment; there is no disagreement about its permissibility.

f: 258. What is the ruling on shaking hands between Muslims?
b: It is permissible and recommended because it is an established practice.

f: 259. What hadith is mentioned regarding shaking hands?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said that when two Muslim brothers shake hands and move their hands, their sins fall away.

f: 260. What is the ruling on selling manure (sarqīn)?
b: It is permissible to sell manure because it has beneficial use as fertilizer.

f: 261. Why did al-Shāfiʿī prohibit selling manure?
b: Because he considered it an intrinsically impure substance, comparing it to human waste and the skin of a dead animal before tanning.

f: 262. Why do the Hanafis allow selling manure?
b: Because it has a recognized benefit: it is placed in fields to increase agricultural production, making it considered wealth.

f: 263. What is the ruling on selling human waste (ʿadhrah)?
b: It is disliked because it has no useful purpose by itself.

f: 264. Is selling mixed manure or waste permissible?
b: Yes, according to the narration from Muḥammad, and this is considered the correct view.

f: 265. Is using mixed impure substances permissible?
b: Yes, according to the correct view, similar to oil mixed with impurity.

f: 266. If someone knows that a slave woman belongs to a certain man, then sees another person selling her and claiming "her owner authorized me to sell her," may he buy her and have intercourse with her?
b: Yes, he may do so because the seller has given a valid report that has no opposing evidence against it. A single person's statement is accepted in matters of transactions.

f: 267. What other claims from the seller are accepted regarding ownership of a slave woman?
b: If he says: "I bought her from him," "he gifted her to me," or "he gave her to me as charity," his statement is accepted because these are matters of transactions.

f: 268. Does the seller need to be trustworthy for his statement to be accepted in transactions?
b: Not necessarily. Even if he is not trustworthy, his statement is accepted if the buyer's strongest opinion is that he is truthful.

f: 269. When is it not permissible to act upon someone's statement in transactions?
b: If the buyer's strongest opinion is that the person is lying, then he may not rely on his statement.

f: 270. Why is a person's strong opinion considered in these matters?
b: Because strong presumption (ghalabat al-ẓann) is treated like certainty when making practical rulings.

f: 271. If someone does not know who owns a slave woman, but the person possessing her says she belongs to someone and he was authorized to sell her, what is the ruling?
b: If the possessor is trustworthy, his statement is accepted. If he is not trustworthy, the buyer considers his strongest opinion.

f: 272. If someone knows that a slave woman belonged to a previous owner, may he buy her from someone else without knowing that ownership transferred?
b: No, because the previous owner's possession is evidence of ownership, so he must know that ownership transferred.

f: 273. If someone does not know that the slave woman belonged to another person, may he buy her from the person possessing her?
b: Yes, because possession itself is evidence of ownership unless another opposing proof exists.

f: 274. Can the possession of a sinful person be considered evidence of ownership?
b: Yes, because the hand (possession) is evidence of ownership for both sinful and righteous people.

f: 275. When should someone avoid buying property despite possession being evidence of ownership?
b: If it appears unusual that such a person would own that property, he should preferably avoid it, although the purchase remains permissible because he relied on legal evidence.

f: 276. If a slave brings property claiming that his master allowed him to sell it, may it be purchased?
b: No, not without investigation, because a slave normally cannot own property and this creates doubt about ownership.

f: 277. If the slave says his master gave him permission and he is trustworthy, is his statement accepted?
b: Yes. If he is not trustworthy, the buyer considers his strongest opinion.

f: 278. What if the slave has no basis for a strong opinion about the truth of the statement?
b: He should not buy it because there is an existing barrier preventing reliance on the claim.

f: 279. If a woman receives reliable information that her missing husband died, may she remarry after completing waiting period?
b: Yes, because the information is from a trustworthy source and there is no opposing evidence.

f: 280. If a woman receives a letter claiming to be from her husband divorcing her, but she is unsure whether it is actually from him, may she remarry?
b: Yes, if after investigation her strongest opinion is that the letter is genuine.

f: 281. Why is a woman allowed to act upon a report of death or divorce from her absent husband?
b: Because the evidence of the change in status appeared later and there is no existing opposing evidence.

f: 282. If a woman says her husband divorced her and her waiting period ended, may another man marry her?
b: Yes, because her statement concerns a new event that occurred after the original marriage.

f: 283. If a woman who received three divorces says her waiting period ended, she married another man, consummated the marriage, was divorced, and completed her waiting period, may her first husband marry her again?
b: Yes, because the new separating events are later occurrences and there is no established contradiction.

f: 284. If a female slave says "I belonged to someone but he freed me," may she be believed?
b: Yes, because freedom is a later event and the original state can be changed by a later cause.

f: 285. If someone claims that a marriage was originally invalid because the couple were siblings through breastfeeding, is his statement accepted?
b: No. Two witnesses, or one man and two women, are required because this concerns an original defect in the marriage.

f: 286. Why is a single person's claim of an originally invalid marriage not accepted?
b: Because entering into marriage is evidence that it was valid, so there is an opposing presumption.

f: 287. If someone tells a man that his wife was his breastfeeding sister, may he marry the wife's sister or four other women?
b: No, unless two trustworthy witnesses testify, because this concerns a defect existing from the beginning of the marriage.

f: 288. If the wife was a child when the marriage occurred and later it is claimed she was breastfed by the husband's mother or sister, is one person's statement accepted?
b: Yes, because the breastfeeding relationship is a later-discovered issue and the original marriage does not prove its absence.

f: 289. What principle explains the difference between a newly occurring defect and an original defect?
b: A later event has no opposing presumption, while an original defect conflicts with the presumption created by entering into the valid action.

f: 290. If a young slave girl in someone's possession later grows up and claims she was originally free, may a man marry her?
b: No, because the current owner's claim creates a valid opposing claim.

f: 291. What is the ruling if a Muslim sells wine and uses the money to repay a debt?
b: It is disliked for the creditor to accept payment from that money.

f: 292. Why is the payment from selling wine by a Muslim not accepted?
b: Because the sale itself is invalid for a Muslim since wine is not recognized as valuable property, so the money remains the buyer's property.

f: 293. If a Christian (dhimmī) sells wine and uses the money, may a creditor accept payment from it?
b: Yes, because wine is considered valuable property in their law, making the sale valid for them.

f: 294. What is the ruling on hoarding food supplies?
b: Hoarding food for humans or animals is disliked when it harms the people of the town. If it does not cause harm, it is permissible.

f: 295. What evidence is mentioned regarding hoarding?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The one who brings goods is provided for, and the hoarder is cursed."

f: 296. Why is hoarding disliked when it harms people?
b: Because the public has a right to essential supplies, and withholding them harms people and makes matters difficult.

f: 297. When is hoarding not disliked?
b: When the town is large and withholding goods does not cause harm to the people.

f: 298. What is the ruling on meeting traders outside the marketplace to buy their goods before they arrive (talaqqī al-jalb)?
b: It follows the same ruling: it is disliked when it harms people.

f: 299. What did the Prophet ﷺ prohibit regarding traders arriving with goods?
b: He ﷺ prohibited meeting incoming traders before they reach the market (talaqqī al-rukbān).

f: 300. When is meeting incoming traders especially disliked?
b: When the buyer deceives them about the market price and takes advantage of their ignorance.

f: 301. What items did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consider subject to hoarding?
b: Essential food supplies such as wheat, barley, straw, and similar necessities.

f: 302. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله broader definition of hoarding?
b: Anything whose withholding harms the public is considered hoarding, even gold, silver, or clothing.

f: 303. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله define hoarding more broadly than Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: He considered the actual harm to society as the reason for prohibition, while Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله considered the commonly recognized forms of harm.

f: 304. What was Muḥammad's opinion regarding hoarding clothing?
b: He stated that hoarding does not apply to clothing.

f: 305. Does a short period of withholding goods count as hoarding?
b: No, because a short period normally does not create harm.

f: 306. Does a long period of withholding goods become hoarding?
b: Yes, because extended withholding usually creates harm.

f: 307. What duration was mentioned as the measure of hoarding?
b: Some scholars said forty days based on the hadith: "Whoever hoards food for forty nights has disassociated himself from Allah."

f: 308. What other duration was mentioned for hoarding?
b: Some scholars said one month, because less than that is considered a short immediate period, while a month or more is considered extended.

f: 309. Does the level of sin differ in hoarding?
b: Yes. Hoarding while waiting for higher prices is sinful, but hoarding while waiting for famine is much worse.

f: 310. What is the general conclusion about trading in food?
b: Trading in food supplies is generally not considered praiseworthy when it involves harming people.

f: 311. Is it permissible to use a legal trick (ḥīlah) to avoid the waiting period (istibrāʾ) after purchasing a slave woman?
b: According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, it is permissible, while according to Muḥammad it is not. The preferred view depends on whether the seller had intercourse with her during her purity period.

f: 312. What is the ḥīlah to avoid istibrāʾ when purchasing a slave woman?
b: If the buyer has no free wife, he may marry the slave woman before purchasing her, then purchase her. If he has a free wife, the seller or buyer may marry her to someone trustworthy before the purchase/possession, then after purchase and possession the husband divorces her.

f: 313. Why does istibrāʾ not become necessary in this case after using the legal stratagem?
b: Because at the time the cause of istibrāʾ (ownership established with possession) occurred, intercourse with her was not lawful for him. The ruling is connected to the condition at the time the cause exists.

f: 314. What are the restrictions upon someone who has made a ẓihār declaration against his wife until he performs expiation?
b: He may not have intercourse with her, touch her, kiss her, or look at her private parts with desire until he performs the expiation.

f: 315. Why are the preliminaries to intercourse prohibited after ẓihār?
b: Because when intercourse is prohibited, the means leading to it are also prohibited, since the cause leading to a forbidden act is itself forbidden.

f: 316. Why are the preliminaries not prohibited during menstruation or fasting like they are after ẓihār?
b: Because menstruation and fasting extend for long periods, and prohibiting all affection would cause hardship. The periods of ẓihār and similar cases are shorter.

f: 317. If a man owns two slave women who are sisters and kisses both of them with desire, what is the ruling?
b: He may not have intercourse with either one, nor kiss, touch with desire, or look at their private parts with desire until he removes ownership of one of them through sale, gift, marriage, or freeing her.

f: 318. Why can a man not have intercourse with two owned sisters?
b: Because combining two sisters in sexual relations is prohibited by the verse: “and that you combine between two sisters” (Qur’an 4:23).

f: 319. Why are the acts leading to intercourse also prohibited with two owned sisters?
b: Because the preliminaries to intercourse take the same ruling as intercourse itself when they lead to the forbidden act.

f: 320. If a man sells, gives away, marries off, or frees one of the two owned sisters, may he then have relations with the other?
b: Yes, because he is no longer considered to be combining them once one sister’s private part is no longer under his ownership.

f: 321. Does renting out or pledging one of the two owned sisters remove the prohibition?
b: No. Renting, pledging, or merely managing her does not remove ownership, so the other sister remains prohibited.

f: 322. If one of the two sisters is married in an invalid marriage, may he have relations with the other?
b: Not until the invalid marriage is consummated and the waiting period becomes necessary, because the waiting period has the same effect as a valid marriage regarding prohibition.

f: 323. If a man kisses two owned sisters but later one becomes owned by someone else, what happens?
b: He may then have relations with the remaining sister because he is no longer combining the two.

f: 324. What is the ruling on a man kissing another man’s mouth, hand, or embracing him?
b: It is disliked according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad. Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله considered it permissible based on reports of the Prophet ﷺ embracing Jaʿfar رضي الله عنه.

f: 325. Is embracing between men always disliked?
b: The disagreement concerns embracing while wearing only one garment. If both are wearing a shirt or outer garment, it is permissible according to the correct view.

f: 326. Is shaking hands between men permissible?
b: Yes. It is permissible because it was a known practice, and narrations mention its virtue.

f: 327. Is selling animal manure (sarqīn) permissible?
b: Yes, because it has a beneficial use, such as improving crops, making it considered wealth that can be sold.

f: 328. Why did al-Shāfiʿī consider selling animal manure impermissible?
b: Because it is impure in itself, similar to human waste and the skin of a dead animal before tanning.

f: 329. Is selling human waste permissible?
b: It is disliked because it does not have benefit except when mixed with something else. The mixed form is permissible according to the correct view.

f: 330. If someone sees a slave woman being sold and the seller says, “Her owner authorized me to sell her,” may he buy and have relations with her?
b: Yes, because statements in transactions are accepted, even from someone whose reliability is not established, due to the need for ease in dealings.

f: 331. When is a person not allowed to rely on someone’s statement in transactions?
b: If his strongest assumption is that the person is lying, he cannot rely on his statement.

f: 332. If a person does not know who owns a slave woman, but the person possessing her says she belongs to him, can he buy her?
b: Yes, if the possessor’s statement is reliable. If he is not reliable, one considers the stronger likelihood.

f: 333. If the current possessor is sinful (fāsiq), is his claim of ownership accepted?
b: Yes, because possession is an apparent sign of ownership unless there is evidence against it.

f: 334. If a slave or female slave claims that her master authorized her to sell something, is her statement accepted?
b: It is not accepted without further verification because a slave normally does not own property. If her master authorized her and she is trustworthy, it may be accepted.

f: 335. If a woman is told by a trustworthy person that her absent husband died or divorced her three times, may she remarry?
b: Yes, after completing the waiting period, because the report establishes the matter and there is no opposing evidence.

f: 336. If someone brings a divorce letter claiming it is from her husband, may she remarry?
b: If she investigates and strongly believes it is genuine, she may wait her waiting period and remarry.

f: 337. If someone claims a marriage was originally invalid due to a forbidden relationship or apostasy, is his statement accepted?
b: No. Two witnesses or one man and two women are required because the invalidity existed from the beginning and the original marriage contract indicates validity.

f: 338. Why is a later claim of invalidity treated differently from a claim that the marriage was originally invalid?
b: A later event can occur after an originally valid situation, so a single report may be accepted. But original invalidity conflicts with the apparent validity of the contract.

f: 339. If a Muslim sells wine and takes its price while owing a debt, may the creditor take repayment from that money?
b: It is disliked because the sale is invalid for a Muslim, so the price remains the buyer’s property.

f: 340. If a non-Muslim sells wine and takes its price, may a creditor take repayment from it?
b: Yes, because wine is considered valuable property in their law, so the seller owns the payment.

f: 341. What is the ruling on hoarding food supplies?
b: Hoarding food is disliked when it harms people in the area. If it does not cause harm, it is not disliked.

f: 342. Why is hoarding food disliked?
b: Because the public has a right to access necessities, and withholding them causes hardship.

f: 343. What is the ruling on intercepting traders before they reach the market (talaggī)?
b: It is disliked when it deceives traders about market prices or harms people.

f: 344. Is hoarding limited only to food according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Yes. He restricted it mainly to necessities such as wheat, barley, and similar food supplies.

f: 345. What was Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله broader definition of hoarding?
b: Anything whose withholding harms the public, even gold, silver, or clothing, can be considered hoarding.

f: 346. How long does hoarding need to continue before it becomes blameworthy?
b: Some scholars estimated forty days based on a narration, others a month. The essential factor is whether harm occurs.

f: 347. Is someone who withholds the produce of his own land considered a hoarder?
b: No, because it is purely his own right and the public does not have a claim over it.

f: 348. Is someone who stores goods brought from another region considered a hoarder?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, no, unless it is brought into the city and connected to public supply. Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad were stricter.

f: 349. Should the ruler fix prices for merchants?
b: Normally, no. Prices belong to contracting parties, and the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah is the One who sets prices.

f: 350. When may the ruler impose price controls?
b: If merchants excessively exploit people and the judge cannot protect public welfare except through pricing, then pricing may be allowed after consultation.

f: 351. What should a judge do with someone who hoards necessities?
b: He orders him to sell what exceeds his needs and warns him. If he repeats it, he may imprison and discipline him to prevent harm.

f: 352. Is selling weapons during times of civil strife permissible?
b: It is disliked if sold to someone known to participate in the conflict because it assists wrongdoing.

f: 353. Is selling weapons generally forbidden?
b: No. If the buyer is not known to use them for wrongdoing, it is permissible because harm is only suspected.

f: 354. Is selling grape juice to someone known to make wine permissible?
b: Yes according to the text, because the sin occurs after the transformation, not from the juice itself.

f: 355. Is renting a building to be used as a fire temple, church, or place selling wine permissible?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, it is permissible because the contract is for the benefit of the building itself, not the sinful act.

f: 356. What did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say regarding renting property for sinful purposes?
b: They considered it disliked because it assists in sin.

f: 357. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish between cities and rural areas regarding non-Muslim religious buildings?
b: Because Islamic symbols are dominant in cities, so allowing such practices there would conflict with public religious order.

f: 358. Is transporting wine for a non-Muslim permissible?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله considered the payment permissible, while Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad considered it disliked because it assists in sin.

f: 359. Is selling buildings in Makkah permissible?
b: Selling buildings is permissible according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله.

f: 360. Is selling land in Makkah permissible?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله disliked selling the land itself, while Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad permitted it.

f: 361. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish between buildings and land in Makkah?
b: Buildings are private property created by individuals, while the land of Makkah has a special sanctity and status.

f: 362. Is renting land in Makkah permissible?
b: It is disliked according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله based on narrations discouraging taking payment from the sacred land.

f: 363. What is the ruling on placing money with a shopkeeper and taking goods whenever needed?
b: It is disliked because it is considered a loan that brings benefit to the lender.

f: 364. How should money be deposited with a shopkeeper instead?
b: It should be treated as a trust (wadīʿah), allowing the person to take from it gradually without it becoming a beneficial loan.

f: 365. What is the ruling on adding section markings (taʿshīr) and vowel dots (naqt) in the Qur’an manuscript?
b: It was originally considered disliked because Ibn Masʿūd رضي الله عنه said: “Keep the Qur’an bare/pure.” Adding markings was seen as leaving the original simplicity of the manuscript.

f: 366. Why was adding section markings to the Qur’an considered disliked?
b: Because it could affect memorization of the verses by relying on markings rather than memory.

f: 367. Why was adding vowel dots to the Qur’an considered disliked?
b: Because it could cause people to rely on dots instead of preserving Arabic grammar and correct pronunciation naturally.

f: 368. Is adding dots and markings to Qur’an manuscripts still disliked in later times?
b: The scholars said that in their time it became necessary for non-Arabs, because leaving them out could lead to neglecting and misreading the Qur’an. Therefore, it became good and beneficial.

f: 369. Is decorating the Qur’an manuscript permissible?
b: Yes. It is permissible because it is a form of honoring and showing respect for the Qur’an.

f: 370. What evidence supports decorating the Qur’an?
b: It is compared to decorating mosques and beautifying them, including with gold-colored decoration.

f: 371. May non-Muslim citizens (dhimmīs) enter al-Masjid al-Ḥarām?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, there is no problem with them entering.

f: 372. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s view regarding non-Muslims entering al-Masjid al-Ḥarām?
b: He considered it disliked based on the verse: “Indeed, the polytheists are impure, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Ḥarām after this year” (Qur’an 9:28).

f: 373. What was Mālik’s view regarding non-Muslims entering mosques?
b: He considered it disliked for all mosques, not only al-Masjid al-Ḥarām.

f: 374. How did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله respond to the argument that non-Muslims are impure and should not enter mosques?
b: He argued that their impurity is a matter of belief, not physical impurity that contaminates the mosque.

f: 375. What evidence did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use to permit non-Muslims entering mosques?
b: The Prophet ﷺ allowed the delegation of Thaqīf, who were non-Muslims, to stay in his mosque.

f: 376. How is the verse prohibiting polytheists from approaching al-Masjid al-Ḥarām understood according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: It refers to entering it in a manner of domination and control, or to the naked circumambulation practiced by Arabs in the pre-Islamic period.

f: 377. What is the ruling on employing eunuchs?
b: It is disliked because employing them encourages the practice of castration, which is a forbidden mutilation.

f: 378. Is castrating animals permissible?
b: Yes, if there is benefit for the animal or people.

f: 379. Why is castrating animals allowed while castrating humans is prohibited?
b: Animal castration can provide benefits, while human castration is harmful mutilation.

f: 380. Is breeding donkeys with horses permissible?
b: Yes, it is permissible.

f: 381. What evidence is given for allowing donkeys to be bred with horses?
b: The Prophet ﷺ rode a mule, which shows that producing such animals is not forbidden.

f: 382. Is visiting a sick Jew or Christian permissible?
b: Yes. It is considered a form of kindness, and there is no prohibition against it.

f: 383. What evidence supports visiting sick non-Muslims?
b: The Prophet ﷺ visited a Jewish boy who was sick and lived near him.

f: 384. Is it disliked to say in supplication: “I ask You by the place of honor of Your Throne”?
b: It is disliked according to the text because it may imply that Allah’s honor is attached to the Throne, while Allah and His attributes are eternal and not dependent on creation.

f: 385. What other wording of this supplication is also considered disliked?
b: Saying: “I ask You by the seat of honor” (maqʿad al-ʿizz), because it implies sitting, which is unsuitable for Allah.

f: 386. Did any scholars permit saying “I ask You by the place of honor of Your Throne”?
b: Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله permitted it because it was reported in a supplication attributed to the Prophet ﷺ. Abū al-Layth also adopted this view.

f: 387. Why did some scholars still avoid saying this supplication despite the narration?
b: Because it was considered a solitary report, so caution was preferred.

f: 388. Is it disliked to say in supplication: “By the right of so-and-so” or “By the right of Your prophets and messengers”?
b: Yes, because creation has no obligatory right over Allah.

f: 389. What is the ruling on playing chess, backgammon (nard), and similar games?
b: It is disliked because they are considered amusement and distraction.

f: 390. Why is gambling with chess or similar games prohibited?
b: Because gambling is explicitly forbidden and is included under the category of maysir (gambling).

f: 391. If someone plays chess without gambling, what is the ruling?
b: It is still disliked because it is considered unnecessary amusement and distraction from remembrance of Allah.

f: 392. What evidence is mentioned against playing chess and similar games?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “The amusement that distracts you from the remembrance of Allah is maysir.”

f: 393. Did any scholars permit chess?
b: Some people, including a view attributed to al-Shāfiʿī, permitted it because it sharpens intelligence and thinking.

f: 394. What happens to a person’s legal uprightness (ʿadālah) if he gambles through these games?
b: His reliability as a witness is removed because he commits a major sin.

f: 395. Does merely playing without gambling remove a person’s uprightness?
b: No, because the person may be following a mistaken interpretation (taʾwīl).

f: 396. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad dislike greeting people who play such games?
b: As a warning and deterrent against their activity.

f: 397. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not dislike greeting them?
b: So that interaction might encourage them to leave their activity.

f: 398. May one accept gifts from a merchant slave?
b: Yes, according to the preferred (istiḥsān) view.

f: 399. May one accept an invitation from a merchant slave?
b: Yes, it is permissible.

f: 400. May one borrow the riding animal of a merchant slave?
b: Yes, it is permissible.

f: 401. Is clothing a merchant slave or giving him money as a gift permissible?
b: It is disliked according to the text.

f: 402. Why would the analogy (qiyās) prohibit accepting gifts from a slave?
b: Because a slave does not normally have full legal authority to make voluntary donations.

f: 403. Why did the scholars allow accepting some gifts from a merchant slave despite the analogy?
b: Because practical necessity exists. A merchant slave needs such dealings in order to function in commerce.

f: 404. Why are clothing and giving gold/silver coins excluded from this allowance?
b: Because they are not necessities of trade, so the original rule remains that the slave cannot make such donations independently.

f: 405. If someone has found a lost child (laqīṭ) with no known father, may he accept gifts and charity on behalf of the child?
b: Yes. The person caring for the found child may accept gifts and charity for him.

f: 406. What are the three categories of actions concerning minors?
b: They are: (1) actions requiring guardianship (wilāyah), (2) actions needed due to the child’s circumstances and necessities, and (3) actions that are purely beneficial for the child.

f: 407. Which actions require legal guardianship and cannot be performed except by a guardian?
b: Matters such as marriage, purchasing, and selling a child’s personal property require a guardian because the guardian acts in place of the child through legal authorization.

f: 408. Who may perform necessary transactions for a minor?
b: The person responsible for the child’s care and maintenance, such as the brother, uncle, mother, or the person who found the child, if the child is under their care.

f: 409. What examples are given of necessary transactions for a minor?
b: Buying necessities for the child, selling such items when needed, and hiring a wet nurse.

f: 410. If someone other than the legal guardian performs necessary transactions for a child, who has greater authority?
b: The legal guardian has greater authority, although the guardian does not need to have the child physically under his care.

f: 411. What type of actions are considered purely beneficial for a child?
b: Accepting gifts, charity, and receiving possessions on behalf of the child.

f: 412. Who may accept gifts and charity on behalf of a minor?
b: The person who found the child, the child’s brother, uncle, or the child himself if he has enough understanding.

f: 413. Why are children allowed to accept purely beneficial things themselves if they understand?
b: Because it benefits the child, and wisdom requires opening the door for such benefits.

f: 414. May the person who found a child hire the child out for work?
b: No, the foundling caretaker cannot rent out the child’s services.

f: 415. May the mother hire out her son’s services?
b: Yes, if the child is under her care.

f: 416. Why may the mother hire out her son but not the finder or uncle?
b: Because the mother has authority over using his benefits for his upbringing, while the finder and uncle do not have the same authority.

f: 417. May the uncle hire out the child’s services?
b: No.

f: 418. If a child hires himself out, is the contract valid?
b: No, because it contains potential harm to the child.

f: 419. When does a child’s self-hiring become permissible?
b: If the work has already been completed, because at that point it becomes purely beneficial and the agreed payment becomes due.

f: 420. What is the comparison between a minor hiring himself and an enslaved person under restriction hiring himself?
b: Both are treated similarly: the contract is not valid initially due to possible harm, but payment becomes due once the benefit has been completed.

f: 421. What is the ruling on placing an iron collar (ṭawq/raayah) around a slave’s neck?
b: It is disliked because it resembles a punishment associated with the people of Hell and resembles cruel treatment.

f: 422. Why is placing a restrictive collar on a slave disliked?
b: Because it is an excessive punishment and resembles practices of oppressors.

f: 423. Is tying a slave with restraints permissible?
b: Yes. It is not disliked because Muslims traditionally restrained criminals and dangerous people to prevent escape and protect property.

f: 424. Is using an enema (ḥuqnah) for medical treatment permissible?
b: Yes, if it is intended for medical treatment.

f: 425. Is there a difference between men and women regarding medical enemas?
b: No. The ruling applies equally to both.

f: 426. Is using unlawful substances such as alcohol for medical treatment permissible?
b: No. Seeking treatment with something prohibited remains prohibited.

f: 427. Is receiving a salary or stipend (rizq) for a judge permissible?
b: Yes. A judge may receive a stipend from public funds.

f: 428. What evidence supports giving judges a stipend?
b: The Prophet ﷺ appointed ʿAttāb ibn Asīd as governor of Makkah and gave him a stipend, and he appointed ʿAlī رضي الله عنه to Yemen and provided for him.

f: 429. Why may a judge receive payment from the public treasury?
b: Because he is occupied with serving the rights of Muslims, so his maintenance comes from their wealth (Bayt al-Māl).

f: 430. What is the difference between a judge receiving a stipend and being paid a fee for judging?
b: A stipend covering his needs is permissible, but making his payment a condition for performing judgment is forbidden because it is payment for an act of worship.

f: 431. Why is taking a salary for judging as a condition prohibited?
b: Because judging is an act of worship, and taking payment as a condition resembles hiring someone to perform worship.

f: 432. Should a poor judge accept a stipend?
b: Yes. It is considered necessary because he cannot properly fulfill his duty of judging while needing to earn a living elsewhere.

f: 433. Should a wealthy judge accept a stipend?
b: Some considered it better for him to refuse out of consideration for the public treasury, but the stronger view is that accepting it is preferable.

f: 434. Why is accepting a stipend better even for a wealthy judge according to the stronger view?
b: To preserve the dignity and independence of the judicial office and to support future judges who may need it.

f: 435. Why is the payment called “rizq” (provision) rather than a wage?
b: Because it is intended only to provide sufficient living expenses, not to pay for the act of judging itself.

f: 436. When was the judge’s stipend traditionally given?
b: Traditionally it was given at the beginning of the year because land taxes (kharāj) were collected then.

f: 437. If a judge receives a full year’s stipend and is removed from office before the year ends, must he return the remaining amount?
b: The stronger view is that he must return the remaining portion.

f: 438. May a slave woman or an umm walad travel without a maḥram?
b: Yes, according to the text.

f: 439. Why may a slave woman travel without a maḥram?
b: Because in matters of looking and touching, unrelated men are treated differently with slave women due to the circumstances of slavery.

f: 440. Why does this ruling apply to an umm walad as well?
b: Because she remains legally a slave woman due to ownership remaining, even though she cannot be sold.
